/api/teleprompter/scripts/demowelc.name: Welcome and thanks
/api/teleprompter/scripts/demowelc.text:
## Welcome [read]
Good evening, and welcome to the Blue Room.
Tonight we have three bands for you, and the first of them
has come all the way from the coast to be here.
Please give a warm welcome to the Harbour Lights!

## Thanks [read]
Thank you all for coming out tonight.
A big thank you to the sound crew, the bar staff,
and everyone who helped make this happen.
Get home safely, and we will see you next month.

/api/teleprompter/scripts/demosong.name: Songs
/api/teleprompter/scripts/demosong.text:
## Lantern Light
Down by the water where the lanterns glow
We sang the old songs soft and slow
And every light along the shore
Called us home to sing once more

recipe.text:
Shakshuka with feta

Ingredients
2 tbsp olive oil
1 onion, finely chopped
1 red bell pepper, diced
3 cloves garlic, minced
1 tsp ground cumin
1 tsp smoked paprika
2 tins (400 g) chopped tomatoes
6 eggs
100 g feta, crumbled
Salt and black pepper, to taste
A handful of fresh coriander

Preparation
1. Chop the onion and dice the pepper.
2. Mince the garlic and measure out the spices.
3. Crumble the feta and pick the coriander leaves.

Method
1. Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over a medium heat. Add the onion and pepper and fry for eight to ten minutes, stirring now and then, until soft. Then stir in a pinch of salt.
2. Stir in the garlic, cumin and paprika and cook for a minute.
3. Pour in the tomatoes and simmer for ten minutes until thick.
4. Make six wells in the sauce with the back of a spoon. Crack an egg into each well; take care not to break the yolks.
5. Cover and cook until the whites are set.
6. Scatter over the feta and coriander and serve from the pan.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.text:
The folders in this repository keep the project's earlier names (`ConcertCamera`, `ConcertCameraManager`).

The manager runs a show from up to 64 Android phones running the camera app (tested with seven): it keeps them in
step in OBS, watches every phone's health, chooses the shots with a local vision model, and keeps the recordings. A
show can be live music (the default), a church service, a podcast or talk show, a panel or conference session, or
theatre, comedy and open mic, cooking, or a Creator Studio set-up you build yourself: see [Kinds of event](docs/DIRECTOR.md#kinds-of-event). It
runs on **Linux or macOS**, and runs live on a **MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro and 48 GB** (see [On a Mac](#on-a-mac)).
See [architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md), [security](docs/SECURITY.md), [OBS commissioning](docs/OBS_SETUP.md) and
[the dashboard's layout](docs/DASHBOARD_REDESIGN.md).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
- **Readiness.** One line on the Show page says whether the show is ready, worked out from this computer (OBS, memory,
  processor, recording disk, camera network, relay, model, and face blur or Creator Studio's consent where they are in
  use) and from every phone (connection, clock, power, battery protection, temperature, phone sounds, Wi-Fi, stream
  target, picture in OBS, frame rate, camera picture, cooler, app version, colour). Each item says what to do; the clock warning has a **Fix** button that takes the camera off air, stops its stream, sets its clock and
  starts it again.
- **Network cameras over NDI.** A camera that is not a phone, such as a PTZ camera on the network, is added by a
  name, a slot and the NDI source it sends (System › Add a network camera, which lists the NDI sources found).
  "Refresh OBS scenes" makes its NDI source and scenes, the readiness checks say whether OBS shows its picture, and
  the director chooses it like any other. In a split screen it fills its half as a phone does: full height, the
  middle of its picture in the middle. It draws no timing strip, so the manager times it by its picture: it watches the
  camera's picture beside the phones', and when the same things are seen to happen in both it sets the camera's delay
  by itself, again and again through the show, and moves it with the phones' common delay in between. Its sound
  (the levels OBS reports) is a second check on that, and stands in when the pictures are still. To time it at once,
  hold the calibrate page up where it and a phone camera both see it (Set up › Calibrate, **Time the network
  cameras**): the page flashes, and the manager sets the delay from the flashes both saw. The manager can also turn and track a network PTZ camera like a gimbal
  that is following: it chooses who to follow and aims the camera, and the camera's own tracker holds the shot. That
  tracker picks its own subject within the area it is aimed at and cannot be handed a named performer. With a phone
  mounted right beside it, showing the whole stage, the camera is aimed from that phone's picture (chosen and lined
  up with Set on its card), with no guess at how far back anyone stands and no room map needed. Its control
  address is set on its card and nothing is sent by itself until Following is armed. With that address it is also
  on the Operate page like a gimbal camera: its picture as OBS has it, aimed and zoomed with the controller or the
  on-screen buttons, its home set and its tracker switched on or off there, its presets as its Positions. It needs the NDI runtime and the DistroAV plugin in OBS; see
  [Network cameras](docs/NETWORK.md#network-cameras-over-ndi).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
- **Feed alignment.** Every phone draws a timing strip on its picture; the manager reads it in OBS and holds each feed so
  all of them line up, behind a look-ahead (5.5 s here) that gives the director time to see a moment before it airs.
- **The director.** A vision model rates every camera from the phones' own pictures, ahead of what OBS shows, and cuts
  to the best (see [The director](docs/DIRECTOR.md)). It can zoom in on a performer and **follow a walker**, leading them and never zooming in on nobody
  (empty or unreadable answers, boxes no person could fill and scenery it keeps mistaking for one are all refused); use
  a camera's **telephoto lens** for tight shots, changed only off air; **cut to the camera the performer is looking at**
  (Apple Vision on a Mac, off unless ticked), and let **a new look into a camera end the hold on a called-out shot**, so a
  host brings the camera back to them with no call (once the called shot has run 4 s,
  `director_gaze_release_after_seconds`, so a glance at what was called and straight back does not undo it), **go back to
  the shot before** when a short look ends, and keep **a host's pace** (quicker cuts to and from a camera given a host's
  role); listen for the instrument to the fore; switch to **whoever is talking**
  from each person's microphone on a mixer (podcasts, panels, services); and show the crowd camera when the
  crowd is lively. Without a model it rotates through the cameras, or leaves the choice to a person (Stage Shots).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
- **Scene Chat.** A chat down the right of the Show and Stage Shots pages for guiding the director through the show:
  a standing brief, and wishes typed as it goes ("more on the keyboards", "less on the drums") that go on top of it,
  newest first. The director answers at once with a canned reply, never by asking the model; a wish sent earlier
  can be sent again with *Again* under it. See
  [Scene Chat](docs/DIRECTOR.md#scene-chat-guiding-the-director-during-the-show).
- **Search and the assistant.** **Search** at the top of the side bar (or `/`, or Ctrl or ⌘ with K) finds a button, a
  setting or a section by what it is for, opens its page and marks it there; it searches this guide too, to read in
  place. A question is answered in words from the guide by the model on this computer (Standard or Plus AI). See
  [Search and the assistant](docs/AI_ASSISTANCE.md#search-and-the-assistant).
- **Sound and voice calls.** The Sound page (Set up) has two sections, listed under it in the side bar (tabs on a
  narrow screen): *Voice shot calls* and *Programme sound*. *Programme sound*: which camera's microphone leads, the
  others staying out, joining while lined up, or an automixer that follows the speaker; **Lip sync** (±1500 ms); and
  **Calibrate sync**, which measures each camera's sound against its picture from a flashing, beeping page on a phone
  or tablet, through OBS's own recording. And *Voice shot calls*: "cut to the stove", zoom calls and, in Cooking, the
  recipe's steps, heard on this computer (and, for camera calls, confirmed by it when only a phone heard them). See
  [Kinds of event](docs/DIRECTOR.md#kinds-of-event).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
- **AI assistance at the level you choose.** No AI (the default: nothing downloaded or run), Standard (the vision model,
  zoom, listening, gaze) or Plus (Standard and the performer library), each set up step by step from the dashboard. See
  [AI assistance](docs/AI_ASSISTANCE.md#ai-assistance-no-ai-standard-or-plus).
- **The performer library (Plus AI).** Consenting performers are enrolled on the day from a camera's picture; stars get
  priority on any camera and a camera can follow a named performer, framed ten times a second by a fast person detector.
  Nobody else is identified, and everything is encrypted and deleted after the show day by default. See
  [The performer library](docs/PEOPLE_LIBRARY.md#the-performer-library-plus-ai).
- **Colour matching.** White balance (kelvin, preset or lock) and exposure (lock or manual) set on every phone at once,
  and a per-camera LUT in OBS, made from a colour chart or by matching the cameras on the scene in front of them. See
  [Making the cameras' colours match](docs/COLOUR_AND_CALIBRATION.md#making-the-cameras-colours-match).
- **Stage Shots.** Shots called by hand from buttons laid out like the stage: rows from the back of the stage to the
  front, each button as wide as its shot, a mark for where its camera stands, and Room view with the buttons standing
  on the room map's stage. See [Stage Shots](docs/STAGE.md#stage-shots).
- **Stage layout.** One page, under Set up, for where the cameras and performers stand: (experimental) the buttons
  placed from the wide camera's picture, on the performers, with suggestions of who is who, as a first guess to check;
  a room map from above with what each camera sees (expanded over the whole window beside the camera's own picture,
  each camera's place, height, aim, tilt and field of view worked out from the stage's corners marked on its picture);
  the buttons arranged by hand. Each kind of event can have **a set
  of its own** under the room map (a kitchen's counter, stove and prep table; a podcast table and its microphones):
  **a map made from a photo or two of the set** (measured with a phone's AR, or with a reference of known size), a
  floor plan (picture or PDF), or a template's shapes, to scale. See
  [Stage layout](docs/STAGE.md#stage-layout).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
- **Face blur (experimental), on the phones.** A camera can blur every face **on its own phone**, before anything is
  recorded or sent (YuNet on the phone since app 0.9.30: turned and small faces too), so no unblurred copy of it exists
  anywhere; with **this computer as its backup** (app 0.9.33), the manager also looks at that camera ahead of OBS and
  blurs any face the phone left showing, told apart by the phone's own report of where it blurred each frame. On the
  computer alone it blurs live in OBS: every face, everyone but consenting performers, or only chosen people, with a
  fail-safe. Hidden and off unless an administrator switches it on. See [Face blur](docs/FACE_BLUR.md#face-blur-experimental).
- **Gimbals that aim and follow (experimental).** A phone on a Hohem iSteady X3 or MT3 is aimed from its camera card
  (hold an arrow, let go and it eases to a stop), and **Follow** has the phone keep the most prominent face in frame
  itself, keeping a person who turns away by their body, or (Plus AI) a named, consenting performer the manager
  recognises; at a Calm, Normal or Quick pace (app 0.9.35), or *By zoom*, Quick at 1x easing to Normal by 3x (app
  0.9.44). **Losing someone** (app 0.9.45; 0.9.46 ends the search where it lost them) it searches for about 15 s,
  swinging out and back each way and zoomed out to 1x, takes them back by their body, then zooms back in; each loss
  and finding is in the audit log and the recording's log (`gimbal_lost`, `gimbal_found`, with what the phone says of
  it); a search that gives up (the phone says *lost* for 20 s, `director_gimbal_home_after_seconds`) has the gimbal
  turned back to its home position, still following, once for each loss (not for a camera aimed from the stage); app
  0.9.48 turns faster after someone close walking by, and 0.9.53 the nearer they are or the faster they approach; app
  0.9.55 zooms to keep the one followed about waist up, in as they walk away and out as they come nearer
  (`gimbal.follow` `keep`); the card says *looking for someone* meanwhile. **Aimed from the stage** (app 0.9.37): a
  gimbal that loses
  its person is turned to where the wide shot sees them, and one given a performer to where the wide shot recognises
  them, from the room map, after one Set at centre stage. **A follow plan** (Plus AI) per gimbal camera: its performers
  in order, a **solo taking over** (whoever plays the instrument the sound hears soloing, or where that instrument stands),
  optionally **prominent players** too, and **anyone** when none of them is in view, so a guest walking on from the other
  side is followed; with holds so it doesn't flit. A **home position** to set and return to. Both are on the card and the
  Operate page alike. **Saved targets** on the card, for each kind of event: "show the pot" turns it there and zooms,
  "back to me" puts it back (*Saved gimbal targets*: [Gimbals](docs/GIMBALS.md#saved-gimbal-targets)). An MT3's own AI tracker is shown on the card. It works hung
  upside down, and coolers and gimbals are paired, moved between cameras and re-paired from the dashboard. See the
  gimbal under [Keeping the cameras going](docs/KEEPING_CAMERAS_GOING.md#keeping-the-cameras-going).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
- **Tracking and zoom, switched off live.** During a performance an operator can switch the automatic tracking and
  the automatic zoom off and on again, apart, for one camera (on its card) or every camera at once (the Show page and
  Stage Shots, and the Operate page: its bar and each tile), at once and with nothing restarted. Tracking off, a gimbal stops where it points; zoom off, the
  director's crop in OBS holds where it is (or as you frame it by hand in OBS), and **Whole picture** puts a zoom gone
  wrong back to the whole picture. On again, each takes up from where things are; Tracking on for one gimbal camera
  by itself starts it following if it was not.
  Also said aloud: "stop tracking", "tracking on", "auto zoom off", "auto zoom on". See
  [Tracking and zoom switches](docs/DIRECTOR.md#tracking-and-zoom-switches).
- **Keeping the cameras up.** A camera whose picture stops while its sound goes on is revived by the phone itself; an
  OBS source that plays with no picture is restarted and then rebuilt; a phone that loses the camera Wi-Fi rejoins it by
  itself while armed; a charging phone holds its battery short of full; an armed phone plays no sound or vibration; a
  Black Shark MagCooler 5 Pro clamped to a phone is kept with its lights off and its fan as chosen, with its
  temperature on the dashboard; the USB charger hubs for the coolers and gimbals can be on Tapo smart plugs switched from the
  dashboard's Power page, which says which gimbals and coolers each one charges. See [Keeping the cameras going](docs/KEEPING_CAMERAS_GOING.md#keeping-the-cameras-going).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
- **Recordings.** The programme is recorded on this computer. Each camera's own stream can be kept as it arrives (camera
  files, from the camera relay) and comes with the cuts as an edit (EDL) and each camera's LUT. The phones' own
  recordings are copied over the network, verified and filed by camera. OBS shows the cameras a few seconds behind real
  life (the sync keeper's hold), so **Record** and **Stop** wait that long before OBS starts and stops: the file begins
  and ends with what was happening as they were pressed (`record_follow_programme`, at most `record_max_lag_seconds`
  10), and a recipe step marked while recording is placed where the file shows it.
- **The camera relay, on by default.** Every camera passes through a small relay on this computer that holds the look-ahead
  as compressed video, so OBS does not hold it as pictures: six 4K cameras took OBS from 11.0 GB to 2.6 GB. See
  [The camera relay](docs/RECORDINGS_AND_RELAY.md#the-camera-relay-the-look-ahead-and-each-cameras-own-file).
- **Setting phones up.** By USB from the dashboard, or with no cable: a factory-reset phone scans a set-up code and
  fetches the signed app from the public repository. App updates are released from CI and rolled out one unarmed camera
  at a time.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What the PC needs
sections.text:
The manager, OBS, the camera relay and (if used) the shot-choosing model all run on one computer, and that computer is
where a show is won or lost. What follows is what it takes, with the figures measured on the two it has run on: the
Linux workstation it was built on (Lenovo Legion: Intel i9-14900HX, 32 GB, NVIDIA RTX 4090 Laptop GPU with 16 GB,
Linux Mint, OBS 32.2 as a Flatpak), and the MacBook Pro that runs it now (M5 Pro, 48 GB; see
[On a Mac](#on-a-mac), and [Performance](docs/PERFORMANCE.md#measured-on-the-mac) for its figures). They are a guide, not a guarantee: check on the computer that will run the
show, with every camera streaming at its intended size for the length of a show. The dashboard's readiness checks (Show
page) report the decoder, memory and disk as they are.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What the PC needs
sections.text:
| | Needs | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **System** | Linux with a systemd user session, or macOS (see [On a Mac](#on-a-mac)); Python 3.12 or later with pip | Built on Linux Mint (Ubuntu 24.04 base); runs live on macOS 26.6. The tests run on macOS here before every pull request, and on Ubuntu 24.04 once merged. |
| **OBS Studio** | With its WebSocket server on; tested with 32.2 (Flatpak on Linux) and OBS for macOS | Run on the same PC; the manager reads its WebSocket password from OBS's own settings. |
| **Graphics** | On Linux, NVIDIA, for decoding every camera (NVDEC) and encoding the programme (NVENC). On a Mac, Apple silicon's own (VideoToolbox, Metal) | The decoder is usually the first limit. On the RTX 4090 Laptop each camera costs about 20% of the decoder at 4K, 9% at 1440p and 5% at 1080p (30 fps): three 4K and three 1440p cameras ran it at 85%, and with six 4K cameras OBS quietly stopped showing some of them. The "Video decoding" check warns at 85%, and the Cameras page estimates the load before a stream size is changed. |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What the PC needs
sections.text:
| | Needs | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Memory** | 32 GB on Linux with the camera relay on (the default). On a Mac, where the model's weights share the memory, **48 GB for five or six 4K cameras with the model**; 32 GB only for fewer or smaller cameras (16 GB may do for a few at 1080p, untested) | OBS holds each camera's look-ahead as pictures unless the camera relay holds it: about 1.5-1.8 GB per 4K camera and 0.65 GB per 1440p camera at a 4-5.5 s look-ahead, against about 0.2 GB per 4K camera with the relay on. Six 4K cameras on the M5 Pro (25 Mb/s, 5.5 s): OBS 11.0 GB with the relay off, 2.6 GB with it on plus 0.13 GB for the relay; the whole Mac 38.8 GB against 30.7 GB. On Linux, with no relay, OBS reached 18.9 GB and the system stopped it. |
| **Processor** | A recent multi-core processor | Decodes the cameras (see [Decoding](docs/PERFORMANCE.md#decoding-on-the-graphics-card-or-the-processor)): six 4K cameras took about 16% of the i9-14900HX in OBS. On the M5 Pro, VideoToolbox decoded six 4K cameras for 27% of one core. |
| **Disk** | Fast local disk with room for the show, and more | The programme recording: about 6 GB an hour. Each camera's own file, only with camera files on (off by default): about 3 GB an hour per camera at 1080p (7 Mb/s), 5 GB at 1440p (12 Mb/s) and 11 GB at 4K (25 Mb/s), up to twice that while the files are made. Six 4K cameras for two hours: about 140 GB, 280 GB at the peak. The relay alone, holding the look-ahead, keeps about a minute of each camera. |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What the PC needs
sections.text:
| | Needs | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Camera network** | A wired gigabit Ethernet adapter on the cameras' network, with a fixed address, or the manager set to follow that adapter's address (System › Network, "Follow the address of") | The streams add up: six cameras at 4K are about 150 Mb/s. Wired phones (USB-C Ethernet adapters) are steadier than Wi-Fi at that rate; the readiness checks can warn of a phone on Wi-Fi when wired was meant. |
| **NDI cameras** (optional) | The NDI runtime and the [DistroAV](https://github.com/DistroAV/DistroAV) plugin installed in OBS, then OBS restarted | Only for a [network camera](docs/NETWORK.md#network-cameras-over-ndi). Checked with OBS 33.0.1 and DistroAV 6.2.2 on the Mac. Without them the manager runs as before, and a network camera says it is not ready and why. The manager itself uses no NDI library. |
| **Internet** | A separate connection (Wi-Fi, say) for streaming out and updates | Kept apart from the camera network, which needs no internet. |
| **Shot-choosing model** (optional) | A vision model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, here llama.cpp with Qwen3-VL 8B (Q4_K_M, with its Q8_0 picture encoder): in Docker on Linux, natively on Metal on a Mac | Linux: about 7 GB of the graphics card's memory and 1.3 GB of system memory; it answered in about a second. Mac: about 2.4 GB of its own plus 5.7 GB of weights held by the graphics, out of the same memory; 0.56 s an answer idle, about 2.2 s a six-camera look under a full show. It shares the graphics with OBS, so leave room for both. |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: What the PC needs
sections.text:
| | Needs | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tools** | ffmpeg and ffprobe, libsrt, avahi-utils, gh, pactl (Linux); Homebrew's python@3.13, ffmpeg, srt, gh and android-platform-tools (Mac) | For particular features; see Installing on a PC and On a Mac. |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Camera and network hardware
sections.text:
What the cameras and their network were tested with, and what is recommended. As with the PC, check a set-up for the
length of a show before relying on it.

**Camera network router**

- **ASUS RT-ACRH13** (tested). It hands out the cameras' addresses; the cameras' network needs no internet.

**PoE switch** (optional: one cable for each phone's data and power; phones can use Wi-Fi instead)

- **TP-Link TL-SG1008MP** (tested): ran three cameras at 4K and three at 1440p.
- **TP-Link SG2210XMP-M2** or **SG3218XP-M2** (untested): 2.5 Gb/s ports, which may allow more 4K cameras.

Six cameras at 4K come to about 150 Mb/s, well within a gigabit link, and in the tested set-up the PC's video
decoder was already about 85% busy (see What the PC needs), so the PC may well be the limit before the switch is.

**Ethernet to USB-C adapter** (for a phone on the PoE switch)

- **Procet Gigabit PoE to USB-C converter**, 10 W charging and data (tested). Other PoE to USB-C adapters may work,
  provided they deliver both power and data. Watch each phone's battery on the dashboard: a phone streaming 4K for
  hours draws a good deal, and must charge faster than it uses.

**Phones** (for 4K streaming)

- **Samsung Galaxy S20 FE** (tested). Takes an SD card, which could allow longer local recording; recording to the SD
  card is untested.
- **Samsung Galaxy S23** (tested), including its 3x telephoto lens.
- **Google Pixel 8 or later** (tested): the app can use its other lenses, including the 2x zoom lens.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Camera and network hardware
sections.text:
The app's choice of lens works on the Pixels and on the Galaxy S23, whose 3x telephoto the app can open; the S20 FE
does not let other apps use its zoom lens. Other Samsung models, the S23 Ultra's 10x lens among them, are untried. Older phones also work at lower sizes: a Pixel 3 and a Pixel 4a streamed at 1440p in testing.

**Phone cooler** (optional)

- **Black Shark MagCooler 5 Pro** (tested on a Galaxy S23 and an S20 FE), clamped to the phone and controlled by the
  camera app over Bluetooth. With it, an S23 streamed and recorded 4K together for 2¼ hours at 22–25 °C. Power it from
  its own USB charger. See the cooler under [Keeping the cameras going](docs/KEEPING_CAMERAS_GOING.md#keeping-the-cameras-going).

**Smart plug** (optional)

- **TP-Link Tapo P125M**, or another Tapo plug the tapo package handles, with a USB charger hub for the coolers and gimbals
  plugged into it, switched from the dashboard over the local network. Up to 8, one for each charger. See the plug under
  [Keeping the cameras going](docs/KEEPING_CAMERAS_GOING.md#keeping-the-cameras-going).

**Gimbal** (optional; app 0.9.19, the MT3 app 0.9.21)

- **Hohem iSteady X3 or MT3** (each tried on a Pixel 8), holding the phone and aimed from its camera card through the camera app,
  over Bluetooth, the right way up or hung upside down. See the gimbal under
  [Keeping the cameras going](docs/KEEPING_CAMERAS_GOING.md#keeping-the-cameras-going).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Installing on a PC
sections.text:
A PC needs Linux with Python 3.12 or later and pip, a systemd user session, and OBS Studio with its WebSocket
server switched on. Some features need more, which `bootstrap.sh` checks for and names without stopping:

| Needs | For | On Debian, Ubuntu and Mint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ffmpeg and ffprobe | checking recordings; each camera's own file | `sudo apt install ffmpeg` |
| the SRT library (libsrt) | the camera relay | comes with ffmpeg (`libsrt1.5-gnutls`) |
| avahi-publish | the phones finding the manager by a `.local` name | `sudo apt install avahi-utils` |
| gh, signed in | bringing a new camera app from GitHub | `sudo apt install gh`, then `gh auth login` |
| pactl | listening for instruments | PipeWire's or PulseAudio's tools, usually there |

Then, from a release download unpacked anywhere, or a clone at a release tag:

```
ConcertCameraManager/scripts/bootstrap.sh --agent-host <this computer's address on the camera network>
```

That checks the PC, installs the release, gives the PC its own certificate, database and first administrator's
password (shown once: keep it; log in with it and no name, and the dashboard asks for your name), registers and starts the service, and prints what is left to do by hand: the firewall
rule, pairing the phones, and the scenes in OBS. Run without `--agent-host` it lists the PC's addresses to
choose from. Nothing secret is ever copied between PCs: each makes its own.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Installing on a PC
sections.text:
- `bootstrap.sh --version v0.9.1`, from a clone, moves an installed PC to another version. Its identity, cameras
  and settings are kept. The same command with an earlier tag goes back.
- `~/.local/bin/mcvsaid` runs the installed manager's commands against this computer's data, for example
  `mcvsaid pair --slot 1 --name Stage-left`, `mcvsaid password`, `mcvsaid --version`.
- Where packages cannot be downloaded, set `PIP_NO_INDEX=1 PIP_FIND_LINKS=<folder of wheels>` first.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: On a Mac
sections.text:
The manager runs on macOS from the same code as on Linux, with OBS for macOS beside it, and that is how it runs live
now: on a **MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro (18 cores) and 48 GB of unified memory**, macOS 26.6, with OBS decoding every
camera in hardware (VideoToolbox) and the shot-choosing model (llama.cpp, Qwen3-VL 8B) running natively on the Mac's
graphics through Metal, up to seven phones. Everything on the dashboard works the same way, and the installation keeps
the same folders (`~/.local/share/mcvsaid`, `~/.config/mcvsaid`). Three launchd agents in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` run
it, each started again by itself if it stops:

| Agent | Runs | Made by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `com.mcvsaid.manager` | the manager and its dashboard | `bootstrap.sh`, from the same unit file as on Linux |
| `com.mcvsaid.relay` | the camera relay | the manager, the first time the relay is wanted (it is on from the start), or switching it on (System › This computer) |
| `com.mcvsaid.model` | `llama-server`, the shot-choosing model | the AI set-up's button (Director page or System › This computer), or by hand ([AI assistance](docs/AI_ASSISTANCE.md#running-the-model-by-hand-on-a-mac)) |

Logs are in `~/Library/Logs/mcvsaid`. What differs from Linux is all in `camera_manager/host.py`:

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: On a Mac
sections.text:
| | Linux | macOS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The services | systemd user units | launchd agents, made from the same unit files |
| A `.local` name | avahi-publish | `dns-sd`, which comes with macOS |
| Hardware decoding in OBS | NVDEC | VideoToolbox |
| How busy the video decoder is | nvidia-smi | not reported by macOS, so the Video decoding check stands aside and **Measure this computer** measures the processor only |
| Listening for instruments | a tap made with pactl | a loopback sound device, BlackHole by default, set as OBS's monitoring device (OBS › Settings › Audio › Monitoring Device); another device can be named in `audio_cues_device` |
| Soundcheck by sound | PipeWire | not available on a Mac (it says so) |
| Cutting to where the performer looks | not available | Apple's Vision framework (`requirements-gaze.txt`, installed by `install-release.sh` on a Mac) |
| The shot-choosing model | llama.cpp in Docker, on the NVIDIA card | llama.cpp from Homebrew, run natively on Metal; Docker on a Mac cannot reach the graphics |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Installing on a Mac
sections.text:
With [Homebrew](https://brew.sh):

| Needs | For | Install |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python 3.12 or later | the manager (macOS's own `python3` is 3.9) | `brew install python@3.13` |
| ffmpeg and ffprobe | checking recordings, each camera's own file, Measure this computer | `brew install ffmpeg` |
| the SRT library | the camera relay | `brew install srt` |
| gh, signed in | bringing a new camera app from GitHub | `brew install gh`, then `gh auth login` |
| adb | setting phones up by USB | `brew install android-platform-tools` |
| OBS | the programme | `brew install --cask obs` |
| BlackHole (optional) | listening for instruments | `brew install --cask blackhole-2ch` |
| llama.cpp (optional) | the shot-choosing model | `brew install llama.cpp` |

```
brew install python@3.13 ffmpeg srt gh android-platform-tools llama.cpp
brew install --cask obs                     # and, for listening for instruments: brew install --cask blackhole-2ch
ConcertCameraManager/scripts/bootstrap.sh --agent-host <this computer's address on the camera network>
```

`bootstrap.sh` finds Python 3.12 or later by itself (`MCVSAID_PYTHON` names one), installs and starts
`com.mcvsaid.manager`, and `scripts/manager.sh restart|status|logs|stop|start` works as on Linux. If the macOS
firewall is on, allow incoming connections for the manager's Python and for OBS; macOS also asks once whether they may
use the local network.

The shot-choosing model is installed by the AI set-up's button (Director page); to install it by hand, see
[AI assistance](docs/AI_ASSISTANCE.md#running-the-model-by-hand-on-a-mac).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Installing on a Mac
sections.text:
What a Mac cannot do: report how busy its video decoder is (the Video decoding check stands aside), soundcheck by
sound (that needs PipeWire, on Linux), or listen for instruments without a loopback device such as BlackHole.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: First run
sections.text:
What is left once `bootstrap.sh` has run, in order, and where each is described:

1. **Log in** with the first administrator's password it showed, and no name; the dashboard asks for yours. More
   accounts: [Who can log in](docs/SECURITY.md#who-can-log-in).
2. **The firewall rule** it printed (on a Mac, the firewall note under [Installing on a Mac](#installing-on-a-mac)).
3. **Pair the phones**: System › Cameras › *Add a phone*, by USB or with a set-up code (see *Setting phones up* under
   [What it does](#what-it-does)).
4. **The scenes in OBS**: **Refresh OBS scenes** on the Director page (see
   [OBS sources](docs/NETWORK.md#camera-capacity-device-storage-and-obs-urls) and [OBS commissioning](docs/OBS_SETUP.md)).
5. **The kind of event**, under the MCVSAID name at the top of the side bar ([Kinds of event](docs/DIRECTOR.md#kinds-of-event)),
   and **the AI level**, asked the first time the Director page is opened ([AI assistance](docs/AI_ASSISTANCE.md)).
6. **Where the cameras stand** (Set up › Stage layout: [Stage layout](docs/STAGE.md#stage-layout)) and **their colour**
   (Set up › Colour: [Colour and calibration](docs/COLOUR_AND_CALIBRATION.md)).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: The dashboard
sections.text:
A side bar groups the pages by when they are needed. Over 1100 px it shows in full; a tablet gets an icon strip that
opens out, and a phone gets Show, Cameras, Stage Shots and Director along the bottom with More for the rest. The show's
state (the kind of event, readiness, on air, REC, LIVE, performer recognition) stays in view in a strip along the top of
every page, at every width, and the kind of event being directed (live
music, worship, podcast, panel, theatre, cooking, Creator Studio) is chosen by the administrator just under the name at the bar's top.

**Search finds where things are.** *Search*, under the kind of event at the top of the side bar on every page (`/`, or
Ctrl or ⌘ with K), takes what you are looking for in your own words ("record the programme", "pair a gimbal", "shot
length"). *Go to* lists the places on the dashboard that match: choosing one opens its page, scrolls to the button,
setting or section and outlines it for a few seconds, opening the fold it is in. *In the guide* lists the parts of this
README and the documents that match, to read without leaving the page. And a question ("How do I add a phone?") can be
put to the assistant, which answers from those; see
[Search and the assistant](docs/AI_ASSISTANCE.md#search-and-the-assistant).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: The dashboard
sections.text:
**The Show page is a programme monitor.** It opens on the programme's picture (what OBS is showing: the scene in its
programme, with its crop) and, beside it, a small picture of each camera, the one on air outlined and labelled (red
while OBS records or streams it, blue when nothing goes out). **Pressing a camera's picture puts it on air**, as a
person's choice, held as any other. The pictures are stills from OBS, one request a second in turn (the programme every
other second, a camera's thumbnail in between, so with six cameras each thumbnail is about 12 s old at most), and only
while the Show page is in front: far lighter than the Operate page's live pictures. A camera with no picture in OBS is
not asked for one and cannot be pressed. `GET /api/programme/picture?width=` (160 to 1920, 960 if not said) is the
programme's; the thumbnails are `GET /api/stage/set/grab/{camera id}?width=320`. Under *All cameras* the start buttons
come first and larger; the three stops (**Disarm all cameras**, **Stop all recordings**, **Stop all streams**) are in a
red-edged box of their own further down, below the line that counts the cameras, and each still asks before it acts.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: The dashboard
sections.text:
If the manager stops answering, the pages say so rather than keep showing the last picture as if it were true: after two
missed answers a red banner ("No answer from the manager for N s; what is shown may be out of date") appears along the
top and the show's state (ready, on air, REC, LIVE) is greyed; both go the moment it answers again. A page left in a
background tab or a tablet put to sleep stops asking until it is looked at. An error stays in the bar at the foot until
it is put away with ×, and a raw answer from the manager is shown as a line with the whole of it behind *details*.
The camera on air is lit in the *Put on air* and split-screen rows, not dimmed.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: The dashboard
sections.text:
| Group | Page | What is on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Show | **Show** | Readiness, the programme (on air, splits, automatic choosing, recording and streaming), start and stop every camera, the heat outlook for the show; Scene Chat down the right |
| | **Recipe** | Cooking only: the recipe, its preparation and steps (the one being cooked, when each began, how long it ran, its key shots), Next, Back, Undo, done and skipped, editing the steps, Prep for the show (concise steps, the room checked, the calls rehearsed), what goes on screen, and spoken cues with what was heard |
| | **Cameras** | A summary card per camera, six to a screen: a small picture of what it sees (OBS's still of it), its name, a chip per fact (*Armed*, *Streaming*, *Recording*, *Offline*), temperature and where it is heading, battery, free storage with the recording time left, and the next step for its state (*Arm*, *Start SRT* or *Start local MP4*, with the stop that undoes the last apart from it and asking first). *Ready* alone when every check passes; the things to look at, and any warning, on the summary itself when not. Everything else opens from the card under *Controls and settings*: all six capture buttons (the stops apart from the starts), its automatic tracking and zoom, the temperature in full, the cooler, gimbal and lens lines, and the *What it shows*, *Picture & stream*, *Cooler* and *Gimbal* (a phone with one) and *Maintenance* folds. Below the cards: band profiles; each charger plug's state and switch, once one is set up. Also the cameras *Not in use here*, and Creator Studio's panel in that kind of event |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: The dashboard
sections.text:
| Group | Page | What is on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| | **Operate** | Chosen cameras live (no look-ahead, all over one connection, so it keeps up on a tablet), steered with Xbox controllers or on-screen buttons: aim a gimbal or a network PTZ camera, zoom, put a camera on air, back to the stage shot or the previous shot; **Arm all cameras** and **Start all camera streams** for every camera in use; Aim and Zoom sensitivity; each gimbal camera's **Positions** (its saved targets) set up with the live picture; also at `https://operate.mcvsaid.local` (administrator or operator, and a setup tech for positions only; see [Operate](docs/OPERATE_AND_REMOTE.md#operate-live-cameras-and-xbox-controllers)) |
| | **Remote** | A remote control for a phone or tablet: programmable keys, all on one page, each one press, with an icon for what it does: a camera on air, a gimbal camera to a saved target's angle and zoom (and then on air), back or home, automatic choosing; one step or several in turn; lit while it is so; also at `https://remote.mcvsaid.local` (administrator or operator; see [Remote keys](docs/OPERATE_AND_REMOTE.md#remote-keys-programmable-buttons-on-a-phone-or-tablet)) |
| | **Teleprompter** | Scripts for whoever speaks to camera, written here with a heading for each section; what is on the teleprompter and its controls; the tablet's PIN (administrator); full screen; also at `https://teleprompter.mcvsaid.local` (see [Teleprompter](docs/TELEPROMPTER_AND_KARAOKE.md)) |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: The dashboard
sections.text:
| Group | Page | What is on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| | **Karaoke** | Karaoke night only: the line of singers (approve, reorder, skip, remove, add by hand), **Next singer**, the QR code and the night's code guests sign up by, *New night* (see [Karaoke night](docs/TELEPROMPTER_AND_KARAOKE.md#karaoke-night-a-line-of-singers-the-words-lit-as-they-are-sung)) |
| | **Stage Shots** | The cameras laid out like the stage, read from the back of it to the audience: press one to put it on air, or two for a split; Automatic, Tracking, Auto zoom, Whole picture and Room view (see [Stage Shots](docs/STAGE.md#stage-shots)); Scene Chat down the right. Until a layout is set up it says so, with a link to Stage layout |
| | **Temperatures** | Opens on the current run (or the latest one when none is live), its time axis fitted to the run, with Show to pick the last hour to 24 hours or any past run. Every phone's temperature, now and run by run, one show set beside another, and each phone's cooler beside it |
| Set up | **Stage layout** | Where the cameras and performers stand, set up once: place the cameras from the wide shot (experimental, a first guess to check), the room map, the buttons arranged by hand, and each kind of event's set (see [Stage layout](docs/STAGE.md#stage-layout)) |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: The dashboard
sections.text:
| Group | Page | What is on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| | **Director** | AI assistance (the level and its set-up steps), then how shots are chosen: the model, zoom, telephoto, gaze, listening for the instrument to the fore, who is talking, crowd camera, shot lengths, feed alignment, look-ahead; *Explain the director* (demo captions: each cut and why, solos heard, gimbals turning, lens changes, voice calls, laid over the programme and recorded with it); face blur, once it is switched on (administrator) |
| | **Sound** | Two sections: *Programme sound* (which camera's microphone leads, the others staying out, joining or the automixer; lip sync; Calibrate sync) (administrator), and *Voice shot calls* (what is listened to and the speech model, the quick phrase spotter, cameras' and zooms' phrases, what was heard) |
| | **Calibrate** | One person calibrates from the stage: the phone's address and QR code, the run the phone drives as it goes (stoppable from here), what it measured, and each camera's state; a setup tech's page (with Operate's positions), and an operator's and the administrator's (see [Calibrate from the stage](docs/COLOUR_AND_CALIBRATION.md#calibrate-from-the-stage)) |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: The dashboard
sections.text:
| Group | Page | What is on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| | **Power** | Keeping this computer awake through a show, on a schedule or for a few hours (see [Keeping the computer awake through a show](docs/KEEPING_CAMERAS_GOING.md#keeping-the-computer-awake-through-a-show)); the smart plugs the USB chargers for the gimbals and coolers are on: each one's state and switch, what is on its charger and which camera each of those is on now, the gimbals and coolers on no plug yet; adding plugs, saying what each charges and the Tapo login (administrator) (see [A charger hub on a smart plug](docs/KEEPING_CAMERAS_GOING.md#a-charger-hub-on-a-smart-plug)) |
| | **Colour** | White balance and exposure on the phones, calibration (chart, grey card or scene) and the LUTs in OBS (administrator) |
| | **People** | Plus AI only: enrol consenting performers from a camera's picture, stars and the cameras that follow them, consent, retention and delete-all (administrator) |
| Library | **Recordings** | *Local recordings (phones)*: copy, check and clean up in four numbered steps, the one to do now marked; each notice at the top carries the button it names, and each paired camera's card shows only the buttons that apply to it. *PC recordings*: the programme recordings with each camera's file and edit, the LUTs, and the camera files switch |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: The dashboard
sections.text:
| Group | Page | What is on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Administration | **System** | *Cameras* (Add a phone, the paired cameras to rename, set aside or remove, camera slots, battery protection, silence while armed), *Updates* (this computer's manager, then the phones' camera app, in one place), *Network*, *Logins*, *Locations & backups*, *This computer* (AI assistance, the camera relay, decoding, experimental features) (administrator) |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Running a show
sections.text:
Where each part of a show day is described:

- **Before**: the readiness line on the Show page, each item with what to do; the phones' health, coolers and charger
  plugs, and keeping this computer awake, in [Keeping the cameras going](docs/KEEPING_CAMERAS_GOING.md).
- **Choosing shots**: the director ([The director](docs/DIRECTOR.md)), or by hand on the Show page,
  [Stage Shots](docs/STAGE.md#stage-shots), [Operate and Remote](docs/OPERATE_AND_REMOTE.md), Scene Chat and
  [voice calls](docs/SOUND_AND_VOICE.md#voice-shot-calls).
- **Recording**: the programme on this computer, each camera's own file and the phones' recordings, in
  [Recordings and the camera relay](docs/RECORDINGS_AND_RELAY.md) and [Offload](docs/OFFLOAD.md).

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Updating from the dashboard
sections.text:
The administrator's **System › Updates** has this manager first ("This manager") and the phones' camera app under it
("Camera app": the release offered to the cameras, which cameras are behind it, and *Update unarmed cameras
automatically, one at a time*), so both are updated in one place. **Check for updates** fetches into the installation's
own copy of the repository (`~/.local/share/mcvsaid/source`, made by bootstrap and never worked in;
`update_repository` names another) and lists what has changed on the
release branch (`update_branch`, `main` unless set) since the version that is installed. **Install and restart**
runs the newer version's own `install-release.sh` and restarts the service into it; the version that was running is
kept, and nothing is made current unless it starts. **Restart manager** restarts the service by itself.

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Where an installation lives
sections.text:
A working installation keeps the program, its data and its settings apart, in the standard per-user places:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| The program, one folder per installed version | `~/.local/share/mcvsaid/releases/<version>` (`current` points at the one in use) |
| Data: database, certificate and key, pairing files, app releases | `~/.local/share/mcvsaid/data` |
| Settings (`config.json`) and secrets (`secrets.json`) | `~/.config/mcvsaid` |
| Bundled tools (ffmpeg) | `~/.local/share/mcvsaid/tools` |
| Tools for building the Android app (JDK, Android SDK, Gradle cache), on a build machine only | `~/.local/share/mcvsaid/build-tools` |
| The copy of the repository that updates are fetched into | `~/.local/share/mcvsaid/source` |
| Backups | `~/.local/share/mcvsaid/backups` |

sections.doc: MCVSAID manager (MultiCam Video Stream AI Director)
sections.title: Where an installation lives
sections.text:
- `scripts/install-release.sh <tag>` installs a tagged version with its own Python environment and makes it
  current. Only what is committed at that tag is installed, so the development copy is never what is on air.
  Earlier versions are kept; installing an earlier tag again goes back to it.
- `scripts/mcvsaid-manager.service` runs `current` against that data and those settings.
- `scripts/move-data.sh <old data folder>` moves an older installation's data into these places, once, after
  taking a backup. It deletes nothing.
- `scripts/backup-data.sh` makes a nightly, dated archive of the data and settings (and `scripts/restore-data.sh` puts one back): see [docs/BACKUP.md](docs/BACKUP.md).
- `config.json` holds only what the operator chooses and is safe to back up or compare between machines.
  `secrets.json` holds the password and passcode hashes, the model server's key and the smart plugs' login, and stays on the machine.

For development, `scripts/run-manager.sh --data-dir "$PWD/data" ...` still runs the working copy against a
folder of its own, as in [Development](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md#run-locally).

sections.doc: OBS setup for the next commissioning milestone
sections.title: OBS setup for the next commissioning milestone
sections.text:
OBS 32.2.2 Flatpak is installed. obs-websocket is present, authentication is
configured, and its server was disabled at inspection. No OBS configuration was
changed by this implementation. Enable the server only when commissioning OBS
integration is approved. Use port 4455, a strong password, and loopback access.
The current preview does not control OBS or claim decoded/recorded media success.

Keep the working scene collection. Export a backup in OBS before creating a
separate five-camera production collection. Then press **Refresh OBS scenes**
(Director page, OBS alignment): the manager makes a Media Source (MPEG-TS, Local
File off) for each camera that has none, with its full-screen scene and split
screens, and nothing is copied from the dashboard by hand. Each source is pointed
at the camera relay, `udp://127.0.0.1:<9999 + slot>?overrun_nonfatal=1&fifo_size=100000&buffer_size=4194304`,
while the relay is on (the default; [Each camera's own file of a recording](RECORDINGS_AND_RELAY.md#each-cameras-own-file-of-a-recording)),
the relay listening on the camera ports in OBS's place. With the relay off it is
pointed at the camera's own SRT listener instead:

| Camera | SRT input (relay off) |
|---|---|
| 1 | `srt://0.0.0.0:9000?mode=listener&latency=200000` |
| 2 | `srt://0.0.0.0:9001?mode=listener&latency=200000` |
| 3 | `srt://0.0.0.0:9002?mode=listener&latency=200000` |
| 4 | `srt://0.0.0.0:9003?mode=listener&latency=200000` |
| 5 | `srt://0.0.0.0:9004?mode=listener&latency=200000` |

sections.doc: OBS setup for the next commissioning milestone
sections.title: OBS setup for the next commissioning milestone
sections.text:
The manager repoints the sources whenever the relay is switched on or off, and
restarts a relayed source as its camera connects and after it goes.

Use 200000/120000/80000 microseconds on OBS for the Stable/Balanced/Low presets.
RootEncoder's sender API takes 200/120/80 milliseconds. Both endpoints contribute
to negotiated latency; these values are not glass-to-glass latency measurements.
Start with the existing software decoder and zero Media Source network buffer;
measure hardware decoding separately rather than assume it is faster.

Select the external soundboard interface explicitly as the production audio
reference, and avoid mixing five delayed phone microphones into it. Configure
scratch camera audio separately for calibration if needed. Record with a format
that can survive interrupted OBS output (typically MKV and later remuxing).
Verify the actual output disk/path/free space and final files, not just a red
recording indicator. Independent ISO recording is not implemented in this preview.

A future production start must block until each required stream is independently
confirmed received and decoded, not merely connected by SRT handshake. This
preview intentionally has no Start Production button or automatic scene edits.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.text: Back to [the manager's README](../README.md). Who can log in from the camera network is in [Security](SECURITY.md#who-can-log-in).

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: The manager's name on the camera network
sections.text:
Phones can be paired to the manager's address, or to a name. Paired to a name, a phone looks it up each time it
connects and follows the manager to whatever address it has: another site, a changed router, a second adapter.
The choice is made on System › Network, under "How the phones find this manager":

| Choice | Needs on the network |
|---|---|
| The address alone | A fixed address for the PC (a DHCP reservation on the router). Every phone is tied to it. |
| `mcvsaid.local`, or another name ending in `.local` | Nothing on the router. The PC announces the name itself (Avahi). The Wi-Fi must let phones hear it: no client or AP isolation, no multicast or mDNS filtering. |
| Any other name | A local name record on the router giving the name the PC's address, and a fixed address for the PC. Do not use a public ending you do not own. |

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: The manager's name on the camera network
sections.text:
- Each name has its own certificate (`data/names/<name>/`). The original certificate goes on being served to phones
  that connect by address; which one a connection gets goes by the name the phone asks for, on the same port.
- "Move … to the name" tells connected phones to use the name, over the connection they already have (app 0.9.0
  or later). A phone tries the name first and keeps its pairing if it cannot reach the manager that way.
- Phones paired by name send their picture to the address their control connection is on, so OBS is found the
  same way.
- An earlier name is answered to until it is retired, so changing the name cuts no phone off.
- `agent_interface` (optional) names the camera-network interface: the manager then listens on whatever address
  that interface has, and restarts itself to follow a change.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Camera capacity, device storage and OBS URLs
sections.text:
Use **Camera slots → Save capacity** on the dashboard to show 1–64 slots. The
default remains five. Capacity cannot be reduced below the highest paired slot;
no cameras or credentials are deleted. Existing five-slot databases migrate
transactionally with a private backup next to the registry. More slots do not
prove Wi-Fi, encoder, workstation or OBS capacity for simultaneous streams.
Stop the manager before provisioning additional devices, then run `pair --slot 6`
(or any configured slot), import its private bundle, and restart the manager.
Camera N uses UDP port `8999 + N`; additional OBS sources must be configured by
the operator. Android 0.5.1 accepts ports through 9063.

Each card shows the device's shared-storage free/total GiB and estimated local
MP4 recording time until the disk is full. Initially this uses local recording
bitrate plus 192 kbps AAC and a 1% MP4 overhead allowance. After at least ten
seconds of local recording, it uses the recent measured local video byte rate
plus audio/overhead. This is approximate: scene complexity, other applications,
filesystem limits and device reserves can change it. It does not promise that
recording is automatically stopped or safely finalized before the disk fills.
Offline values are last reported. No telemetry means unavailable, not zero.
Older 0.5.0 agents supply free space and bitrate only while armed; 0.5.1 adds
free/total storage and local bitrate while unarmed as well. Phone replacement
requires approval; the newly built APK is not installed automatically.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Camera capacity, device storage and OBS URLs
sections.text:
OBS needs no URL copied from the dashboard: **Refresh OBS scenes** (Director page, OBS alignment) makes in
OBS a Media Source for each camera that has none, its full-screen scene and its split screens, and points each
source at the right address: the camera relay's when the relay is on (the default), otherwise the camera's own SRT
listener port. Nothing already in OBS is changed or removed. **Refresh names in OBS** beside it gives every
camera's source, scenes and split screens its name here, as renaming does: for a camera renamed while OBS was
closed, or sources made by hand under other names (`POST /api/obs/names`).

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Network cameras over NDI
sections.text:
A camera that is not a phone, such as a PTZ camera on the network, can be one of the show's cameras. OBS takes its
picture over NDI; the manager knows it by a name, a slot and the name of the NDI source it sends. Nothing is installed
on the camera and nothing connects to the manager: OBS is asked what it has and shows.

**What it needs.** The NDI runtime and the [DistroAV](https://github.com/DistroAV/DistroAV) plugin installed in OBS
(both free; their installers ask for an administrator's password), and OBS restarted. The kind and the setting names
the manager uses were read from OBS 33.0.1 with DistroAV 6.2.2 on the Mac (`ndi_source`, `ndi_source_name`, `latency`,
`ndi_behavior`, `ndi_behavior_timeout`, `ndi_bw_mode`). The manager itself links no NDI library. Without the plugin
the manager starts and runs as it always has; the network camera's card says "OBS has no NDI source: install the NDI
runtime and the DistroAV plugin, then restart OBS", and "Refresh OBS scenes" makes everything else and names the
camera it left out.

**Adding one.** System › Cameras › *Add a network camera* (an administrator), or the button on an empty slot's card.
The page lists the NDI sources to choose from: as OBS's plugin lists them when OBS already has an NDI source to ask
through, otherwise as they announce themselves on the network (multicast DNS, `_ndi._tcp`, read without the NDI
library). The name can always be typed instead, exactly as OBS shows it: the sending device, then the source in
brackets, as in `STAGE-PTZ (Camera 1)`.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Network cameras over NDI
sections.text:
**In OBS.** "Refresh OBS scenes" makes an NDI source for it in the scene that keeps every stream open, with its
full-screen scene and its split screens, as for a phone. In a split screen the sync keeper crops its picture to the
upright middle, so it fills its half at full height with the centre of the shot in the centre (logged as
`obs_split_crop_fitted`); a crop of your own that is the shape of the half is left as it is. The source is set to the plugin's lowest delay
(`latency` 2), kept receiving while it is not shown (`ndi_behavior` 0), and cleared three seconds after the camera
stops sending (`ndi_behavior_timeout` 0), so that a camera that has gone is seen to have gone. A source made by hand
is found too: by the NDI source name kept for the camera, or failing that by being called what the camera is. One
made by hand with the plugin's own default keeps its last frame when the camera stops, and would go on counting as a
picture.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Network cameras over NDI
sections.text:
**Readiness.** Four checks, and none of a phone's: whether OBS has the plugin, whether it has a source for the camera
(and whether that source takes the NDI name kept here), whether OBS shows its picture, and what it is held by. OBS is
asked every two seconds (`network_camera_seconds`). A source just made shows nothing until one of the camera scenes
has been on programme once (seen with DistroAV 6.2.2: the plugin connected at once, and the picture came half a
second after its scene was first shown). A camera whose source shows a picture counts as streaming, so the
director, voice shot calls, Stage Shots and the Remote page's keys choose it like any other.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Network cameras over NDI
sections.text:
**Its delay: timed by its picture.** A phone's delay is measured from the timing strip it draws; a network camera
draws none. The manager times it another way (`picsync.py`): when two cameras look at the same room, things happen in
both pictures at the same instant: someone moves, a stage light changes. While OBS sync is on, the sync keeper takes
small pictures (160 by 90) of the network camera's OBS source and of two phones' sources 25 times a second for 20
seconds, works out how much each picture was changing at each instant, and finds how far the one has to be slid along
the other for the busy moments to fall together. That is how much earlier or later OBS shows the same moment from the
network camera than from a phone already lined up, and so how late the camera is by itself; its delay in OBS (its
sound with it) is then set so that it is shown as far behind real life as the phones are. It does this again every
15 seconds or so for as long as the manager runs, so a camera whose own lateness changes in the middle of a show is
brought back without anyone touching it.

It answers only when it can tell, and otherwise leaves the camera as it is:

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Network cameras over NDI
sections.text:
- At least four separate things have to be seen happening in both pictures during a watch, the two have to be alike
  there (0.6 or better of 1), and no other fit may come near (0.7 of the best at most). A still room, a camera being
  turned, or two cameras looking at different things give no answer. So does a picture whose only change is the pulse
  an encoder gives it at each keyframe: changes of less than two grey levels in a dot are not counted.
- One watch seldom holds four such things (a cook at a stove gave two to four in twenty seconds), so the last few
  watches of the same two cameras are fitted together (`picsync.newest`): the newest alone, then the newest two, up to
  six from the last five minutes (`network_sync_watches`, `network_sync_pool_seconds`), as few as give an answer.
  The true gap is the same in every watch and a chance fit is not, so what the watches share adds up. Only watches
  taken with the same delays are put together: when the camera's delay, the phone's or the phones' common delay
  moves, it starts again. And the newest watch has to be part of the answer, so that a room gone still does not go
  on confirming where the camera was. In made-up quiet rooms one watch answered 7 times in 120, two together 97,
  six together 113, and two cameras seeing unrelated things were answered 0 times in 480.
- Nothing is changed on one reading: two in a row have to agree within 50 ms.
- A watch during which a phone's delay, the network camera's, or the phones' common delay was changed is thrown away.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Network cameras over NDI
sections.text:
- The phone that placed it last time is watched again, with one other beside it, each of the lined-up phones in turn,
  since not every phone sees what the network camera sees. Two phones that place it more than 80 ms apart: no answer.
- It is light that is compared, which reaches every camera at the same instant.

**Its sound, as a second check.** While it watches, the sync keeper also listens (`soundsync.py`): OBS reports how
loud each of its inputs is about 18 times a second, a muted input included (its level before the fader and the mute),
and the network camera's loudness is slid along a phone's by the same rules as the pictures. That says how much later
its sound *reaches* OBS than the phone's, and from it how late the camera is by itself. Sound is not light: it
reaches a camera further from the stage later (3 ms a metre), and a camera's sound and picture need not leave it
together. So the sound is never believed by itself to begin with. Whenever the pictures and the sound both tell, the
difference between them is kept for that pair of cameras (`network-sound.json` in the data folder, the last nine).
Once three or more have settled:

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Network cameras over NDI
sections.text:
- when the pictures cannot tell (a still or dark stage with music playing) and the sound can, the sound stands in,
  corrected by that difference; the card says "timed by its sound";
- when both tell and they part by more than 120 ms (`network_sync_sound_agree_ms`), neither is believed for that
  watch (`network_camera_sound_disagrees` in the audit log). What the sound said is kept all the same, so a camera
  moved to another place in the room comes to agree again after about nine watches.

Only levels are listened to, about 18 numbers a second for each input; nothing said or played is kept or could be
made out from them. `network_sync_sound: false` leaves the sound out. In tests with made-up rooms the sound placed a
camera within 30 ms. Against the real OBS (2026-11-19): the levels arrive as expected, every 55 ms, for muted inputs
too; but the Tenveo PTZ's own input was flat at about -76 dB while the phone beside it heard the room, so its sound
could not be tried. A network camera with no microphone, or none switched on, is timed by its picture alone.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
The picture matching needs something to happen in both pictures, and takes a few watches of a quiet room. The
calibrate page's third run, **Time the network cameras** (Set up › Calibrate; `flashsync.py`,
`SyncKeeper.time_by_flash`), makes it happen: somebody holds the page up where a network camera and at least one
phone camera both see it, and it lights its screen for an eighth of a second about once a second, at uneven gaps,
without the beeps. Light reaches every camera at the same instant, and neither the page's clock nor its screen's own
delay comes into it: only how much later OBS shows each flash from the one camera than from the other.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
- One watch of 16 seconds (`network_flash_seconds`) of every network camera and up to three lined-up phones
  (`network_flash_phones`) at once, as small pictures like the picture matching's.
- In each picture, the dots that lit about as often as the page does are found (a phone across a room is a dot or
  two; a stage light or a hand is another part, and is told apart by going bright at other times). When each lit is
  paired between the two cameras by the page's uneven gaps: only the true slide pairs more than a few, and a light
  blinking evenly pairs as well one way as the next and is refused. How those dots were changing, slid until they
  fall together about there, gives the answer more finely than the time between two looks.
- At least five flashes have to pair, most of what either camera saw, agreeing within 60 ms; OBS has to have
  answered at least eleven times a second for each source; two phones may not place the camera more than 80 ms
  apart; and a delay changed during the watch throws it away. Otherwise that camera is left as it was, and the page
  says why.
- A camera that is timed is held by what brings it to the phones at once, on this one reading (it was made to
  happen, and is checked against itself), kept as a delay set by the picture matching is, and that matching goes on
  from it. Its card says "timed by the calibrate page's flashes", and the audit log `network_camera_timed` with
  `by: flash`.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
In tests with made-up pictures the answer was within 26 ms of the truth at twelve looks a second or more (5 ms in
the middle). Not yet tried with a real phone held up to real cameras.

Its card says when it was last timed, against which phone, how late it is by itself, and why the last look gave no
answer when it gave none; each change is in the audit log (`network_camera_timed`). Why a camera could not be timed
is in the audit log too (`network_camera_not_timed`, with what each look found: how alike, how many things seen in
both, the rival fit), each time the reason changes and at most once a minute, so that a recording that went out
unsynchronised can be explained afterwards. In tests with made-up rooms, the
answer was within 35 ms of the truth, and two cameras seeing unrelated things were given an answer once in 450
watches (and never twice alike). `network_sync_enabled: false` in the configuration switches the timing off; the
watch is `network_sync_watch_seconds` (20) long, `network_sync_rate` (25) pictures a second, with
`network_sync_gap_seconds` (15) between watches.

**Between timings it follows the phones.** The delay is kept with the phones' common delay it is right for. When that
common delay moves, because the slowest phone changed or the hold was changed, the network camera's delay is moved by
as much at the next round. A delay that would have to be less than nothing (the phones lined up closer to real life
than the camera can be) or more than 6000 ms is held at that end, and its sync line says by how much it is late or
early.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
**By hand.** The delay can still be set on its card (Maintenance › Delay, 0 to 6000 ms) by eye against a phone until
a clap lands on the same frame. That is a starting point: the next timing that can tell replaces it. With OBS sync off
nothing is timed and nothing follows, and a delay set by hand stays as set.

**Tried so far.** Against a real OBS 33.0.1 with a Tenveo PTZ over NDI beside a Galaxy S23+ (2026-11-19, read only,
nothing changed in OBS): a still room is told as still, the once-a-second encoder pulse is not taken for something
happening, and when the camera was moved the picture placed it 5.5 s before the phone (before the rule that four things must be seen in both, which one movement would not pass), as it should be when held by
nothing beside phones held for 5.5 s. 50 small pictures a second cost OBS nothing that showed (no frame skipped,
render time unchanged at about 2 ms). The first recordings made with it (same evening) went out with the camera never timed: the one phone streaming
looked at a different part of the kitchen from the camera, no single watch held four things seen by both, and the
camera's sound was silent. That is what fitting several watches together is for; five real watches kept from that
rig, of which three gave no answer alone, give the same answer (within 40 ms) when the fifth is fitted with the two
before it. Not yet tried: the whole loop setting a real camera's delay, people moving in
front of both, or a show's length.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
**What does not apply to it.** Arming, starting and stopping its stream, recording on the camera, battery,
temperature, storage, lenses, gimbal and cooler, the clock, app updates, stream encryption, the camera relay (so it
has no camera file of its own, and face blur, which reads the relay, does not cover it) and the choice of decoder.
None of them is shown for it and none counts against it. The "All cameras" actions leave it out. Its sound is left
as OBS has it: Programme sound does not mute or line up a network camera's microphone.

**Turning and following.** The manager can turn and track a network PTZ camera (a Tenveo TEVO-X60 and its like) as
it does a phone on a gimbal that is following. The work is split the same way: the manager chooses who to follow
(the camera's follow plan: the soloist, a prominent instrument, the performers it follows in order, or anyone) and
gives the coarse aim from the wide shot and the room map, and the camera's own onboard tracker (single person,
autoframe, zone or stage) holds the fine framing within the area it was aimed at. It is controlled over the camera's
own control API (VISCA, carried over the HTTP interface the camera's web page uses), so the manager links no NDI
library for it.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
*Setting it up.* An administrator sets the camera's control address on its card (an address such as `192.0.2.10`),
then arms **Following**. The address is kept on the local registry, never committed or logged, and the interface
asks for no password, so none is kept. Nothing is sent to the camera by itself until Following is armed, so a camera
can be set up with nothing ever sent to it; only a person steering it or using its presets, on its card or the Operate
page, reaches it before then. The card's Following section also has the onboard tracker's mode (single, autoframe,
zone, stage or hybrid) and framing size (close, half, full or custom), tracking on and off, the parts of the follow
plan, and the camera's named shots. It has no performer picker.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
*A phone mounted beside it.* The coarse aim from the room map has one weak spot: the wide shot shows which way
someone is, but how far back they stand is a guess from their feet, and a camera somewhere else in the room needs
that to know which way to turn. A phone fixed right beside the PTZ camera, showing the whole stage, removes the guess:
the two look from the same place, so where someone is in the phone's picture is the way the camera turns, however
far away they are. On the camera's card an administrator chooses the **Phone mounted beside it**, then lines the two
up one of two ways. *Set:* aim the camera by hand at whatever is in the middle of that phone's picture and press
**Set**; the camera is asked where it points (nothing moves it) and that is kept, which also tells the manager how
far the phone tilts. *The room map:* with no Set, both cameras' aims on the room map are used (and the phone's tilt
there, if it has one; without it only the pan is aimed). Set is the more exact, and neither camera needs to be on
the room map with it. Press Set again if either is moved. Then whoever the follow plan wants is found in the
phone's picture and the camera is turned to them, at about chest height; with "anyone", to the middle of everyone
the phone sees. Keep the two lenses close (within about 30 cm puts the aim within 3 degrees for someone 6 m away),
the phone still (not on a gimbal) and at one zoom. While the phone's picture cannot be used, the camera is aimed
from the room map as before, and its card says why. This has been checked against simulated cameras
(`tests/test_beside.py`), not yet with the real camera and a phone beside it.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
*Shots and voice.* A named shot recalls one of the camera's own presets: aim the camera, name and save the shot, then
say its name ("show the pot"); "back to me" lets it follow again. "Stop tracking" and "start tracking" and the zoom
calls ("close up") work on it. The director cuts to it as a following camera and trusts its onboard framing.

*The limit.* The camera picks its own subject within the area it was aimed at. It cannot be handed a named performer,
and it reports no one it is tracking, so the manager cannot say who it has. It matches a phone on a gimbal in every
way but this one. Where performers keep to fixed places, a preset for each stage area (a zone), recalled for whoever
the plan wants, aims it at one spot. The exact control commands are modelled on VISCA and the camera's web page and
are still to be confirmed on the camera itself.

sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
*By hand, on the Operate page.* A network camera has a tile on the [Operate](OPERATE_AND_REMOTE.md) page like any
other, and one added later is shown there without being ticked. Its live picture is its OBS source's, asked of OBS
eight times a second at 640 pixels wide while somebody is watching (`network_camera_picture_rate`,
`network_camera_picture_width`): the phones' pictures come from the camera relay, which it never passes through. It
is the source as OBS shows it, so a delay set for the camera holds this picture back too, and the tile says by how
much; aim with that in mind. With its control address set, the right stick or the on-screen arrows turn it, the
triggers or the zoom buttons zoom it, B or **Stop camera** stops it, and the right stick's press or **Go home** sends it
home, whether or not Following is armed. **Set home** keeps where it points now, and its zoom, as that home, as on a
gimbal camera: it is saved on the camera as one of its own presets (number 60, `network_camera_home_preset`, clear of
the 1 to 12 its Positions take), so it holds across restarts and there is nothing to find again. Until a home is set,
Go home is the camera's own home position (straight ahead). A VISCA move carries on until the camera is told to
stop, where a phone stops its gimbal by itself, so the manager does that part: it stops the camera when a reading
says so or when none has come for 0.6 seconds (the page closed, the network lost, the controller unplugged), and
tries a stop again if the camera did not take it. Its **Positions** are its presets: Save as… keeps where it points
as the camera's next free preset, Go recalls it. The tile's **Tracking** (X on a controller) turns the camera's own
tracker on or off, whether or not Following is armed: on, it frames its own subject where it points (and an armed one
is aimed from the stage); off, it stays where you aim it. The camera does not say whether its tracker is on, so the
button shows what was last set from here ("not set" until something has been), and every press is sent to the camera. With its tracker on, it takes the
camera back after a hand move, and the page says so. Without a control
address the tile shows its picture and puts it on air, and says where to give the address. None of this has moved a
real camera yet.
