sections.doc: The camera network, camera slots and OBS sources
sections.title: Timed at once by the calibrate page
sections.text:
**Locations and fleet files.** A network camera is not in a fleet file (it has no credential for another PC to trust)
and stays when the fleet of phones is replaced; if a phone arrives with the slot it has, the network camera moves to
the highest free slot.

sections.doc: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.title: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.text:
How much AI helps the director, and how each level is set up. Back to [the manager's README](../README.md).

How much AI helps the director is a choice per installation (`ai_tier`, camera_manager/ai.py), so a modest computer can
still run a show:

| Level | Shots | Zoom | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **No AI** (the default) | by hand, on Stage Shots or by timed rotation; the safety rules still cut away from a camera that breaks | off | OBS and the manager only: nothing is downloaded or run for AI |
| **Standard AI** | a vision model on this computer rates every camera, guided by what each camera shows (its instruments, or the roles of a service, podcast, panel or play) and your wishes; instrument listening and cutting to where the performer looks; in Cooking, spoken cues from what the cook says, and voice shot calls ("cut to the overhead") in Cooking, Creator Studio and wherever switched on (Whisper on this computer, optional) | follows the performer | the model, about 7 GB of graphics memory: an Apple silicon Mac with 32 GB or more (24 GB at the least), or an NVIDIA card with 8 GB or more |
| **Plus AI** | Standard, and consenting performers recognised from reference pictures taken on the day in what they perform in: stars given priority on any camera, cameras that follow a named performer | follows a named performer, with the fast person detector | Standard's, and the detector (very little); under the performer library's privacy rules (docs/PRIVACY_PERFORMER_LIBRARY.md) |

sections.doc: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.title: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.text:
A new installation starts at No AI. `bootstrap.sh --ai standard` (or `plus`) chooses a level on a new PC; otherwise the
administrator is asked the first time the Director page is opened, and can change the level at any time under
System › This computer. Each level's set-up is shown as steps, each checked as it stands:
On the Director page the panel is one line ("Plus AI: 10 of 16 steps done", with *Continue set-up*, or *Show what did not
work* and a note when a step failed); the steps and the other levels sit in a fold, closed until opened, which stays as
it was when the panel redraws. Home-folder paths are shown as `~` and other long ones by their last two parts (the full path is the tooltip; buttons and the Copy
button still use the full path):

- what the manager can do by itself has a button: downloading the model (about 5.8 GB, to `~/models/qwen3-vl-8b`),
  installing and starting the model as a service on this computer only (`mcvsaid-model`: a launchd agent on a Mac,
  a systemd user service on Linux, from `scripts/mcvsaid-model.service`), checking it answers, pointing the director
  at it, and for Plus, adding the detector's runtime and downloading the detector (YOLOX-s, Apache-2.0);
- what needs an administrator's password, installing llama.cpp with Homebrew or a package manager, is shown as the
  command to run in Terminal, ready to copy (as the account that owns Homebrew, where that is another account). The
  dashboard never asks for, or keeps, that password.

sections.doc: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.title: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.text:
Listening for instruments, when it is switched on, adds its own steps: the runtime (ai-edge-litert) and Google's YAMNet
sound model (about 4 MB, to `<data>/audio`) have buttons; BlackHole on a Mac (or PulseAudio's tools on Linux) has its
command (and a reinstall command when Homebrew lists BlackHole but its driver is missing); and the last step, hearing
the programme, is done once sound actually arrives. For that, OBS has to send the programme to the loopback device: in
OBS › Settings › Audio, **Monitoring Device** is *BlackHole 2ch*, and each camera's (or the sound desk's) source has
**Audio Monitoring** set to *Monitor and Output* (not *Monitor Only*, which takes it out of the programme). Set up this
way on the Mac, the listener hears the programme (checked live on 2026-10-17).

From a terminal, `mcvsaid ai` shows the same steps, and `mcvsaid ai setup standard` chooses a level (with the manager
stopped; while it runs, use the dashboard). At No AI the model, listening and gaze stay off however they are set, and
the Director page shows only what works without a model. An installation from before the levels keeps what it was
doing: Standard if its model, listening or gaze was on, No AI otherwise.

sections.doc: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.title: Search and the assistant
sections.text:
**Search** is at the top of the side bar on every page, and opens with `/` (when nothing is being typed into) or Ctrl
or ⌘ with K. It works at every AI level, No AI included, and looks through two things as you type
(`camera_manager/helpdesk.py`, `static/help.js`):

- **Places on the dashboard**: buttons, settings and sections, each with the page it is on and the words people look
  for it by (*Record programme to file*, *Shot lengths*, *Add a phone*, *Keep this computer awake*…). Choosing one
  opens its page, scrolls to it, opens the fold it is in and outlines it for a few seconds. You are shown only the
  places your login may open: an operator is not offered the administrator's pages, and a setup tech has Calibrate and
  Operate.
- **The guide**: the manager's README and the documents of `docs/` this installation came with, cut at their headings.
  Choosing one opens that part to read in the search itself, with *Next* to read on and its links to other parts
  working.

sections.doc: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.title: Search and the assistant
sections.text:
**The assistant** answers a question in words. Type one ("How do I pair a gimbal?", "What does Arm do?") and choose
*Ask the assistant*, the first thing listed for a question: the model the director uses, on this computer, is given
the question with the few parts of the guide and the places the search found for it, and is told to answer from those
alone and to say so when they do not cover it. Under its answer are *Go to* buttons for the places and *Guide* buttons
for the parts it was given, so what it says can be checked against the guide's own words; a model can still get a
detail wrong. An answer takes about 2 to 7 s on the M5 Pro (three questions asked of Qwen3-VL 8B, 2026-11-20). A
follow-up question is answered knowing the last two.

sections.doc: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.title: Search and the assistant
sections.text:
- **It needs Standard or Plus AI**, with the model set up (the steps above). At No AI, or when the model does not
  answer, the best-matching part of the guide is shown in place of an answer, with the reason.
- **Not while the programme is on air.** While OBS records or streams and the model is choosing shots, the assistant
  does not ask it: the model has two places, the director wants both, and a rating kept waiting is a cut made late. The
  guide's own words are shown instead, and the search says why. `help_ai_on_air: true` in the settings lets it answer
  on air too (not tried during a real show). One question is answered at a time.
- **Nothing asked is kept.** A question and its answer live in the page that asked, and are gone when it is left; the
  audit log notes that a question was answered and from which parts of the guide, never its words. Nothing leaves this
  computer: the model is the one on 127.0.0.1.
- `help_ai_timeout_seconds` (45) is how long an answer is waited for.

The places are written by hand in `helpdesk.py` (`PLACES`); `tests/test_help.py` holds each one to a page the side bar
has and to words or an id that page's own files have, so a renamed button fails there until its place is put right.

sections.doc: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.title: Running the model by hand on a Mac
sections.text:
The model runs as its own launchd agent, so it starts at login and comes back if it stops. The AI set-up downloads the
model and installs this agent with a button; to do it by hand instead, download Qwen3-VL 8B
Instruct as GGUF (the Q4_K_M model and its Q8_0 `mmproj` picture encoder), then save this as
`~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.mcvsaid.model.plist` with your own paths, and load it with
`launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.mcvsaid.model.plist`:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>com.mcvsaid.model</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key><array>
    <string>/opt/homebrew/bin/llama-server</string>
    <string>--model</string><string>/Users/YOU/models/qwen3-vl-8b/Qwen3VL-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf</string>
    <string>--mmproj</string><string>/Users/YOU/models/qwen3-vl-8b/mmproj-Qwen3VL-8B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf</string>
    <string>--alias</string><string>qwen3-vl-8b</string>
    <string>--host</string><string>127.0.0.1</string><string>--port</string><string>8082</string>
    <string>--n-gpu-layers</string><string>99</string><string>--ctx-size</string><string>8192</string>
    <string>--parallel</string><string>2</string>
  </array>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key><true/>
  <key>ProcessType</key><string>Interactive</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/Users/YOU/Library/Logs/mcvsaid/mcvsaid-model.log</string>
</dict></plist>
```

sections.doc: AI assistance: No AI, Standard or Plus
sections.title: Running the model by hand on a Mac
sections.text:
On the Director page the model server is then `http://127.0.0.1:8082/v1/chat/completions` and the model
`qwen3-vl-8b`. `--parallel 2` lets the zoom's quick "where is the performer" questions in beside the slower ratings.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.text: The kinds of event, where the host looks, band profiles, switching tracking and zoom off live, Scene Chat and Explain the director. The AI levels are in [AI assistance](AI_ASSISTANCE.md); sound and voice calls in [Sound and voice](SOUND_AND_VOICE.md); cooking in [Recipe and kitchen](RECIPE_AND_KITCHEN.md).

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: How the director zooms and cuts
sections.text:
- **Following a performer.** With the zoom on, the model is asked about every second, apart from its ratings, where the
  performer is in the newest picture from the camera relay (else the phone's, else OBS's), which runs about 5 s ahead
  of the programme. Between two finds the shot is interpolated, after the last one extrapolated only when three finds
  agree, and it leads a walker with room ahead. An answer that arrives too late to use is thrown away.
- **Never zooming on nobody.** The model may answer that nobody is there; a box no standing or walking person could fill
  is refused; scenery it keeps finding a "person" in while rating the picture empty is remembered for five minutes; and
  a picture rated poorly is shown whole. Replayed on a recording where the old zoom sat on a litter bin, the walker was
  wholly in shot all of the time they were in the picture (38% before) and the zoom was on nobody 2% of the empty time
  (43% before).
- **The telephoto lens** (see [Camera and network hardware](../README.md#camera-and-network-hardware)): only off air, at most every 30 s per camera.
- **Where the performer looks** (Director page, off by default; Mac only). About twice a second each stage camera's
  picture is read with Apple's Vision framework for a face turned to it and centred eyes, in 4-5 ms a picture on the
  M5 Pro. A look held for two looks in a row cuts to that camera, which then stays on air at least 2.5 s; when the
  performer looks at no camera the model chooses again. Not yet checked on a real face.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: The telephoto lens
trail: How the director zooms and cuts
sections.text:
With the zoom on, the director can use a camera's telephoto lens for tight shots ("Use its telephoto lens" on the
camera's card; off unless ticked). It changes lens only while that camera is off air, keeps the camera out of the
choosing until the telephoto's picture is in OBS, changes any camera's lens at most every 30 seconds, and goes back to
the main lens when a wider shot is wanted. A telephoto that will not open, or whose picture does not reach OBS within
20 seconds, is given up on for that camera and the camera goes back. Every change is in the log with its reason.
On a Galaxy S23 the 3x telephoto opens for the app (tested).

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Kinds of event
sections.text:
The kind of event is chosen under the MCVSAID name at the top of the side bar, and shown on every page (in the strip
along the top of the page). It is the administrator's to change; an operator sees it. It belongs to the location, and
travels with its settings. Live music is the default, and a show set to it is directed exactly as before.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Kinds of event
sections.text:
| Kind | What a camera can be given to show | Sound | Pace, where you have not set your own |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Live music / concert** | singers and instruments, the whole band | the instrument to the fore; solos | shots 6–18 s; the crowd at most every 45 s, for 6 s |
| **House of worship** | pastor or preacher, worship leader, reader or lector, choir, the band's instruments, the congregation | music as at a concert; speech favours the pastor's and readers' cameras; whoever talks into their microphone | shots 8–25 s; the congregation at most every 2 min, for 5 s |
| **Podcast / talk show** | host, co-host, guests 1–5, a wide shot of everyone | whoever talks into their microphone; the wide shot when several talk at once or nobody does; no solos | shots 3–30 s; wide after 5 s of quiet |
| **Panel / conference / meetup** | moderator, panelists 1–6, the speaker at the lectern, audience Q&A, the whole panel, the audience | whoever talks into their microphone; laughter and applause favour the audience camera | shots 4–30 s; wide after 6 s of quiet |
| **Theatre / comedy / open mic** | performer on stage, host or MC, singers and instruments, the whole stage, the audience | speech and song favour the performer; laughter and applause favour the audience camera | shots 5–20 s; the audience at most every 30 s |

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Kinds of event
sections.text:
| Kind | What a camera can be given to show | Sound | Pace, where you have not set your own |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cooking / recipe** | host (talking to camera), cutting board / knife work, mixer and mixing bowls, countertop (prep and plating), stovetop with pots and pans, oven, grill, the wide kitchen | the kitchen's sounds favour their station: chopping the board, frying, sizzling and boiling the stovetop, the blender the mixer, cutlery the counter, the host's voice the host; no solos | shots 9–35 s: a recipe step holds |
| **Creator Studio** | framings you build yourself from body regions ([Creator Studio](CREATOR_STUDIO.md#creator-studio-on-the-dashboard)) | not used | cameras in turn, 6–20 s, until you set your own cutting |

What changes with the kind of event:

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Kinds of event
sections.text:
- **What each camera shows.** The Cameras page offers the kind's own roles in place of the instruments; "other" takes a
  name of your own (an interpreter, a second host). A camera keeps what it was given when the kind changes. A camera
  given only the congregation or the audience is the crowd camera, unless another is chosen on the Director page.
- **How the model is asked.** Its instructions are put in the kind's words: a sermon, a reading, a guest speaking, a
  panelist answering, a laugh in the house, in place of a performer, a band, a solo and a crowd. The zoom looks for the
  moderator or the person at the lectern as it looks for the drummer.
- **Who is talking.** With a mixer or audio interface that gives the computer each microphone on its own channel (a
  RØDECaster, a Zoom PodTrak, a digital desk over USB), name its sound device on the Director page and give each camera
  its person's channel on the Cameras page. Each channel's level is read ten times a second against its own
  background; the loudest one talking is the speaker, a second one counts only when nearly as loud (every microphone
  hears its neighbours), a cough does not take the floor, and a pause between sentences does not end a turn. With the
  model, the speaker's camera is lifted as a soloist's is (by 4, where its picture shows a person); without one (No AI),
  the programme cuts to whoever is talking once the shot on air has run its shortest length, and to the wide shot when
  several talk at once or nobody has for a few seconds. Without a mixer, the model rates the person who is visibly
  speaking; the programme's mixed sound cannot tell one voice from another (`camera_manager/talk.py` says more).

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Kinds of event
sections.text:
- **A kitchen**, **a recipe to follow** and the rest of Cooking: see [Recipe and kitchen](RECIPE_AND_KITCHEN.md).
- **The pace.** Shot lengths and how often and how long the audience is shown take the kind's values above, unless set
  on the Director page, which always wins.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Where the performer looks: gaze cuts
sections.text:
**Looking back to a camera ends a called shot's hold** (with gaze on; `Director.gaze_releases`,
`director_gaze_overrides`, for each kind of event). A shot called aloud is held for *Hold after a person chooses*; with
this, a confirmed look into another camera ends the hold and the gaze cuts to it, so a cook calls "cut to the stove" and
brings the camera back to themselves by looking into the front camera, with no call. Only a look that began after the
held shot was cut to counts: the look given while calling the shot does not undo it. Calling the camera already on air
keeps it there with no cut (it might have been put there by the recipe or the model); that is a call too, and a look can
end it 4 s after the call. While someone looks at a camera, each look is in the cut log (`gaze`: every camera's score,
where its picture came from and how old it was, the camera leading and the hold the director was under). *After a called-out shot* by
default in Cooking and Creator Studio, *never* elsewhere; *after any chosen shot* also ends an operator's or the Operate
page's hold. Set on the Director page under the gaze settings.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Where the performer looks: gaze cuts
sections.text:
**Looking away goes back** (`Director.gaze_return`, `director_gaze_return`, on by default). When the performer stops
looking at the camera their gaze cut to, and the gaze lets go (2 s), the programme goes back to the shot the gaze took
over from (the first, if the look moved from camera to camera), cut `gaze_return`. Only to a shot chosen a short while
ago (it went on air at most `director_gaze_return_seconds`, 20, or 30 with a host, before; timed from when it went on
air, not from the look): after longer the host is talking to their camera, and a split from over a minute before came
back with nothing happening in it. Not when anything else has chosen a shot since (a voice call, the operator, the
recipe's key shot), when the recipe has moved to another step meanwhile, when that shot can no longer be shown, or
after a recording was started. Not before the gaze's shot has had its least time (`director_gaze_min_hold_seconds`).
And not while the camera on air is still the one to show (`Director.gaze_keeps`): the microphones hear whoever it
shows talking, or the model's fresh ratings put it at least `director_ai_margin` (1.5) above every camera of the shot
before; then the old shot is forgotten, the rest of the director chooses, and the recording's log says why it stayed.
A look that ends before the gaze's cut reaches the programme calls that cut off. (2026-11-15: a host looking down at
the work while talking was cut away from to a 25 s old split, and a late cut back flashed on air for 26 ms.)

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Where the performer looks: gaze cuts
sections.text:
**A host's pace** (`gaze.HOST_PACE`, `director_gaze_host_pace`, on by default). Where a host talks to camera (a camera
given a host's role: Host, Co-host, Host / MC, Moderator, Cooking's Host talking to camera; or Creator Studio), the gaze
is quicker, for a back and forth between the host and the shots: looked for three times a second (not twice), a look
cut to on its first confirmed reading (not two), from a score of 0.5 (not 0.55), the cut made 0.8 s before the
programme shows them turning (not 0.4), held at least 1.5 s (not 2.5), let go after 1.5 s looking away (a glance of two
seconds had cut away and straight back), and gone back from after a look of up to 30 s (not 20). Each yields to its own `director_gaze_` setting where one is set.

**Record starts fresh.** Pressing Record forgets every look the gaze has had, the model's last answer, a cut planned and
the shot to go back to, and puts the recipe back before its first step. The recipe follows by itself only while the
programme is recorded (`recipe_needs_recording`, on by default): before that, the model's looks, the kitchen's sounds,
spoken cues and camera calls move no step (a cue says "press Record first"); the operator's own step buttons, and a
phrase typed on the Recipe page to try it, always do.

People (Plus AI) works the same in every kind of event: the people on stage it recognises may be performers or
speakers, under exactly the same consent and privacy rules ([the performer library's privacy](PRIVACY_PERFORMER_LIBRARY.md)).

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Band profiles
sections.text:
A band profile (a service, show, session or production profile in the other kinds of event) is the same thing: a set-up
that comes back the same each time. The kind of event itself is not part of it, since a profile is loaded by an operator
and the kind is the administrator's to choose.

A band that sets up the same way each time is shot the same way each time. A band profile keeps who is where on
stage for the location in use: what each camera shows, each camera's solo zoom, the stage picture, the crowd camera,
the default shot, the zoom choices (each camera's telephoto among them) and the wishes given to the model. It is saved, loaded, saved over, renamed and
removed on the Cameras page (below the cameras' cards), by an operator as well as the administrator.

Loading sets those things to exactly the profile, keeping how they were as a restore point, and leaves the room's
own settings (look-ahead, feed alignment, the model's address) alone. A profile belongs to its location, since it is
written in terms of that location's cameras, and travels with the location when it is exported.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Tracking and zoom switches
sections.text:
The automatic tracking and the automatic zoom switch off and on during a show, apart, for one camera or for every camera
at once, by an operator or the administrator (`camera_manager/autoswitch.py`; `POST /api/auto` with `{"kind": "tracking"
or "zoom", "on": true or false}`, and `camera_id` for one camera). It takes effect at once; nothing restarts.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Tracking and zoom switches
sections.text:
- **Where.** Each camera's card, under its state line: *Tracking* (only for a camera with a gimbal) and *Auto zoom*.
  The Show page, under *Choose shots automatically*: both for every camera, saying which cameras are off on their own.
  **Whole picture** beside *Auto zoom* (on the card, *Whole picture on every camera* on the Show page, *Whole picture*
  in Stage Shots' bar): the whole picture now, gliding there on air, and the zoom switched off so that it stays so, for
  a zoom that has gone wrong (`{"kind": "zoom", "whole": true}`, audit `auto_zoom_whole`).
  The Operate page: *Tracking*, *Auto zoom* and *Whole picture* in its bar for every camera, and on each camera's tile
  for that camera, beside its zoom (amber while off).
  Stage Shots at the dashboard: *Tracking* and *Auto zoom* in its bar, for every camera (not on the Stage Shots page
  offered to phones, whose accounts run shots only). Voice calls too (see [Tracking and zoom said aloud](SOUND_AND_VOICE.md#tracking-and-zoom-said-aloud)).
- **Every camera overrides each camera.** Off for every camera, each is off whatever its own switch; switched on
  again, each camera is as its own switch says. A camera switched on on its own while every camera's is off stays off,
  and the dashboard says why.
- **Tracking off.** The manager stops pointing it at its performer (its follow plan), its phone stops following (which
  stops the gimbal where it points; a turn under way is stopped), and aiming from the stage, the home-position fallback
  when a search gives up, Creator Studio's framing aims and "I'm over here" all leave it alone. The arrows, Home, Set
  home and saved targets still work: they are a person's own choices. **Follow** pressed meanwhile (the card, the
  Operate page's X) is refused with the reason and remembered: it follows when tracking is switched on. A phone found
  following anyway (it reconnected, or was switched on at the phone) is told to stop, at most every 30 s
  (`auto_every_seconds`).

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Tracking and zoom switches
sections.text:
- **Tracking on again.** A camera that was following when it was switched off follows again, by its plan if it was,
  from where it points; one that was not stays where it is and is aimed from the stage again. A camera on a saved
  target waits for "back to me", which then puts it back and follows. Switched on for one camera by itself (its
  card, its Operate tile, or said with its shot call), a phone on a gimbal that was not following starts following
  from where it points, as a network camera's own tracker is started: so the switch does something after the manager
  has restarted, or where Follow was never pressed. The every-camera switch only takes up what was following, so a
  gimbal left still on purpose stays still.
- **Zoom off.** The director's zoom on that camera (the crop of its picture in OBS) stays exactly where it is: a glide
  under way stops where it has got to, the performer is no longer followed, and going on air later does not put it
  back to the whole picture. Its telephoto is not changed either way. So a shot can be **framed by hand in OBS** (the
  source's Edit Transform, or Alt-dragging its edges) and it stays as framed, for a show or while the zoom is being
  tried out. It is the OBS crop alone: the gimbal's tracking and the phone's own zooming while it follows someone
  (keeping them waist up, widening to search) go on, and stop with *Tracking*. Zoom calls aloud, the Operate page's
  zoom and saved targets still zoom the phone. The director keeps looking where people are, so that:

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Tracking and zoom switches
sections.text:
- **Zoom on again** frames from where they are now, at its next look, taking over from a crop set by hand.
- Kept in the settings (`auto_switches`: `{"tracking": {"all": true, "off": [camera ids]}, "zoom": {...}}`), so a
  restart leaves the switches as they were (what each gimbal was doing when switched off is kept only while the
  manager runs). Each change is in the audit log (`auto_switched`, with who, which cameras it changed and any phone
  that did not take it).

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Scene Chat: guiding the director during the show
sections.text:
The model that chooses the shots is told what the operator wants in two parts, and Scene Chat, down the right of the
Show and Stage Shots pages, holds both:

- **The standing brief**: the wishes for the shot that hold all show ("stay on whoever is singing; the drums for fills; a
  wide shot between songs"). It is the same setting as *Your wishes for the shots* on the Director page, kept in the
  installation's settings (and in a band profile), and can be edited from either place.
- **Rolling wishes**, typed into the chat during the show: "more focus on the keyboards", "less on the drums", "stay on
  Drum Cam", "clear". Each goes on top of the brief, newest first, and the model is told that where the two differ the
  newer wishes win. They steer its next look, about a second and a half later.

How they combine, kept small because the model reads them again on every look:

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Scene Chat: guiding the director during the show
sections.text:
- A wish **about the same thing** as an earlier one replaces it: "less on the drums" after "more drums" leaves only the
  newer. "The same thing" is what a camera has been given to show (an instrument, or a role of the kind of event, and
  other names for it such as "keys" or "the drummer"), the audience, or a camera by its name.
- **Sending a wish again.** Every wish you have typed this show has **Again** under it in the chat: press it and the
  same words are sent as a new wish, without typing them a second time. A wish still in force is renewed rather than
  doubled: it becomes the newest and its 15 minutes start over. To change one before sending it, press the up arrow
  in the empty box: it brings back the wish before, and the one before that (the down arrow steps forward again).
- At most **four** wishes are in force; a fifth drops the oldest, and the reply says which.
- Each lasts **15 minutes** unless cleared or replaced first, so a wish for one song does not steer the encore; the chat
  notes when one expires.
- **Clearing**: type "clear" (or "reset", "forget it", "back to the brief") for all of them, "clear the drums" for one
  topic; each wish in force also has its own × and there is *Clear all*. **New show** empties the chat and the wishes
  and keeps the brief.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Scene Chat: guiding the director during the show
sections.text:
**The replies are canned.** The director answers every wish at once ("More on the keyboards.", "Less on the drums.",
"Changing focus: more on the drums.", "Cleared. Back to the brief.") from the wish's own words: the model is never asked
to reply, so the chat costs it no time. Where it is honest to say, a later line reports what came of a wish: the first
cut within three minutes of it, with the reason the director already logs ("Cut to Keys: rated best by the model.").
Replies and the box's example follow the kind of event: "more on the host" for a podcast, "more on the cutting board"
for cooking, "the congregation" at a service.

**Who and where.** The administrator and the operator can both use it, at the PC or on a tablet; it is not on the Stage
Shots page for a phone on the camera network. Over 1180 px wide it sits beside the page and can be shut to a tab at the
right edge; on a tablet it opens over the page from that tab; on a phone it is a sheet from the bottom. The box
to type in is three lines high and grows with what is typed: Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line.

**At No AI** there is no model to tell: the box says plainly that wishes need AI assistance (Standard or Plus) and the
history is still shown. With Standard or Plus but the model not choosing shots, wishes are kept and the reply says they
wait until it is.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Scene Chat: guiding the director during the show
sections.text:
**Kept per show**, in the data folder (`scene-chat.json`, readable by this user only): the wishes in force and the
chat survive a page reload and a manager restart, until *New show*. Like everything else they stay on the production
computer; the wishes reach only the model the director already uses.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Explain the director: captions for demo videos
sections.text:
**Explain the director** (`camera_manager/explain.py`; Director page, off unless switched on, `explain_mode`) lays the
director's decisions over the programme as caption cards, so a video made with it shows what the AI did and why: for
demo videos that prove the idea and show where it stands. OBS's recording and stream carry them, because they are drawn
by the overlay page (`overlay.py`) that OBS has as a browser source on top of every scene; switching the mode on puts
it there, in any kind of event (it was Cooking's alone).

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Explain the director: captions for demo videos
sections.text:
- **What makes a card.** Each cut, with who made it (the AI director, the director's rules, who is talking, where the
  host looks, a voice call, the operator) and its reason, and the zoom and lens it went on air with ("Cut to Stage Left ·
  AI director: the guitarist is soloing and in shot · framed 1.8x"); a solo heard starting and ending; a gimbal camera's
  follow plan turning to someone else ("Stage Right follows · solo: guitar"); a camera kept off air because its gimbal
  lost its person, and its return; a gimbal camera's own tracking, from what its phone reports the moment it changes
  ("Stage Right is tracking", "…is tracking by their body", "…found them again", "…operator aiming"), and aiming from
  the stage turning it towards where the wide shot sees them, each once it has held a second and at most every 6 s a
  camera; a telephoto change made off air, or one that did not come up; a voice call acted on,
  with what was heard. Only what happens after it is switched on: never a backlog.
- **Spotlights.** While nothing else is showing, every 45 s (`explain_spotlight_seconds`, 0 for none) a card on one of the
  features in use, in turn: the AI director, performer recognition, listening to the band, automatic framing, gimbals that
  follow, face blur on the phone, voice calls, phones as cameras.
- **On screen.** At most three cards at once, newest at the bottom, each for 7 s (`explain_seconds`, 3 to 20), in the top
  left (or top right, or bottom left: `explain_position`), coloured by kind, fading in and out. In Cooking they always
  take the top corner away from the recipe card, whichever side it is on, so they never cover the recipe or a step
  popping up. What happened in real life (a call heard, a phone's gimbal, a lens change) is shown as the programme
  reaches it, the sync keeper's hold later (at most 10 s; `explain_follow_programme`), so it no longer comes up before
  what it explains; a cut, made as the programme shows it, at once.

sections.doc: The director: how shots are chosen, zoomed and cut
sections.title: Explain the director: captions for demo videos
sections.text:
- **Privacy.** Never a performer's name: their instrument or role, and camera names. What was said aloud is shown as heard,
  which the audience heard anyway.
- The Director page's panel has the switch, the timings and corner, whether OBS has the overlay, and the last captions;
  `GET`/`POST /api/explain`.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.text: Back to [the manager's README](../README.md).

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Stage Shots
sections.text:
A page for calling shots by hand during the show, laid out like a stage plot and read from the stage outward. Where the
buttons stand is set up on [Stage layout](#stage-layout); until that is done (no button placed and no camera on the room
map) the page says "Cameras are in a default row. Set up the stage layout.", with a link. It works at the PC, on a
tablet logged in as the operator, and on a phone on the camera network with the Stage Shots passcode (the switch that
offers it to phones, and the passcode, are at the foot of the page, for the administrator). Offered to phones, it is
also at `https://stageshots.mcvsaid.local`, with no port to type (see [Who can log in](SECURITY.md#who-can-log-in)).

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Stage Shots
sections.text:
- **Rows.** At the top, a button for each camera on one performer or instrument, placed where it stands, from the back
  of the stage to the front. Under them, the wide (whole band) shots, across the full width. At the bottom, under
  "Front of stage", the crowd camera, as the audience sits in front of the stage. Which row a camera is in comes from
  what it shows (Cameras › What it shows; the crowd camera from the Director page), not from where it was dragged.
- **Left and right are the performers'.** Stage left is on the performers' left as they face the audience: the right
  of the page. The page says so at the top (Stage right · house left, Stage left · house right) and marks SR and SL at
  the sides, so "the stage-left camera" means the same to the band, the crew and the page.
- **Width is framing.** A tight shot of one player is a narrow button and the whole band a wide one. Each kind of shot
  has a default (one performer or instrument 18% of the stage, wide shots and the crowd the full width), which the
  administrator changes on Stage layout (*Default widths*); any camera can have its own width, and a height of its own (1 to
  4 times the usual, never less than its words need). On a phone a button is never
  narrower than a thumb (about 92 px), and buttons that would cover each other are eased apart as shown, without
  changing what is saved.
- **The camera mark.** A small dot on each button's edge, with a wedge opening from it, shows where the camera stands,
  which way it points and how wide it sees: the same wedge as on the room map, a sliver for a telephoto and a broad fan
  for an ultrawide. A stage-left camera shooting across the stage is told from a stage-right one at a glance. Faint
  while shots are called.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Stage Shots
sections.text:
- **What each camera sees, across the stage.** For the cameras on the room map, their wedges from the map are drawn
  across the performers' stage too, in each camera's colour (the same as on the map, and its button's mark), only the
  part of each that falls on the stage: faint and dashed, and the camera on air (or, on Stage layout, the one pressed)
  filled. The map's stage is stretched to the page's, so a wedge covers the same performers here as there. For a camera on the room map (below) the mark always follows the map; otherwise it is set on
  Stage layout, or stands in front of the button pointing up at the stage.
- **Programme and next.** The camera on air has a red border and says ON AIR (as a vision mixer's tally); the cut the
  director has decided and is waiting to make is green and says NEXT; the first camera picked for a split is amber.
  Every state is said in words as well as colour, and the line above the stage names them.
- **Room view** (at the manager's dashboard, on a screen at least 720 px wide): the buttons and the room map in one
  picture. The room is drawn from above. The performers' buttons stand on its stage where the performers do, the
  wide shots are in a row along the front of the stage, and the crowd camera's button is out in the house. Each camera
  is drawn as a dot with its wedge, and each button is striped in its camera's colour to find them by. Pressing a
  button puts it on air as usual; nothing is moved here. Each browser remembers whether Room view is on. The phone version keeps the plain
  buttons, which are bigger to press.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Stage layout
sections.text:
Under **Set up**: where the cameras and the people they show stand, set up once for each place and each band, and what
Stage Shots lays its buttons out from. It is at the manager's dashboard only (`/stage-layout`: the PC, or the operator's
tablet), and has four parts, in the order they are best done:

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Stage layout
sections.text:
1. **Start from the wide shot** (experimental): one button, *Place cameras from the wide shot*, has the manager find
   each camera's picture in the wide camera's and place and size its button from that. It is a first guess to check:
   nothing changes until it is applied, it can be undone, and where it cannot run (or finds nothing) the parts below do
   the same by hand. See [Placing cameras from the wide shot](#placing-cameras-from-the-wide-shot-experimental).
2. **Room map**: where each camera stands in the room and which way it points (below).
3. **Arrange the buttons by hand**: the same picture of the stage as on Stage Shots, with everything in it draggable.
   Drag a button to where its camera's subject stands, drag any of its four corner
  handles to resize it (the opposite corner stays where it is), drag the camera mark round its edge (it turns to face the button's middle; fine-tune with the
  eight directions or the exact angle). For a camera on the room map the mark is the map's: pressing its button
  offers turns of 5 and 15° (they turn it on the map) and *Show it on the room map*. Press a button to set its size and mark exactly, or put either back to the
  default. Each change is saved as it is let go. Wide and crowd buttons are dragged along their row to change the
  order. The administrator's *Default widths* are under it.
4. **The set**: this kind of event's own map under the room map's cameras (below).

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Stage layout
sections.text:
On a phone (375 px) and a tablet each part is the full width and they follow one another down the page. The room map
has no smallest size, but under about 560 px of map only the chosen camera is named on it, and the page says so:
cameras are chosen from the list under the map. Dragging works by touch at any width.

Before this page (to 2026-11) these were on Stage Shots, behind its Arrange button; what is saved, and the requests
that save it, are the same, so a layout set up there is here unchanged. The phone version of Stage Shots chooses shots
and no longer arranges.

Saved in the settings and kept with each location (the layout in band profiles too): `stage_layout` gives each camera id any of
`x`/`y` (its place, 0 to 1 from house left and from the back of the stage), `w` (its width, 0.08 to 1 of the stage),
`h` (its height, 1 to 4 times the usual) and `cam` (`{"at": 0 to 1 clockwise round the edge from the top left, "aim": degrees clockwise from up the page}`);
`stage_widths` holds the administrator's defaults for `single`, `wide` and `crowd`. A layout saved before widths and
marks keeps its places and gets the defaults. `POST /api/stage` with `{"layout": {id: {field: value or null}}}` changes
one camera field by field (null puts that field back to its default); `{"widths": {...}}` is the administrator's only.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The room map
sections.text:
Stage layout's **Room map** shows the room from above, to lay out once while setting up: the stage at the top with SR and
SL marked, the house below with house left and house right, as the buttons have them. Each camera is a coloured dot
with an arrowhead the way it points and a wedge for what it sees.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The room map
sections.text:
- **Place and aim.** Drag a camera to where it stands. Drag the round handle in front of it to turn it; it settles on
  a multiple of 15° when within 4° of one. Press a camera, or its name in the list beside the map, to set its aim
  exactly: a dial, a number in degrees, and ±1° and ±15° steps. With the keyboard, Tab to a camera; the arrow keys
  move it and Shift with an arrow key turns it. Cameras not on the map yet are listed beside it, each put on with a
  press (in the middle of the house, pointing at the stage). "Take it off the map" removes one again. On a narrow
  screen only the chosen camera is named on the map; the list names them all.
- **What it sees.** The wedge's angle is worked out from the lens in use and the phone's zoom. A phone that reports
  its lens's focal length and sensor width (the camera app does from 0.9.19) gives it exactly: twice the
  arctangent of half the sensor's width over the focal length. Otherwise the angle is typical for the lens: about 70° for a main
  lens, and each other lens by how much tighter or wider the phone says it is (about 100 to 110° for a 0.5 to 0.6x
  ultrawide, 27 to 39° for a 2 to 3x telephoto). A digital zoom narrows it by the same rule: 2x makes 70° about 39°.
  The panel says which angle is used and why. The administrator can set a camera's angle by hand (2 to 170°), for a
  phone in a case, an add-on lens or anything else the phone cannot know, and put it back to the lens's.
- **What Stage Shots takes from it.** Each button's camera mark follows from where its camera stands relative to what
  the button shows: a performer where the button is placed, the whole stage for a wide shot, the house for the crowd.
  The mark sits on the side of the button nearest the camera and points the way the camera does. Where the wedge
  crosses the stage at that depth it gives a width; the button's panel offers it ("Use the room map's 24% wide") rather than
  changing a button by itself, and a width set by hand stays. The mark always follows the map: one set earlier by
  hand is kept, and comes back if the camera is taken off the map.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The room map
sections.text:
- **Height and tilt (optional).** A camera can also be given its height (metres above the floor the performers stand
  on) and its tilt (degrees, up positive, down negative, 0 level). The map then draws what it really sees of the floor
  in place of the flat wedge: its picture's frame cut by the floor, a long trapezoid for a camera tilted a little down
  and a closed patch for one pointing steeply down. With a height and tilt, the panel shows **a side view**: the camera
  at its height, what it sees up and down, and a performer 1.7 m tall in the middle of the stage. *Back to a flat wedge*
  takes them off. Heights are in metres, so the map has a **width in metres**: the set's when its layout has one
  (from its scale), otherwise set in the panel (*Map width*), otherwise a guess of 12 m, which the panel says. A camera
  without a height and tilt is drawn and used exactly as before; Stage Shots' marks and widths still come from the
  flat wedge.
- **Expand, and check against the picture.** *Expand* (on the map's corner) opens the map over the whole window, and
  Esc or *Close the big map* closes it; on a phone the map and the panel follow one another down. Dragging, turning
  and the panel work as ever. On Stage layout, with a camera chosen, its picture now is shown beside the map (from
  OBS, as a set's photos are; *New picture* takes another), with where the map says the stage's corners are drawn
  on it: an outline for a camera with a height and tilt, otherwise upright lines where its wedge's sides say the front
  corners are. If they sit on the real corners, the camera is placed right.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The room map
sections.text:
- **Fit it from the picture** (`roomfit.py`). *Mark the corners*, then press each corner of the stage (or the set's
  main area) in the picture as asked: front left, front right (left and right as the map has them: the map's left is
  stage right), back left and back right (each back one can be skipped if it is hidden). *Work it out*: with all four,
  the manager works out the camera's place, height, aim, tilt (and roll, when clear) from where they are in the
  picture, the floor being a plane; with two or three, the camera stays where the map has it and only its aim is
  worked out, the corners' bearings from it less how far across the picture each is (and how far apart they are says
  whether the place or the lens is off). The result is drawn dashed on the map and written out with any doubts;
  *Use this* saves it as any change to the map, *Not this* leaves the map as it was. Nothing changes until then. The
  field of view is the lens's unless four corners clearly fit another much better (a zoom it did not report): then
  theirs is offered, and taken only by the administrator. Looking steeply down, the corners cannot tell the field of
  view, so the lens's is always used: set it first if the camera is zoomed. On synthetic cameras with the corners
  clicked up to about 5 pixels out in a picture 960 across (`tests/test_roomfit.py`: level at the back of the house,
  tilted down 20°, 3 m up over a table pointing steeply down, and nearly straight down over the stage) the place came
  within about 0.3 m nine times in ten and the height within 0.3 m; it is only as good as the clicks and the map's
  width in metres. Not yet tried with a real camera at a real venue.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The room map
sections.text:
- **Who.** Anyone logged in to the manager's dashboard, the operator's tablet included, can place and
  turn cameras, give their heights and tilts, and fit them from their pictures; the field of view is the administrator's. The phone version of Stage Shots shows the marks that
  follow from the map but cannot change the map.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The room map
sections.text:
Saved as `stage_room`: each camera id has `x` and `y` (where it stands, 0 to 1 from house left and from the back wall
of the stage to the back of the house), `aim` (degrees clockwise from up the page, as the marks) and, when the
administrator set it, `fov` (degrees across); optionally `height` (metres, 0 to 30), `tilt` (degrees, -90 to 90) and
`roll` (degrees, clockwise as the camera looks). The map's own width is `stage_room_width_m` (a set layout keeps its
`width_m`). The room is drawn 0.8 times as deep as it is wide, with the stage from
12% to 88% across and reaching 36% of the way down. It is kept with each location, travels with exported settings,
and is cleared for a camera that is removed. It is not part of a band profile: where the cameras stand belongs to the
room, not the act. `POST /api/stage` with `{"room": {id: {"x", "y", "aim", "fov", "height", "tilt", "roll"}}}` changes a
camera field by field: a camera is first put on the map with `x`, `y` and `aim` together, `x` and `y` set to null take
it off, `fov` set to null goes back to the lens's angle, and `height`, `tilt` or `roll` set to null take them off.
`{"room_width_m": metres or null}` sets the plain map's width. `POST /api/stage/room/fit` with `{"camera": id,
"points": {"front_left": [across, down], ...}, "aspect": width over height}` (the corners as shares of the picture)
answers what the corners say (`method` corners or bearings, `proposal`, `error`, `fov_from`, `notes`) and saves
nothing.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The set: each kind of event's own map
sections.text:
A concert has a stage; a cooking show has a counter, a stove and a prep table; a podcast a table with microphones.
Under the room map's cameras (**The set**, at the foot of Stage layout), each kind of event at a location can have
a set of its own. Without one the room map is the plain stage, as above.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The set: each kind of event's own map
sections.text:
- **A map from photos.** The quickest way to a true map of a set. Take a photo or two of it from where its floor can
  be seen (any phone; high and well back is best), or press **Use what it sees** to take what a camera here sees now.
  In the first photo press four points on the floor round something whose size you know, far left, far right, near
  right, near left: the corners of a rug or a run of floor tiles, tape marks put down for it, the foot of a riser or a
  counter. Give its width and depth in metres and press **Straighten**: the photo is turned into a view from above,
  and the map is to scale. A further photo is joined on by pressing four points in it and the same four on the map so
  far; where photos overlap each spot is taken from the photo that sees it closest. **Trim to a box** keeps the part
  that matters, and **Use this map for the set** keeps it. It is all done in the browser: the photos are never sent
  to the manager, only the map made from them. How: a flat floor seen in perspective is the same floor seen from
  above through one 3x3 matrix (a homography), fixed by four points; each photo's is solved from the points pressed,
  and the map is drawn back through it. Its limits: only the floor's level is true. Anything above it (a counter top,
  a person, a lamp) leans away from where the photo was taken, so a counter's foot is in the right place and its top
  looks stretched; mark floor points, not a table top. The map reaches only as far as the floor is seen clearly (at
  most twice the reference's size round it, and nowhere one pixel of the photo covers nine times the floor it does at
  the reference). Lens distortion is not corrected: phones correct their main lens themselves, but an ultrawide's
  straight lines bend near its edges. Tested with made-up photos of the demonstration's made-up kitchen: two photos from
  different sides, joined, came back 6.0 by 4.8 m, as drawn.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The set: each kind of event's own map
sections.text:
- **Measured on a phone (AR).** No reference to measure: in the camera app, disarmed, **Measure the set (AR)** opens
  the camera with ARCore (Google Play Services for AR), which finds the floor as a plane in real metres. Aim the circle
  at each corner of the set's floor in turn and press **Mark point**: each side is shown on the screen along the floor
  in metres, so it doubles as a tape measure. Then **Take photo** from where the audience is, and more from other sides
  (up to six), and **Send to manager**. Each photo goes with where its pixels are on the floor (its homography, worked
  out on the phone from ARCore's pose of the camera and its lens), all in one frame: on The set, *Map from photos*
  offers "*phone* measured the set at *time*", and **Use these** straightens and joins them with no points to press,
  the four marks drawn as the outline. The phone's photos pass through the manager: sent over the pairing's pinned
  HTTPS connection from the camera network, checked and cleaned as kept pictures are (a JPEG only, what is not the
  picture taken out), held in memory only (never in the data folder), the latest measuring of each phone, forgotten
  after 30 minutes or once the dashboard has taken them. The same limits as photos marked by hand: only the floor is
  true, and the map reaches as far as the floor is seen clearly. ARCore's own: it needs a floor with some texture
  (a plain glossy or black stage floor, or a dark one, may not be found; tape or a rug helps) and light, and drifts by
  a few centimetres over several metres. ARCore takes the camera for itself, so it will not open while the camera is
  armed, and closes if the camera is armed meanwhile. **Not yet tried on the phones**: the floor's maths is checked
  (`ConcertCamera/tools/tests/FloorMathTest.java`), and the dashboard's side with made-up photos of the demonstration's
  kitchen (6.0 by 4.8 m, as drawn), but not ARCore on a Pixel or the S23.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The set: each kind of event's own map
sections.text:
- **A floor plan.** A picture (PNG or JPEG, up to 15 MB and 40 million pixels) or a PDF (up to 25 MB and 50 pages,
  and the page to use). The map takes the plan's shape. A picture is drawn afresh in the browser first (turned as it
  was taken), and every picture is checked again and cleaned on the manager: only PNG and JPEG are kept, and what is
  not the picture is taken out (EXIF with a phone's GPS place, comments, text, colour profiles). A PDF is never kept:
  its page is drawn into a PNG on the manager by PDFium (pypdfium2), in a process of its own run in Python's isolated
  mode, given the file on its input and limited in memory (1 GB, where the system enforces it: Linux), processor time
  and open files, killed after 30 seconds; PDFium as pypdfium2 ships it has no JavaScript engine and no XFA forms, and
  the page is drawn without its form fields, so nothing in the file runs. Then mark two points a known distance
  apart (**Scale**) to put it to scale.
- **Templates and shapes.** **Start from a template** gives each kind of event's usual set as shapes to move and size
  (a concert stage with a drum riser, a platform and lectern, a podcast table with four microphones, a panel table, a
  theatre stage, a kitchen counter, stove and prep table, a studio desk, a karaoke stage), or a blank floor. Shapes are
  stages, risers, counters, stoves, prep tables, tables (square or round), microphones, audience, screens and named
  zones; drag one to move it and its corner to size it, and rename, retype or remove it in the list. Over a plan or a
  photo map they are drawn as outlines.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The set: each kind of event's own map
sections.text:
- **The main area.** One shape is where the shots are (ticked *Main*, else the first stage, counter or table): the
  room map's measures are taken against it in place of the plain stage. Stage Shots' buttons stand on it, its middle
  is what a gimbal is aimed at for **Set** (calibrate after changing the kind of event if the main area moved), and
  the wide shot is read across it.
- **Cameras and targets.** A set has its own room map: the cameras are where they stand for this kind of event (they
  start where the location's room map has them), and moving one moves it in this set only. Saved gimbal targets ("show
  the pot", see [Saved gimbal targets](GIMBALS.md#saved-gimbal-targets)) can be put on the map where they are.
- **Who.** An operator or the administrator, at the manager's dashboard. Not the phone version of Stage Shots.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The set: each kind of event's own map
sections.text:
Saved as `set_layouts`: `{kind of event: {depth, width_m, shapes, background, cameras, targets, template}}` (see
`camera_manager/setlayout.py`). Pictures are kept apart, in the data folder's `set_pictures`, named by their SHA-256,
so the same picture is kept once however many layouts and restore points use it. Layouts travel with the location's
settings, and **a location file carries their pictures** too (each checked and cleaned again when it is brought in, and
left out if it is not the picture its name says); a settings file carries the layouts without their pictures.
`POST /api/stage/set` with `{"use": kind or "blank"}`, `{"remove": true}`, or any of `shapes`, `depth`, `width_m`,
`scale` (`{"a": [x, y], "b": [x, y], "metres"}`), `background: null` and `targets` (`{"camera id/target id": {"x", "y"}
or null}`), with `mode` for another kind of event; `POST /api/stage/set/background?kind=image|pdf|photos&page=&width_m=&photos=&depth=`
with the file as the body; `GET /api/stage/set/picture/{sha256}`; a phone's measuring (`camera_manager/setmeasure.py`):
`POST /set/measured` on the agents' port, from a paired phone on the camera network
(`{"photos": [{"jpeg", "to_floor"}], "reference", "taken_ms"}`), listed as `measured` in `/api/stage`'s `room.set`
(not on the phone page), `GET /api/stage/set/measured/{camera id}/{n}` and `DELETE /api/stage/set/measured/{camera id}`; `GET /api/stage/set/grab/{camera id}` (a camera's
picture now, from OBS; `?width=` 160 to 1920 for a smaller one, as the Show page's thumbnails ask).

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The set: each kind of event's own map
sections.text:
**Could the system make the map by itself, from photos?** What was looked at, and why the four-point photo map is what
was built:

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: The set: each kind of event's own map
sections.text:
- *A top-down map from a photo or the wide camera's own frame, through four marked floor points* (built). Needs nothing
  new: a phone, or a camera already in place, and a known size on the floor. Seconds of work, exact on the floor's
  level, wrong above it.
- *Finding the floor points by itself* (not built). The four points could be found as the corners of a printed marker
  (an ArUco or AprilTag sheet of known size laid on the floor) with OpenCV, already an optional package
  (requirements-people.txt). It would save four presses; a sheet must be printed and put down, and the corners pressed
  by hand are as good.
- *Several phone photos with structure from motion* (COLMAP and similar; not built). A real 3D model of the set, things
  above the floor included. Heavy: 30 to 100 overlapping photos, minutes to an hour of processing on a GPU, a large
  install, a scale still to be given, and failures on plain walls and shiny counters. Too much for a map whose job is
  where things are on the floor.
- *ARCore's floor* (built, as *Measured on a phone* above). The Pixels and the Galaxy S23 have no depth
  (time-of-flight or LiDAR) sensor; ARCore runs on both and finds the floor as a plane in real metres. Used for what
  the photo map lacked, a scale and the joins with no reference, and nothing more: the map is still the photos
  straightened. A step of its own in the camera app before the show, since ARCore takes the camera for itself.
  Not used: its Depth API (depth from the phone moving), which could outline what stands on the floor.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Placing cameras from the wide shot (experimental)
sections.text:
The first part of Stage layout sizes and places the buttons from the cameras' own pictures, and can suggest
who each performer's camera shows. Choose the camera
that shows the whole band and press **Place cameras from the wide shot** (**Look again** after the first look). Over about 15 seconds it takes every camera's picture from OBS five
times. Each time, it looks for where each camera's picture is inside the wide camera's picture. It then draws what it
found as outlines over the wide picture and lists each camera with how much of the stage it takes in and where. A
camera is placed only when at least 3 of the 5 looks found it and agreed; otherwise it says why not. Nothing changes
until **Apply to the ticked cameras**, and **Undo** puts the buttons back. With the wide camera on the room map, places
are measured along its line of sight from where it stands; without it, the wide picture is taken to span the stage.
Where both cameras are on the room map, it also offers a new aim for the other camera, unticked: it is less sure of
the aim than of the place. Where a camera stands is not worked out.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Placing cameras from the wide shot (experimental)
sections.text:
- **On the performers.** With the person detector (Plus AI), the people in the wide picture are found as well. A
  performer's camera that shows one of them puts its button on that person: across the stage where they stand, and
  down it by where their feet are compared with the other performers' (lower in the wide picture means nearer the
  front). That depth is rough. It only puts the performers in order from back to front, and is left alone when fewer
  than two are found or they stand in a line. Everyone found is outlined faintly on the wide picture, and a camera's
  performer in its colour. Without the detector, a button goes where the middle of its camera's picture is and keeps
  its place down the stage. It works best from a look taken at soundcheck, with everyone at their spot.
- **Who is who.** With a vision model set up for choosing shots (Director page), each performer's camera is asked what
  the person in its own picture plays, from what the kind of event offers. It uses the camera's own close picture,
  because across a wide shot a performer is too few pixels to tell instruments apart. Drums, keyboards and singers
  should be the easiest. A guitar and a bass look alike (a bass usually has four strings, a longer neck and a bigger
  body), so unless the model is at least 75% sure, it asks "guitar or bass?" with a button for each. A suggestion is
  shown beside what the camera is set to show now, and changes it only when pressed. A suggestion the camera already
  shows is just confirmed, so a camera given two things is never cut down to one. It has not been tried on concert
  pictures yet.

sections.doc: Stage Shots, Stage layout and the room map
sections.title: Placing cameras from the wide shot (experimental)
sections.text:
It is **experimental** and labelled so. On test pictures (no concert footage yet), cameras that see part of what the
wide camera sees were found almost every time, and their places were steady to within about half a percent of the
stage's width. A camera seeing something else was never placed. It usually finds nothing for a camera more than about
45° round from the wide camera, a tight telephoto on someone moving, a dark or out-of-focus picture, or the audience.
Once in a while it puts a camera in the wrong place, most often next to repeating things like a lighting rig, so check
each outline before applying. It needs OpenCV (`requirements-people.txt`); without it, the panel says so. The manager
asks OBS for the pictures at full size and compares them on this computer. The results are not saved: `GET` and
`POST /api/stage/place` (`{"wide": camera id}`) and `GET /api/stage/place/picture`. Applying places uses `POST
/api/stage`, and a who-is-who suggestion uses `POST /api/director` with `camera_focus`.

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.text: Back to [the manager's README](../README.md). The gimbals these pages steer are in [Gimbals](GIMBALS.md).

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Operate: live cameras and Xbox controllers
sections.text:
The **Operate** page (Show group, for the administrator and operators alike) shows the cameras chosen there live and
lets a person steer them, for a gimbal camera that needs a human hand on it. It works from a tablet logged in as the
operator, at `https://operate.mcvsaid.local` once the dashboard is offered on the camera network (see
[Who can log in](SECURITY.md#who-can-log-in)).

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Operate: live cameras and Xbox controllers
sections.text:
- **A network PTZ camera too.** A camera taken into OBS over NDI has a tile here: its picture as OBS has it, and,
  once its card has its control address, the same stick, arrows, triggers and zoom buttons, **Stop camera**, **Go
  home** and **Set home**, **Tracking** on or off (its own tracker) and its presets as Positions. See
  [By hand, on the Operate page](NETWORK.md#network-cameras-over-ndi). A camera added since you chose *Cameras shown*
  is shown without being ticked; untick it to leave it out.
- **Positions, set up before the show.** Under each gimbal camera's picture, its saved targets for the kind of event
  chosen (the same ones as *Saved targets* on its card, Remote's keys and voice calls): aim and zoom it with the live
  picture, then **Save as…** and give it a name. Each position shows its angles and zoom, with **Go** (turn there and
  zoom, to check; asks first while the camera is on air), **Update to here** (where it points now and its zoom kept in
  its place, under its own name and phrases: `{"action": "update", "id"}` to `/api/cameras/{id}/gimbal-targets`),
  **Rename** and **Delete**. On a controller, hold **Menu** (≡) and press **A**, **B**, **X** or **Y** to go to positions
  1 to 4, or the **left stick** to save a new one (named *Position N*, renamed under the picture). A position saved
  before the phone restarted its rotation sensor no longer lines up, and says so, unless the camera is aimed from the
  stage (Stage layout), which carries it across, or it is aimed where its home was and **Set home** pressed again,
  which brings them all back. A **setup tech** account opens this page too, to set positions from a
  phone or tablet away from the PC: its tiles have the aiming, zoom, Stop gimbal, Home and the Positions, read from
  `GET /api/operate/cameras` (each camera's name, zoom and gimbal, and which is on air; nothing else of
  `/api/cameras`), and nothing that cuts, arms, streams, records, follows or changes the bar's settings. The way back
  from a target and a spot remembered live stay the show's. Not yet tried on a real gimbal from this page.

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Operate: live cameras and Xbox controllers
sections.text:
- **Every camera at once.** **Arm all cameras** and **Start all camera streams** in the bar (administrator and
  operators; not a setup tech) are the Show page's *All cameras* actions, with the same rules (`fleet.js`, shared by
  both pages): for every camera in use here, not only those shown, each with how many it would touch. Each first asks,
  listing the cameras it will touch and those it leaves out and why (offline, not armed, or not device owner so it
  must be armed on the phone); Start all camera streams sets any clock that is off first and shows each camera's
  readiness in the question. They are sent a third of a second apart, and what was done, and any failure, is said
  under the page. Arming never starts recording, and starting a camera's stream is not **Start OBS stream**. Not yet
  tried on real phones from this page.
- **Without a controller.** *On-screen controls* (kept in the browser) puts arrows under each picture that aim its
  gimbal while held, a stop, and zoom − / + while held, sent as a controller's readings are (`/api/operate/control`).
  **Reset zoom** on a tile left zoomed in puts it back to 1x, gliding on a phone that zooms by itself, and keeps 1x on
  the phone. **Record programme** and **Start OBS stream** in the top bar are the Show page's programme recording and
  OBS stream, with their running times; stopping either asks first.
- **Tracking and Auto zoom** (see [Tracking and zoom switches](DIRECTOR.md#tracking-and-zoom-switches)): on the bar for every
  camera, with **Whole picture** for a crop zoom gone wrong; on each tile for that camera, beside its zoom. A switch
  that is off is shown in amber. The zoom the triggers and buttons make here is the phone's own and works either way.

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Operate: live cameras and Xbox controllers
sections.text:
- **Live, with no look-ahead.** Each camera's picture comes from the camera relay as it arrives, not from OBS's
  delayed programme: a small JPEG stream (960 wide, 12 a second, about 50 KB each; `operate_width`, `operate_rate`)
  that any browser or tablet shows, decoded by one ffmpeg per camera being watched, stopped about ten seconds after
  the page closes (live.Viewer). It needs the camera relay on. Which cameras are shown is kept in the browser; at
  first, every camera in use, up to six; a camera with no gimbal has zoom, *Put on air* and what it shows.
- **Xbox controllers**, through the browser's Gamepad API (Bluetooth or USB, no driver): the right stick aims the
  gimbal (the further, the faster: a dead zone for stick drift, then a mostly cubic curve, so small pushes make small
  corrections), the right and left triggers zoom in and out on the sensor (a light squeeze creeps, a full one goes from
  1x to 8x in under two and a half seconds, `operate_zoom_speed` = 1.25 doublings a second; in proportion, so 1x to 2x
  feels like 4x to 8x, sent in small steps up to twelve times a second, without waiting for the phone's answer; on a phone with app 0.9.38
  the trigger's rate itself, renewed while held, and the phone glides a frame at a time, handing over to its telephoto on
  the way, `camera.zoom`), **A** puts the camera on
  air, **B** stops the gimbal, **X** switches Follow, **Y** goes back to the previous shot, **View** puts the stage
  shot on air, a **right stick press** sends the gimbal to its home position, **LB/RB** (or the d-pad's left and right)
  change camera, and the d-pad's up and down step **Aim**. **Aim** and **Zoom** on the page's bar (1 to 10, kept on
  each device) set how quick they are: Aim is the most a full push asks of the gimbal (6, the default, is 60% of its
  top speed; the on-screen arrows follow it too), Zoom is the trigger's zoom speed against `operate_zoom_speed` (6 is
  1.6 times it, sent as `zoom_speed`, 0.1 to 5; a phone that glides its own zoom is never asked for more than the 4
  doublings a second it takes, so 10 is 4). A camera's refusal of a reading (not streaming, say) is shown on the
  page's bottom line until a reading works again. The stick is a third straight, two thirds cubic, so a part push moves
  too: the old default (a sixth of the gimbal's speed, mostly cubic) asked under 2% of it for half a push, "incredibly
  slow" on a tablet. Several controllers can drive several cameras; each is shown on its camera's tile.

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Operate: live cameras and Xbox controllers
sections.text:
- **How it reaches the camera.** Ten readings a second while a stick or trigger is held go to
  `POST /api/operate/control`, which never waits for the phone: a gimbal move lasts 0.4 s and is renewed by the next,
  so a dropped controller, tab or network stops the gimbal by itself; letting go sends a stop at once. Moving a gimbal
  this way counts as hands on it, so Follow and the director's gimbal-lost handling leave it to the person.
- **Which lens, and the zoom.** Each tile and each camera card has a chip saying which lens makes the picture and the
  whole zoom ("Telephoto 2.9× lens · zoom 3.3× (1.1× crop)"; `lenses.now`), coloured by lens: from the phone's own report
  each moment with app 0.9.38, which hands over between lenses by itself as it zooms; before, the lens chosen.
- **Less delay.** A stick or trigger first pushed, or moved clearly, is sent at once rather than at the next tenth of a
  second; and the live pictures can be **24 a second** instead of 12 (the page's *Picture* choice, `operate_rate`), for a
  smoother zoom or pan to judge by, at about twice the decoding and network per camera watched.
- **All the live pictures over one connection** (`/api/operate/feeds`, a WebSocket: the camera's id, then its JPEG,
  for each new picture). A browser keeps only six connections to an address, and a picture stream for each camera took
  them all, so nothing else the page asked for got through: on a tablet, Arm reached the camera but the page never
  showed it, and the controller's moves trickled through. Measured on the demonstration manager with six cameras: the
  page's status request had not answered after 8 s; over one connection, 15 to 40 ms.

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Operate: live cameras and Xbox controllers
sections.text:
- **Arm, stream and record on each tile**, for an operator as for the administrator: *Arm* when it is not armed;
  once armed, *Start stream* / *Stop stream*, *Record* / *Stop recording*, and *Disarm* when it is doing neither.
  Stopping asks first, as on the camera card; starting syncs the phone's clock first when it is off. A small **REC**
  in the tile's heading while it records.
- **Its temperature**, small at the right of the heading ("41°"), grey while fine, amber when warm, red when at the
  phone's stop temperature, pulsing when critical (thermal.py's levels); pointed at, it says the trend and how long
  until the phone's stop at this rate.
- **What it shows, on each tile.** The camera card's own *What it shows* (`shows.js`, the same setting in both places):
  its instruments or roles, the solo framing, its microphone channel, its telephoto for tight shots, folded to one line
  until opened. An operator may change it mid-show ("this camera is on the keys now"). In Creator Studio it is the
  framing the camera leads with instead.
- **Follow and home on each tile.** Each gimbal camera's tile has the camera card's own Follow control and follow plan
  (`follow.js`, the same setting in both places), and **Go home** and **Set home**.
- **Main stage and Previous shot** (buttons, and View and Y): the director's default shot, or the shot before the one
  on air, put on air as a person's choice and held as Stage Shots' are (`POST /api/operate/main`, `/previous`).

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Remote keys: programmable buttons on a phone or tablet
sections.text:
The **Remote** page (Show group, for the administrator and operators) is a remote control on a phone or tablet: every
key on one page, as many across as the screen has room for, and each one does its whole job in a single press, with
nothing to choose or confirm. Press a key instead of calling a shot aloud. It is at `https://remote.mcvsaid.local` once
the dashboard is offered on the camera network (the operator's login, as on `operate.mcvsaid.local`), and at `/remote`
on the dashboard. `camera_manager/remotekeys.py` keeps the keys (`remote_keys`, in order), and `static/remote.js` draws
them.

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Remote keys: programmable buttons on a phone or tablet
sections.text:
- **Steps.** A key does one step or several in turn (at most six), as a Stream Deck's Multi Action does: **Put a camera
  on air** (`take`, as a shot chosen by hand), **Turn a gimbal camera to a saved target** (`target`: its angle and its
