  zoom: the *Saved targets* on its card, for the kind of event chosen), **Put a gimbal camera back from its target**
  (`back`, "back to me"), **Turn a gimbal camera home** (`home`), **Automatic choosing** on, off or each in turn
  (`auto`), and **Wait** up to 10 s (`wait`). "The pot" can be: Stage Right to its target *pot*, a wait of 1.5 s while it
  turns, and Stage Right on air; a turn followed straight by a cut to the same camera gets that wait by itself.
- **What a key shows.** A large icon for what it is for: a camera (on air), a crosshair (to a saved target), a return
  arrow (back), a house (home), sparkles (automatic choosing); a small badge on the icon's corner for each other kind of
  step, a red camera for "then on air". Under its label, the camera it moves or puts on air, and a colour of eight. It is
  lit while what it does is so: red *LIVE* for its camera on air, green *THERE* for its gimbal camera on its target,
  yellow *ON* for automatic choosing on. It is faint while it cannot be done, and says why when held or read aloud: its
  camera not connected, no gimbal that can turn to a position (app 0.9.37), no home set, its target saved in another kind
  of event, or saved before the phone restarted its rotation sensor. A phone that can buzz does so at each press.

sections.doc: Operate and Remote: live cameras, Xbox controllers and programmable keys
sections.title: Remote keys: programmable buttons on a phone or tablet
sections.text:
- **Pressing** (`POST /api/remote/press {"key"}`) runs the key as the manager keeps it, never steps sent with the
  press. The steps go in order, and the first that cannot be done stops the rest, so a camera is never put on air before
  it has turned; the page says what was done and what was not. Each press is in the audit log (`remote_key_pressed`).
- **Setting them out.** With no keys yet, *Add a key for each camera* makes one per camera to put it on air. *Edit keys*,
  small at the foot of the page, adds a key, changes or deletes one, and moves one (dragged onto another's place, or
  *Move earlier* and *Move later*). In a target step, *Save where it points now…* saves a new target from the camera's
  aim and zoom, as *Save as target* on its card does. Every change is kept at once (`POST /api/remote {"layout":
  {"keys": [...]}}`, checked whole by `remotekeys.tidy`; at most 32 keys).
- **Not yet.** A real Stream Deck (or Bitfocus Companion) pressing the keys, and keys for the coolers and smart plugs.

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.text: A phone on a Hohem iSteady X3 or MT3, aimed and followed from the dashboard. Pairing gimbals from the dashboard, and the smart plugs that charge them, are in [Keeping the cameras going](KEEPING_CAMERAS_GOING.md); the Operate page and its Xbox controllers in [Operate and Remote](OPERATE_AND_REMOTE.md); switching tracking off live in [the director](DIRECTOR.md#tracking-and-zoom-switches).

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Hohem gimbal
sections.text:
**Hohem gimbal** (app 0.9.19; optional; tried on an X3 on a Pixel 8, the right way up and hung upside down, and
with app 0.9.21 on an MT3). A phone on a Hohem iSteady X3 or MT3 shows it on its card, with its model, and its *Gimbal* fold has arrows to aim the camera: hold one and the
camera turns (Slow, Medium or Fast), let go and it eases to a stop (a third of a second, since app 0.9.21: an MT3
stopped at once jerks). An MT3's AI tracker (app 0.9.24) is shown on the card and in its summary line ("AI
tracking", "AI tracker ready"); while it tracks, the arrows are outlined and the fold warns that they will fight
it. It is started and stopped at the gimbal (a gesture or the trigger), never from the dashboard: Hohem's own app
has no way to either. With app 0.9.27 the fold also has **Follow**: nobody, **the most prominent face**, or (app
0.9.29, Plus AI, an administrator) **a performer by name**: the enrolled, consenting performers recognised now. Choosing
one sets the People page's cameras that follow them (so the director's zoom on that camera follows them too), and
about once a second the manager takes the camera's newest picture from the relay, recognises them as the director
does, and points the phone at their head, but only when the phone is not already on them (following, with them at
its mark, and whom its plan wants unchanged): a point a little old only unsettled a phone that had them. Others see that it follows its performer, never a name. For the face, the phone finds faces in
its own picture (with or without face blur), and since app 0.9.30 people too, so that someone who turns away or is
too far for their face to be found is still followed by their body (the fold says so; it never starts on a body alone,
app 0.9.35), and turns the gimbal to keep that face a little above the middle (on a phone set to 180°, the right way
only since app 0.9.35; Calm, Normal or Quick beside Follow, app 0.9.35; By zoom, app 0.9.44),
calmly and at most at 45% speed; the arrows take over for three seconds whenever they are used, and the fold and the
summary line say whether it is following, looking for someone, has lost them, or has no picture (the camera is not
running). **When the gimbal loses its person** (app 0.9.36 tells the manager the moment following changes): after
1.5 s lost (`director_gimbal_lost_seconds`), or looking for someone after following them, the camera is out of the
director's choosing; if it is on air it comes off at once, whatever the holds and shot lengths, to the camera the
model rates best when its ratings are fresh and worth showing, and otherwise to the default shot (the stage shot).
It is not cut back to until it has been following again for 2 s (`director_gimbal_settle_seconds`). Not while
someone steers it with the arrows, and not a camera a person put on air already lost: that is their call. The card
says when the director is keeping it off air, and each cut's reason says why.

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: The follow plan
sections.text:
**The follow plan** (`gimbalpick.py`; Plus AI, `gimbal_follow_plan`): **Follow → By its follow plan** on the card or
the Operate page. Whom, best first: **a solo** (when *Solos take over* is ticked: while the sound hears an instrument
taking a solo, `listener.soloing`, whoever plays it, from the instruments on their People record ("Guitar", "keys",
"lead vocals" are understood), even if they are not in this camera's list; when nobody enrolled plays it, a gimbal
aimed from the stage is turned to that instrument's Stage Shots button), then **a prominent player** (when *Prominent
players too* is ticked: an instrument at 0.6 or more in the sound for 3 s, `gimbal_prominent_level`; voices are left
out, as a singer is to the fore most of a song), then **its performers in order** (an administrator puts them in order
with ↑, adds and removes them; the list is the People page's cameras that follow them), then **anyone** (when *Anyone
else when none of them is in view* is ticked: the phone's own choice of face, so an unplanned guest who walks on from
the other side is in shot rather than an empty spot). Who is in view comes from both the camera's own picture and the
wide shot (seen in the last 2.5 s), so both ways of aiming agree. It stays on someone at least 4 s before a better
choice takes over (a solo, already heard for seconds before it is called one, takes over at once), and 2 s more after a
solo or prominent part ends. A gimbal aimed from the stage that is following someone else while its plan wants another
person it sees well away in the wide shot is turned to them. The arrows and controllers win: nothing is sent while
the phone says someone is aiming it by hand. The card and the tile say why it is on whom it is ("on: solo: guitar ·
Ravi Moss seen 0.6 s ago"). An operator may tick what takes over and start or stop it; whom, by name, is an
administrator's (`POST /api/cameras/{id}/gimbal-plan`).

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: The zoom frames whom the plan is on
sections.text:
**The zoom frames whom the plan is on** (the plan's *The zoom frames whom it follows*, on unless unticked): while a
gimbal camera follows by its plan, the director's zoom (`director.pick_planned`) frames the soloist, the next in its
order, or for anyone, whoever is nearest the middle of its picture (where the phone keeps the face it follows), enrolled
or not, rather than choosing by itself (a listed performer, then a star).

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Home position
sections.text:
**Home position** (app 0.9.37's `gimbal.point`, `gimbal_home`): **Set home** keeps where the gimbal points now, and
its zoom (`zoom_percent`; **Go home** puts the zoom back as a saved target does, over `gimbal_target_zoom_seconds`; a
home set before zooms were kept has none and leaves the zoom alone). Where it points is read (from
the phone's rotation sensor, read once it has come to rest: a stop that finds it still turning is followed by a
second `gimbal_settle_seconds`, default 0.7, later, as for a saved target and a stage Set); **Go home** stops following (or following would steer it off again) and turns it back
there; a camera that was following (or was before a saved target it was on) follows again from home once it has got
there and its picture is checked, by its plan if it was (`gimbal_home_following` in the audit log). Anything else
that moves it first (the arrows, a stop, a saved target, Follow on its card) keeps it from following again, and with
its tracking switched off it follows again only when tracking is switched on. On the card, the Operate page's tiles, and a controller's right-stick press. The phone's angles start afresh when
it restarts its sensor, so after that it asks to be set again (`POST /api/cameras/{id}/gimbal-home`). Aim it where
its home was and Set home: how far the pan moved is how far the sensor's zero moved, so every saved target from the old
home's session, in every kind of event, is turned by the same and lines up again (the answer's `restored` says how
many; the tilt is from gravity and needs nothing). Not yet tried on a real gimbal.
A camera app from 0.9.60 to 0.9.65 moved that zero by itself, with no restart and the same session, at every turn to a
position (its sensor's rate changed, and a Galaxy S23+ starts the pan afresh at that), so its home and positions went
wrong within minutes and nothing here could tell; app 0.9.66 listens at one rate and they hold. Set home and save the
positions again after updating it. From app 0.9.67 a turn to a position stops within 0.5° of it (it was 1.5°) and is
checked once at rest.

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Find home
sections.text:
**Find home** (`matchhome.py`, with OpenCV from `requirements-people.txt`) does the same from the picture, with nobody
aiming it. As a home is set or a position saved, the room it sees is kept as a view: the features found in a fresh
picture (the phone's own snapshot, else the relay's; OBS's is too late), with the pan, tilt and sensor session they
were taken at and how wide it saw. Only the features are kept, never a picture, in the data folder's
`gimbal-views/<camera id>/`; a view goes with its home or position (`gimbal_room_views: false` keeps none). After a
restart the card and Operate offer **Find home** (`POST /api/cameras/{id}/gimbal-home` `{"action": "find"}`): the
camera stops (and stops following), zooms out to 1x, and two pictures a moment apart are matched against its views.
The camera only turned, never moved, so the fit is a pure turn through its lens; it is believed only when 25 or more
features agree with it, the turn redrawn lands within 5 % of the fit, and the two pictures agree within 0.6°. It
turns to the view it matched, measures what is left close up and takes that off, carries home, positions and views
across, ends at home and puts its zoom back. On air it is refused unless confirmed (`"on_air": true`): the audience
sees it move. Measured on made-up rooms turned by known angles: within 0.3° up to 25° round, and 0.5° with the lens
guessed 10 % wrong; another room and a blank wall are not found. Not yet tried on a real gimbal or in a dark room:
what autoplace.py found for matching holds here too (nothing in the dark, out of focus or on repeating truss).

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: The picture check
sections.text:
**The picture check** (`Manager.picture_check`, the same views): the angles a turn closes on are the phone's rotation
sensor's, whose pan drifts slowly over a show, so a turn that stops within 0.5° of them can still be a degree or two
off the place itself. After **Home** or a turn to a saved position (Go, a remote key, a call aloud), once the phone
says it has arrived and its zoom has got there, its picture is matched against the view kept there (the same tests
as Find home), at the lens's width at that zoom. Within 0.5° it is left alone (the phone would not move for less);
0.5° to `gimbal_picture_check_most_deg` (3°) off, it is turned onto the view and looked at again, and put back if
that left it further off; further than that it is not believed enough to turn by itself, and said. Not turned on air
(`gimbal_picture_check_on_air: true` allows it); a target called aloud is cut to once its check has ended
(`gimbal_picture_check_cut_seconds`, 4 s at most). Anything else that moves the gimbal (the arrows, Stop, following,
another turn) ends a check under way. The card says how the last went (how far off, which way, what was left); the
audit has `gimbal_picture_checked`. `gimbal_picture_check: false` switches it off; a home or position saved without
a view (no OpenCV, no fresh picture) is not checked. Measured on made-up rooms with the sensor drifted 2° in pan and
1° in tilt: back within 0.3° of the place. Not yet tried on a real gimbal or in a real room.

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Aiming from the stage
sections.text:
**Aiming from the stage** (`stageaim.py`, app 0.9.37; Set and Centre stage tried on an MT3, 2026-10-23: back within
0.7° after a 110° turn away, in 3.7 s; the aiming from a live wide shot not yet tried): coarse from the manager, fine on
the phone. About once a second (`gimbal_stage_every_seconds`) the manager finds the people in the wide camera's
picture (the one given the whole band, a wide shot or a group; the person detector, Plus AI, and the relay), places
them on the room map along the wide camera's line of sight (how far back each stands from their feet against the
others'), and works out which way each is from every calibrated gimbal camera on the map. While a gimbal follows, the
one in the wide shot in its view is remembered; when it loses them (or the director has it out for that), it is
sent `gimbal.point` towards where the wide shot sees them now (or last saw them, for 30 s), and the phone turns
there, closed on where its own camera points (its rotation sensor: an MT3 reports its own angles only every ten
seconds or so), and hands back to its own following once someone is in the middle of its shot. A gimbal given a performer is turned to where the wide shot recognises them, before the
director needs that camera. To calibrate, aim it at the middle of the stage with the arrows and press **Set: it
points at centre stage** in its *Gimbal* fold (it needs the camera and the wide camera on the room map); **Centre
stage** turns it back there to check, **Forget** stops it. The phone's sensor has no fixed zero for the pan and
drifts slowly, so the manager keeps it anchored: while the phone follows someone by their face and nobody else in the
wide shot is near the way it points, the anchor moves a fifth of the way to that person's bearing, each look. After
the app restarts (a new sensor session) Set no longer holds; it is anchored again by itself the first time the phone
follows someone while the wide shot sees only one person, or by Set. Tilt: for a gimbal camera with a height and
a tilt on the room map, it is pointed at 1.4 m up on the person (between chest and head), turned up or down from
its Set tilt by as much as the way to them rises or falls more than the way to centre stage did (Set is taken as
aimed there at that height; the phone must report which way its tilt grows). Without a height and tilt the tilt it
had at Set is asked for, as before (`gimbal_stage_tilt` false leaves the tilt alone). On a simulated stage the aim came within 1.7° (median) of the
person for a gimbal camera in the middle of the house or at the back, and 4° for one beside the stage looking across
it, where how far back someone stands decides it (`tests/test_stageaim.py`). Nothing is said of anyone beyond a place,
and performers only as performer recognition allows.

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Arrows, mounting and connection
sections.text:
It works the same on an X3 and an MT3, and on any gimbal the app can aim. The card sends a move every 300 ms while an arrow is held
and the phone turns the gimbal for half a second after each, so a closed page or a lost network stops it by itself;
a stop is never held back by the dashboard's limit on commands. On an X3 or an MT3 the arrows turn the way they point
as it comes; for a gimbal that differs, the fold can **swap pan and tilt**, **reverse pan** and **reverse tilt** for that phone.
**Mounted upside down (hanging)** is for a gimbal hung from a bar or truss: it turns both arrows round, so they still
go the way they point. The picture is turned round separately, with **Turn picture 180°** under *Picture & stream*
(any phone mounted upside down, gimbal or not, since a phone may already be set that way). The phone turns its
picture as its camera starts, so on a camera that is streaming or recording the card asks first, then stops it,
turns the picture and starts it again, as **Send to UDP** does.
If the gimbal hangs up (switched off, or its mode changed), the phone waits for it to come back and reconnects.
The phone takes a gimbal paired with it (pair it once, with Hohem's app) without looking over the air, and keeps it
connected; **Forget this gimbal** lets it go. Close Hohem's app: it holds the gimbal while open. Experimental: the
commands were worked out from a Bluetooth log of Hohem's app, so a firmware update could change them.

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: An X3 rolls the phone
sections.text:
**An X3 rolls the phone** (app 0.9.56; an X3 only, the MT3 is not tried). Its *Gimbal* fold has **Portrait**,
**⟲ Landscape** (the phone's top to the left, seen from behind it) and **Landscape ⟳**: the phone rolls itself there
over Bluetooth (`gimbal.orient`, 0x67 roll speed, closed on how the phone hangs by its own rotation sensor, or on the
gimbal's roll without one; it slows at the end and stops at an end stop, after 12 s per 90° or when the readings
stop), by way of portrait, and turns its picture to match as its camera next starts (capture rotation 90 for
portrait, 0 and 180 for the landscapes). The picture turns only as the camera starts, so on a running camera the card
asks, stops its stream and recording, rolls, waits until the phone says it is there, and starts them again; from
portrait to landscape the picture changes shape, so check its scene in OBS. **Recentre** (`gimbal.recentre`, as the
trigger does) rolls the phone back to how it hung if recentring rolled it. **Mode** sets its work mode
(`gimbal.mode`: pan and tilt follow, pan follow, all locked, POV), echoing the gimbal's own settings back to it, and
the fold and summary line show its **battery** (volts, roughly how full, charging), read every half minute.
With app 0.9.57 the phone stays rolled while the camera is aimed, pointed or following someone (an X3 is steered
with the same frames as its roll; the older ones levelled it back to portrait). A phone top down in the clamp is
rolled to either landscape the way round that keeps clear of the gimbal's end stops, and **Portrait**, past them,
is greyed out (turn the phone over, then Recentre).

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Saved gimbal targets
sections.text:
**Saved gimbal targets** (`camera_manager/gimbaltargets.py`; the same listening). A gimbal camera's aim at a thing, kept
by name for the kind of event chosen: in Cooking, "show the pot" swings it to the pot and zooms in, and "back to me"
puts it back on the host.
- **Saving one** is for whoever runs the cameras (an operator or the administrator; a Stage Shots account opens no
  dashboard): on the camera's card, under *Gimbal*, aim it with the arrows and zoom, name it ("pot") and press **Save as
  target**. Its pan and tilt (read from the phone with a stop, as *Set home* does) and its zoom are kept, up to 12 for
  each camera in each kind of event (`gimbal_targets`). **Rename** changes its name or the other words it is called by
  (up to 6, "the big pan"; a call word typed in front, "show the pot", is left to the matching), **Delete** drops it,
  and **Go** turns it there to check. Needs app 0.9.37 (`gimbal.point`); a target is tied to the phone's rotation
  sensor, so after the phone restarts it the card asks for it to be saved again, unless the camera is aimed from the
  stage, when centre stage carries it across, or its home is set again ([Home position](#home-position)), which brings back every target saved
  with the old home (`gimbaltargets.rebased`).
- **Calling it.** Like a shot call: after a call word ("show the pot", "let's see the chopping board", "cut to the pot")
  or said alone ("The pot!"); in passing ("the pot is hot"), denied ("don't show the pot") or asked ("can you show the
  pot?") it does nothing. A target's name and phrases are your own words, so heard exactly they need 50% of the
  recogniser (`voice_own_min_confidence`); a phrase two targets share acts for neither. A target call is heard before
  shot calls, so its words are not taken for another camera's shot, and a zoom call in the same breath ("show the pot,
  close up") zooms that camera.

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Saved gimbal targets
sections.text:
- **What it does.** The camera stops following (or following would steer it off again; a follow plan is paused), turns
  to the target and zooms there (gliding over 1.5 s with app 0.9.38, `gimbal_target_zoom_seconds`). The director shows
  it whole meanwhile: no zooming in on people in its picture, and aiming from the stage and the home-position fallback
  leave it alone. Where voice shot calls are on, it is put on air once it is there (the phone says it has arrived, or
  `gimbal_target_settle_seconds`, 4 s) and the programme, held behind real life, has reached that moment, so the swing
  is not seen; the shot on air is held until then (`gimbal_target_cut` false turns this off).
- **The way back.** "Back to me", "back on me", "follow me again", "eyes on me", "back to the presenter", "back to the
  host", "let's bring it back", "bring it back", or phrases of your own for the kind of event (`gimbal_target_back_phrases`, the Sound page), or **Back** on the
  card: every camera on a target is put back as it was before its first target, its aim (unless it is aimed from the
  stage, which turns it to whoever it should be on), its zoom, and following, by its plan if it was. From one target
  to another, back still means as it was before the first. **Home** also lets go of a target. With tracking switched
  off ([Tracking and zoom switches](DIRECTOR.md#tracking-and-zoom-switches)), a target is still turned to and back is still made,
  its aim and its zoom, but it does not follow again until tracking is switched on, when it follows from where it is.

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Saved gimbal targets
sections.text:
- **A spot remembered live.** "And remember where we are" ("remember this spot", "remember this shot", "remember
  this position", "mark this spot", "keep this spot"), or **Remember where it is** on the card, keeps the gimbal
  camera's aim and zoom as they are now, and whether it follows, as its way back instead. Which camera: the gimbal
  camera on air, else the only one that can turn to a position (two, neither on air: it asks which). Nothing moves and
  following goes on. A host who has walked away from the stove says it, then "let's check out the pot" ("check out" and
  "check on" are call words, for shot calls too), then "let's bring it back": the camera turns back to that spot, zooms
  as it was and follows again if it did then, so a host who stayed put is back in shot and one who moved is found. The
  spot is not used up: with no camera on a target, the way back turns a camera with a spot to it (stopping following
  while it turns). It lasts until the next "remember", **Clear** on the card, another kind of event or a restart of the
  phone's sensor, and is kept in memory only; the card shows it. With no spot, the way back is as before the first
  target. Heard wherever a target is saved or a gimbal camera can turn to a position (`gimbal_spot_remembered`,
  `voice_target_remember` in the audit log).
- **Home by voice.** "Let's bring it back home" ("bring it back home", "back to home", "go home", "home position",
  "camera home") turns the gimbal camera on air, or the only one with a home position, to its **home position** (Set
  home on its card), as its Home button does: following stops while it turns and a saved target is let go of, and a
  camera that was following (or was before the target) follows again once it is home. "Let's bring it back"
  without "home" is still the way back. Said in passing ("time to go home") it does nothing (`voice_target_home`).

sections.doc: Gimbals: aiming, following, home and saved targets (experimental)
sections.title: Saved gimbal targets
sections.text:
- On by default wherever a target is saved; switched off for a kind of event under *Saved gimbal targets* in the Sound
  page's voice panel (`gimbal_targets_voice`), which lists every target and what it is heard as. Each go and back is in
  the audit log (`gimbal_target_go`, `gimbal_target_back`, `voice_target`). Following a target that moves (the pot lifted
  off the stove) is not done yet: it needs a detector for things rather than people.

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.text: The Sound page, in two sections (under Sound in the side bar, tabs on a narrow screen): **Voice shot calls**, everything said aloud that the director acts on, and **Programme sound**, with lip sync and its calibration, which is the administrator's. How speech is recognised (Whisper, on this computer) is described with Cooking's [spoken cues](RECIPE_AND_KITCHEN.md#spoken-cues). Saved gimbal targets called aloud are in [Gimbals](GIMBALS.md#saved-gimbal-targets).

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Programme sound
sections.text:
**Programme sound** (Sound page, administrators; `camera_manager/programmesound.py`). *Stay out* is the recommended
choice and the default: phone microphones in different places, mixed, sound hollow however closely lined up. **Follow
the speaker** is an automixer (`camera_manager/automix.py`): only the microphone hearing whoever is talking most
clearly is open, judged from each camera's sound live from the relay against its own background, the chosen camera's
while nobody is heard; another opens when 4 dB clearer for 0.6 s and the one open has had 2 s, crossfaded over 0.3 s
in OBS (volumes, each put back when it stops) as the programme reaches the moment.

Every camera's OBS source is in the scene that keeps every stream open, part of every programme scene, so every
streaming phone's microphone is in the programme. A camera whose picture, and so its sound, is a little off the others
is heard as an echo (2026-10-24: Pixel8_2's delay in OBS wandered by about 350 ms).

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Programme sound
sections.text:
**Programme sound from** a chosen camera: its microphone is always heard; the other cameras either *join it, each
while lined up with it* (muted in OBS while the sync keeper says its feed is not steady: not in sync, wandering,
fallen behind, or moved more than 100 ms in the last 3 minutes, and joining again once it is) or *stay out*. Every 2
minutes each camera's sound is also measured against the chosen camera's, from the relay's copies of their streams,
each placed on the phones' shared clock by its timing strip, and any difference is made its sound trim
(`sound_trim_ms`), so it is heard when the chosen camera hears the same thing. Nothing changes until a camera is
chosen; choosing *every camera* again unmutes what it muted.

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Lip sync and Calibrate sync
sections.text:
**Lip sync** (under Programme sound on the Sound page; `lip_sync_ms`, -1500 to 1500 ms) moves every camera's sound
against its picture by the same amount, negative earlier, for a phone that stamps its sound later than it heard it.

**Calibrate sync** (`camera_manager/avsync.py`) measures it for each camera instead:

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Lip sync and Calibrate sync
sections.text:
- the sync page (`/sync-flash`, no login, nothing on it but the flashes; reached from the calibration pages too:
  [Calibrate from the stage](COLOUR_AND_CALIBRATION.md#calibrate-from-the-stage)) on a phone or tablet flashes white
  and beeps at 2 kHz together, at uneven times;
- held where the cameras see it, **Measure** (pressed while it flashes) has OBS record 12 s of the programme with the
  camera Programme sound comes from on air, to a folder of its own, then puts the shot, the recording folder (once OBS
  has finished the file) and the director's hold back and removes the file (never while the show is being recorded;
  the director does not take that recording for one started in OBS by hand);
- it finds the flashes (in whichever of 40 different parts of the picture flashes in step with the beeps: in the
  programme, the overlay's cards changed more than a small screen in a wide shot) and the beeps in that recording, and
  in each streaming camera's own stream in the relay over the same moments (picture and sound on one clock, before
  OBS), pairing them by the page's uneven gaps (the one shift, up to 1.5 s either way, that puts most beeps on their
  flashes; at least 4 pairs and most of each, agreeing within 40 ms, else it says why: paired by nearness within half
  a second, a programme with its sound 0.53 s late could not be measured).

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Lip sync and Calibrate sync
sections.text:
What the programme shows less what the heard camera's stream had (and its lip sync then) is OBS's own part, and each
camera's lip sync (`lip_sync_by_camera`) is set against its stream and that part together (`avsync.settings`):
measured in the relay alone, the stream said 13 ms and the recording came out further off than the -90 ms set by ear.

Without the programme measured, or with OBS's own part over 1.5 s (`avsync.OBS_MOST`, a misreading), nothing is
changed; the last calibration recording is kept (`data/calibrate/last-calibration.*`, replaced each time) for a look;
**Forget measurements** puts every camera back on the one setting. With the others *joining* the chosen camera, every
camera is moved as the chosen one is, so their sounds stay lined up.

`POST /api/sync/calibrate` (`{}` or `{"clear": true}`), audit `lip_sync_calibrated`.

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Voice shot calls
sections.text:
**Voice shot calls** (optional, at the Standard and Plus AI levels; `camera_manager/voicecalls.py`). The host says a
camera's shot aloud and the director puts that camera on air at once: "cut to the overhead", "show the stove", "back to
the wide", "over to camera 3", or just "Wide shot!". It is heard by the same speech recognition as Cooking's spoken cues
(one listener, one model, on this computer; nothing sent anywhere, the last ten phrases kept in memory only).
- **On air with the call.** Heard live (a camera's own microphone from the relay, a microphone input, a phone's
  spotter), a call comes before the programme, which the sync keeper holds behind real life, gets to it. The cut waits
  that long less a second (`voice_cut_lead_seconds`, 1.0, so it looks planned), holding the shot on air meanwhile, so it
  goes out just ahead of the call, together with a zoom the same call asks for (made by the phone, so as late as its picture). Heard in the programme's
  own sound, typed, or with `voice_cut_on_air` false: at once, as before. A call heard only by a phone's own spotter, while
  this computer listens too, is cut to only if this computer's spotter or Whisper hears it as well before the cut is due
  ("…this process of making coffee" was spotted on a phone as "coffee maker"; `voice_shot_dropped` otherwise). Another camera called within 1.5 s of one
  still waiting is the recogniser changing its mind over one stretch of speech, so neither is cut to
  (`voice_shot_dropped`).

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Voice shot calls
sections.text:
- **What a camera answers to.** Its name, its slot ("camera 2"), what it has been given to show in the words Scene Chat
  knows for it (a camera given the stovetop answers to "stovetop", "stove", "hob", "pan"; the crowd camera to "crowd" and
  "audience"), and phrases of its own, set under **Voice shot calls** on the Sound page ("overhead", "the bench").
  Each camera's card lists what it answers to. A phrase of a camera's own wins over another camera's default; a default
  two cameras share (two wide cameras) is struck through and not acted on until one has a phrase of its own.
- **A call, not a word in passing.** The phrase must follow a call word ("cut to", "switch to", "go to", "over to",
  "back to", "show", "let's see", "let's take a look at", "have a look at", "give me", or one of your own, below) or be all that was said, give or take "shot", "camera" or "please". "The
  stove is hot", "I'll pop it in the oven later", "don't cut to the stove" and a question ("shall we look at the oven?")
  do nothing. How sure the recogniser was, times how clear the call is, must reach 70% (`voice_shots_min_confidence`,
  60 to 90% on the Sound page): a call word and the phrase as set count fully; said alone, or heard a letter out
  ("stovetopp"), counts for less. A phrase of your own (a camera's, or a zoom call's), heard exactly as you set it,
  counts fully however it is said and needs only 50% (`voice_own_min_confidence`): Whisper is unsure of itself on very
  short phrases, and a chosen phrase matched word for word is evidence of its own. A camera with no usable picture is not put on air.

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Voice shot calls
sections.text:
- **The cut** is the director's own cut by hand: the camera goes on air at once and the director holds it for *Hold
  after a person chooses* (30 s by default) before the automatic choosing may cut away. Calling the camera already on
  air keeps it there for another hold. Each call is in the cut log (by *voice*, with the phrase heard), and is noted in
  Scene Chat on the Show page ("Heard “cut to the stove”: cut to Stove; the director holds it 30 s.").
- **Where it is on.** By default in **Cooking** and **Creator Studio**, where one host talks to their own cameras with no
  music. Off by default in **live music**, **worship** and **theatre** (sung words, a congregation and scripted lines
  through the PA would call cameras by mistake) and in a **podcast** or **panel** (several people talk freely and call
  each other by the names cameras are given: "over to Sam"). Each kind of event can be switched on or off on the Sound
  page, and *Listen to the host* switches the listening off altogether (the same switch as the Recipe page's spoken
  cues). Its set-up steps are in **AI assistance**, as for spoken cues.
- **Call words of your own.** Under *Call words* in the Sound page's *Voice shot calls* panel, up to 12 for each kind of
  event (`voice_call_words` {mode: [...]}, `voicecalls.call_words`), heard beside the built-in ones by shot calls,
  zoom calls and saved gimbal targets alike: "let's pop across to the stove", "peek at the pot", "pop in for a close
  up". Each is two words or more besides "the", not only small words ("to the", "on it" would call cameras from
  ordinary talk) and never a denial ("don't cut to"); a "the" typed at the end is dropped, since it is heard anyway
  (`voicecalls.tidy_call_words`; `POST /api/voice` `{"call_words": [...]}`, `[]` for the built-in ones alone). A
  question or "don't" before one still calls nothing. When the Heard list shows a camera or a target named in passing,
  the words just before it (two to five, `voicecalls.lead_in`) are offered as a call word with a button. The quick
  phrase spotter is not told call words: it listens for your own phrases, and Whisper hears what comes before them.

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Voice shot calls
sections.text:
- The Sound page's *Voice shot calls* panel lists what was heard and what each phrase did or why it did nothing, and **Try a phrase**
  acts on one typed as if the host said it.

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Voice zoom calls
sections.text:
**Voice zoom calls** (`camera_manager/voicezoom.py`; the same listening). A tighter or wider shot asked for aloud zooms
the camera on air, or the one a phrase names: **tighter** and **wider** (1.5 times each way), **close-up** (just past
the telephoto's handover on a phone that has one, else `voice_zoom_close_percent`, 3x; with app 0.9.50, no tighter
than leaves a followed face a third of the picture high) and **back to normal** (1x). **Find me** ("I'm over here",
"over here", "find me", "look over here", or a phrase of your own with that action) turns the gimbal camera on air, or
every gimbal camera when the camera on air has none, to whoever called (`Manager.find_me`): with its gimbal calibrated
and on the room map, and a wide camera there, it is pointed where the wide shot sees the largest (nearest) person;
otherwise it searches at once, zoomed out and swinging each way (app 0.9.51, `gimbal.follow` `find`; an older app is
put back to 1x and following).
Called like a shot ("give me a close up", "camera, zoom in") or said alone ("Close up!"); with a shot call in the same
breath ("cut to the stove, close up") it zooms the camera just called. A phone with app 0.9.38 glides there (`camera.zoom`:
0.6 s a step, 1 s to a close-up or back to normal, or twice as long with *smooth* in the Zoom calls panel;
`voice_zoom_seconds`), an older one changes at once (`camera.lens`); the director holds a camera on air while it zooms, so
a performer's close-up is not cut away from. **Built-in phrases** ("zoom in", "tighter", "close up", "tight shot",
"pull back"…) only where voice calls are on by default (Cooking, Creator Studio); **phrases of your own** for each kind
of event everywhere (`voice_zoom_phrases`, up to 12, each with its action and camera), so a band can give the director a
cue nobody sings ("camera, close on me"). On or off for each kind of event (`voice_zoom`), by default as shot calls are;
under **Zoom calls** in the Sound page's *Voice shot calls* panel. Over loud music recognition is unreliable: a cue between songs,
or into a talkback microphone, works best.

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: Tracking and zoom said aloud
sections.text:
**Tracking and zoom said aloud** (the same listening, as zoom calls: `voicezoom.SWITCHES`). "Stop tracking" or
"tracking off", "start tracking" or "tracking on", "stop zooming" or "auto zoom off", "auto zoom on" or "start
zooming" switch tracking or the zoom for every camera ([Tracking and zoom switches](DIRECTOR.md#tracking-and-zoom-switches));
with a shot call in the same breath ("cut to the stove, stop tracking"), or as a phrase of your own given a camera, for
that camera only. Built in where voice calls are on by default (Cooking, Creator Studio); elsewhere as phrases of your
own (the Zoom calls panel's actions *Tracking off*, *Tracking on*, *Auto zoom off*, *Auto zoom on*; "the camera on air"
there means every camera). In the audit log as `voice_auto_switch`.

sections.doc: Sound, lip sync and voice calls
sections.title: The quick phrase spotter
sections.text:
**The quick phrase spotter** (`camera_manager/spotter.py`; Vosk, Apache-2.0, with its small English model, about 40 MB,
both set up from AI assistance once you have phrases of your own). Your own phrases (zoom calls, cameras' own shot
phrases) are listened for beside Whisper by a recogniser told those phrases and nothing else, and acted on as each ends:
measured on the M5 Pro, "Bring it back" said alone 0.02 s after it ended, and within a longer sentence 0.4 s after,
where Whisper takes a quarter to three quarters of a second to begin. Since it hears other speech as the nearest of its
phrases, it acts only on a phrase said alone with the speaker stopped, or one whose every word is 90% certain ("the ring
is back on the table" is not "bring it back"); Whisper's transcription of the same moment leaves out what it acted on,
so nothing is acted on twice. The Heard list marks what it spotted; a switch beside Zoom calls turns it off
(`voice_spotter`). A phrase spotted by a phone's own spotter moves no recipe step while this computer listens too (this
computer hears the same microphone a third of a second later; a phone heard "step two" as step three): it acts only
on camera and zoom calls, and each step cue's audit entry says which listener heard it (`listener`: `whisper`,
`alone`, `within`, `typed`; never the words). **The recipe's calls** are on its list too in Cooking, while step cues are on (`voice_spotter_steps`,
on by default): "step one" to the last step, "prep step one"…, "next step", "previous step", and each step in its own
words (its first clause, the first 8 words, steps of 3 or more, and again with "the" after its first word, as it is
usually said: "start the coffee maker"), acted on as the recipe's cues are. Whisper wrote
"step three" as "we've got three of them" and missed it; replayed through the spotter, every step call of that
recording was caught and nothing in the talk before it. Heard inside a sentence, a step call begins only the step
expected next (the next still to come, or the method's first during the preparation): any other, and "previous step",
is left in Whisper's transcription for Whisper to act on, and the Heard list says it waits. Told only its phrases, the
spotter read "…two sticks, one tightly packed cup" as "step six" with both words 100% certain, and the recipe went
from before its first step to its last (2026-11-16). Said alone, a step call still goes to any step. A step with a word the spotter's model does not know ("sauté")
is left to Whisper. Phrases are given to it in words, numbers spelled out ("step 3" was a phrase it could never hear). **On the phone itself** (app 0.9.41, `voice_phone_spotter`): a phone with its cooler connected can
spot your phrases from its own microphone and tell the manager at once (a "voice" message), a quarter to a third of a
second sooner than hearing them in the relay. Ticked per camera under Zoom calls, offered only while its cooler is
connected; the phone listens only below the warning temperature (`thermal_warn_c`, 45 °C) and with its cooler
connected, pausing itself otherwise, and this computer's spotter hears the relay meanwhile; a phrase heard by both is
acted on once. The manager keeps each phone told its phrases (`voice.settings`) and serves it the model
(`/app/spotter-model.zip`, zipped from the spotter's own, with its SHA-256).

sections.doc: Colour matching, and calibrating from the stage
sections.title: Colour matching, and calibrating from the stage
sections.text: Back to [the manager's README](../README.md). Lip sync and Calibrate sync are in [Sound and voice](SOUND_AND_VOICE.md#lip-sync-and-calibrate-sync).

sections.doc: Colour matching, and calibrating from the stage
sections.title: Making the cameras' colours match
sections.text:
Phones of different makes see the same scene differently. Measured on 2026-10-16, three cameras on one street: a
neutral sidewalk was strongly yellow on the S20 FE (b* +13.5), nearly neutral on the Pixel 8, and the cameras differed
by 10-22 ΔE on lawn, trees and road. OBS decodes each phone correctly; the difference is each phone's own automatic
white balance, exposure and processing. The Colour page (administrator only) has two remedies:

sections.doc: Colour matching, and calibrating from the stage
sections.title: Making the cameras' colours match
sections.text:
- **White balance and exposure on the phones** (app 0.9.7 or later). White balance: automatic, a preset, a kelvin
  value (where the phone allows setting it by hand, from its own sensor calibration), or locked on what it sees now
  (point every camera at the same grey card first). Exposure: automatic with compensation, locked, or shutter and ISO by
  hand. "Set white balance" and "Set exposure" send it to the cameras ticked (all by default); one kelvin for every camera is the usual choice, and a
  phone that cannot be set in kelvin takes its nearest preset and says so. Each phone keeps its setting across stream
  restarts and lens changes, and reports what it is actually doing (including the temperature its white balance is
  at). Readiness warns when cameras in a show have their white balance set differently.
- **A LUT per camera from a colour chart.** Point every camera at an X-Rite ColorChecker (24 patches), or a plain grey
  card for white balance and exposure only, lit as the stage will be. Without one, the **Colour card** on a tablet
  (`https://calibrate.mcvsaid.local`, see [Easy addresses](SECURITY.md#who-can-log-in)) shows the same 24 patches in the same layout, and an 18%
  grey; a screen gives off its own light rather than the stage's, so it is good for matching the cameras to one
  another ("match") and less so for "accurate", and only with its brightness up and Night Shift or True Tone off.
  Logged in on that page, **Calibrate colour** does all of this from the phone, finding the chart in each camera
  without any clicking (see [Calibrate from the stage](#calibrate-from-the-stage)). "Take pictures from OBS" takes each camera's
  picture from its OBS source at full size, losslessly (BMP). Click the four corners of the chart's patch area on each
  picture, in any order round it, then "Calibrate": the patches are sampled, and a correction fitted, per-channel
  curves through the six greys and then a 3x3 matrix for the colours, either to the chart's published colours
  ("accurate") or to one camera ("match"). Each is written as a 33-point .cube LUT and listed with its fit (mean and
  worst ΔE2000 on the chart, before and after), by camera and lens. "Put every LUT in OBS" adds an "Apply LUT" filter
  (`Camera colour match`) to each camera's source. Calibrate again when the light changes: the corners are kept.

sections.doc: Colour matching, and calibrating from the stage
sections.title: Making the cameras' colours match
sections.text:
- **Without a chart: the scene in front of them.** Choose "the scene in front of them (no chart)" and the camera to
  match. Point every camera at the same thing (the stage as lit, with some grey and some colour in it), take pictures,
  and where cameras frame it differently, click two corners of a box on each picture round the view they share (a
  window frame or a part only one camera sees is left out). "Match" pairs the colours of each boxed picture with the
  reference's by optimal transport (sliced colour transfer), takes per-channel curves from what is grey in both, and
  fits the same matrix as for a chart. It makes the cameras alike, not accurate. On the 2026-10-16 street pictures it
  took the S20 FE from 10.7 ΔE from the Pixel 8 to 3.5 and the S23 from 10.6 to 3.8, on sidewalk, road, lawn and
  trees; whole pictures without boxes did worse (7.2 and 5.3). Its ΔE scores are rougher than a chart's.

A 4K picture through a 33-point LUT costs about 0.4 ms of the M5 Pro's GPU (0.1 ms more than drawing it plainly),
measured with Metal doing what OBS's filter does, so the LUTs are put on the sources rather than the scenes.

With camera files on, each camera's LUT also goes beside a recording's camera files (`01 S20 FE.cube`, ...) and is
listed in `<name>.cameras.json` (`luts`, with whether the programme had it applied), for Resolve, Premiere or Final
Cut. Apply it to the camera file as decoded to Rec.709, as OBS shows it.

sections.doc: Colour matching, and calibrating from the stage
sections.title: Calibrate from the stage
sections.text:
**Calibrate from the stage** (Set up › Calibrate; `camera_manager/calibrate.py`, `screenfind.py`). Once the cameras are up
and streaming, one person walks on stage with a phone, opens `https://calibrate.mcvsaid.local` (or scans the QR code on
the Calibrate page), logs in as a setup tech or an operator and holds the phone up where the cameras see it; the
manager measures from what the page shows. One run at a time; only the phone that started it shows its steps, and the
Calibrate page at the PC follows it and can stop it.
- **Calibrate sound** opens the sync flash (`/sync-flash?manager=1`): it flashes and beeps as soon as it is started
  and the manager runs Calibrate sync meanwhile (as in [Calibrate sync](SOUND_AND_VOICE.md#lip-sync-and-calibrate-sync), each camera's lip sync set against its stream and OBS's own
  part), then stops by itself and says what each camera was set to. It needs the camera relay, as Calibrate sync does.
- **Time the network cameras** (offered when there is a network camera) opens the same sync flash without its beeps
  (`/sync-flash?manager=timing`). While it flashes, the manager watches every network camera and up to three
  lined-up phones in OBS for 16 seconds and times each network camera by the flashes it and a phone both saw, then
  sets what it is held by; see [Timed at once by the calibrate page](NETWORK.md#timed-at-once-by-the-calibrate-page).
  It needs OBS sync on and at least one phone camera lined up and seeing the page; the relay is not needed. It can be
  stopped at any time, and changes nothing unless it finishes.

sections.doc: Colour matching, and calibrating from the stage
sections.title: Calibrate from the stage
sections.text:
- **Calibrate colour** finds the phone in every camera by itself: the manager asks the page, step by step, to show
  black, the chart's patch area lit white, black and white again, and waits each time for the page to say it shows
  it (numbered steps, `POST /api/calibrate/shown`) and for the picture to reach OBS (`calibrate_settle_seconds`, 1.5,
  plus however far the sync keeper holds the programme behind), then takes each camera's picture at 480 wide. What is
  brighter in both lit pictures than in either dark one is the screen (a light that comes on between pictures does
  not go off again with it); the largest such shape is taken, its corners are its outermost points along the two
  diagonals, and one that fills less than 60% of them, or is under 60 pixels, is refused with a reason. Then the page
  shows the chart, each camera's picture is taken at full size, its patches read at the corners found, and a LUT fitted
  as on the Colour page: matched to the camera that sees the chart biggest (or one chosen, or the chart's own colours)
  and put in OBS unless asked not to. A camera that did not see the phone says why, and the rest go on. The phone
  stays still for about 30 seconds: a stand or a clip helps. The page covers itself in black but does not go full
  screen, since that would resize it after the phone had been found; turned mid-run, it says to stop and start again. `GET /api/calibrate`, `POST /api/calibrate/start`
  (`{"kind": "sync"}` or `{"kind": "colour", "reference": "auto"|"chart"|id, "obs": true}`), `/shown`, `/stop`; audit
  `calibration_run`.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.text: Back to [the manager's README](../README.md).

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: Keeping the cameras going
sections.text: Phones mounted out of reach have to look after themselves. Each of these is on by default and reported in readiness:

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: Keeping the cameras going
sections.text:
- **A picture that stops while the sound goes on** (app 0.9.10). Seen live: a phone's encoder stopped while its sound
  kept the link alive, so nothing noticed. The app now watches its own frame count while streaming or recording: no new
  frame for 5 s reopens the camera, still none 6 s later restarts the whole capture (a recording carries on in a new
  file), and further tries follow 12, 24 and 48 s apart, then every minute. Readiness ("Camera picture") fails while a
  phone reports a stall and warns for ten minutes after it recovers; for older apps the relay notices a camera sending
  under a tenth of its rate.
- **An OBS source that plays with no picture.** Every streaming camera's source is looked at every 10 s. One that plays
  but shows nothing is restarted, and if a restart (its own, the relay's or the sync keeper's) does not bring the
  picture back within 15 s it is rebuilt, which brings back its decoder (seen live after a phone moved from Wi-Fi to
  Ethernet). At most one rebuild every two minutes and six an hour per source; never a source on air that shows a
  picture.
- **Rejoining the camera Wi-Fi** (app 0.9.8). An armed phone that loses the camera network (a router restarted, say)
  rejoins it by itself, 3 s after and then up to a minute apart, and keeps Android from dropping a network that has no
  internet. Optionally (System › Network) its other saved networks are switched off while armed, and given back on
  disarm or after five minutes without the camera Wi-Fi. The app needs location access for Android to show it the
  networks; the set-up grants it.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: Keeping the cameras going
sections.text:
- **Rejoining when this computer is out of reach** (app 0.9.23). A phone on the camera Wi-Fi whose every connection to
  the manager times out for 2 minutes drops the Wi-Fi and joins it again, then switches it off and on, 5, 10 and then
  every 30 minutes apart (seen 2026-10-22: an S23+ that roamed between the router's 2.4 and 5 GHz access points reached
  the router but not this computer for 35 minutes, until its Wi-Fi was switched off and on). A manager that is switched
  off refuses the connection, which the phone takes as the network working, so it is left alone; and never while the
  phone records to its own storage. Its card says so under Maintenance for an hour after (“Wi-Fi: dropped and rejoined
  the camera Wi-Fi 5 min ago; it could not reach this computer for 2 min (9 tries)…”), from `wifi_rejoin.manager_rejoin`
  in its telemetry.
- **Battery protection** (app 0.9.9). A phone kept charging all show is held short of full (80-85%), which keeps it
  cooler: Samsung's protect-battery setting, Pixel 8's charge limit, granted over USB. The Pixel 3 and 4a have no
  charge limit, and readiness says so once they are warm. Switched off on System › Cameras.
- **Silence while armed** (app 0.9.11). A camera's microphone feeds the show, so an armed phone plays nothing: Do Not
  Disturb at total silence, its sounds muted and touch vibration off, all given back 10 s after it is disarmed.
  Readiness ("Phone sounds") warns of a phone that is not silenced.
- **Black Shark cooler** (app 0.9.12 to 0.9.18; optional). A phone with a MagCooler 5 Pro clamped on shows it on its
  card: the cooler's fan mode, fan speed (rpm), temperature and lights, and in its *Cooler* fold the fan choice (Smart by
  default, Overclock while streaming, Overclock, Silent, or a fixed speed 1 to 5), which cooler is this phone's
  (**This one** from those nearby, or **Forget this cooler**) and its firmware, and since when it has been connected or
  off and why it last dropped (audit `cooler_connected` / `cooler_dropped`, with how long it had been on or off; from app 0.9.54 a drop also has
  the cooler's own shutdown timer as last read, `shutdown_timer`, so a drop near half an hour is told from the radio). **Flash its lights** (app 0.9.47) blinks
  the connected cooler's lights five times, to check which cooler is on which phone; and a cooler the phone let go of is
  shown as *Let go of*, nearby or not, with **Take it back**, since the phone never takes it back by itself. The phone finds its cooler by name as
  well as by its Bluetooth service, takes one that is close and alone by itself, and keeps it connected. Its lights are
  always kept off while the phone holds it, armed or not (they sit beside the lens): the phone asks the cooler what its
  lights and fan are every 10 s and sends the lights setting again every 30 s. A fan mode the cooler refuses (the one
  tested refuses Overclock, as it does Black Shark's own app) is not asked for again for 5 minutes: the cooler runs
  Smart meanwhile and the card says so. The Temperatures page lists each cooler beside its phone. Readiness ("Cooler")
  warns of one that has gone, or of its lights on while armed, never more. A cooler asking to pair (app 0.9.28) shows
  as *asking to pair: tap Pair on the phone once*: Android's Pair prompt cannot be accepted by any app, and unanswered
  the cooler drops every 30 s; tapped once, the phone and cooler stay paired. Phones without one show only a line under
  Maintenance, with **Look for a cooler** (close the Black Shark app first: while it holds the cooler, the cooler cannot
  be found; no cooler is looked for while streaming or recording). *Test: Switch off in 30 min* tries the cooler's own
  Auto Shutdown from the card, to find out whether it can be woken afterwards; it is a trial, not for a show.
  Experimental: the commands were worked out from Black Shark's app, so a firmware update could change them.
  **Measured** (one evening each): a Galaxy S23 with the cooler streamed and recorded 4K together for 2¼ hours at
  22–25 °C, where streaming alone without one took it to 43–44 °C, near the 47 °C at which the app stops recording; an
  S20 FE ran at 5–15 °C with one, against up to 50 °C without. So a cooler makes recording on the phone while it
  streams practical. Keep the fan in **Smart**; watch for **condensation**, since the cooler can chill a phone below
  the room's temperature (water on or in it, or on the lens, in a humid room); the cooler's own **Auto Shutdown** is kept off by the phone (when it runs out the cooler turns
  off and cannot be woken over Bluetooth until its button is pressed): set off on connecting since app 0.9.49, and read
  every 30 s and set off again whenever it is found set since app 0.9.54 (with an older app, switch it off in Black
  Shark's app); and power it from its own USB charger, not a PoE-to-USB-C adapter on the camera switch.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: Keeping the cameras going
sections.text:
- **Hohem gimbal** and **an X3 rolling the phone**: see [Gimbals](GIMBALS.md).
- **All coolers at once** (administrator; *Coolers* under System › Cameras; on the Show page until
  2026-11-13). **Re-pair all
  coolers**: every phone that is not streaming or recording lets go of its cooler and looks for 10 s; each cooler heard
  then goes to the phone that hears it loudest (it is clamped to that phone), one cooler a phone, a cooler a phone took
  by itself (close and alone) believed first. About half a minute; the row says what each phone got, which phones were
  left as they were and any cooler heard but given to none (audit `coolers_repaired`). **Forget all coolers**: every phone
  lets go of its cooler, an offline one when it is next connected (audit `coolers_forgotten`).
- **Pairing coolers and gimbals from the dashboard.** A phone without a cooler or gimbal has a line under
  *Maintenance* with **Look for a cooler** or **Look for a gimbal** (the phone looks for 10 s, not while it streams or
  records; one found close and alone is taken, several are listed with **This one**; a gimbal paired with the phone is
  among those found whether it advertises or not; since app 0.9.22 a look hears an MT3 with the phone's screen off,
  and before that only with it on). Below it, **Move here** lists the coolers and gimbals other cameras
  have: that phone lets it go and this one takes it. A phone with one has **Pair a different cooler** (or gimbal) in
  its fold: it lets go of this one and looks, and is not offered the one it let go of. A look asked for later (app
  0.9.34) lists that one again, to be chosen with **This one**, never taken by itself. The manager notes which camera
  each was given to (`accessory_owners`, kept on this computer), so a phone that was off when one was moved, and still
  tries to reconnect to it, is told to let go when it is next heard (audit `cooler_let_go` / `gimbal_let_go`); a
  phone actually connected to one for over a minute is believed over an older choice. A look asked from here is
  usually made with the phone's screen off, when Android passes on only coolers the app knows by name; if none is
  found the card says to use the phone's own *Black Shark cooler…* button, which hears every cooler (app 0.9.20 also
  knows the MagCooler 5 Pro by the name it advertises, so it is found from here too). Not offering the one let go of
  back, and taking another gimbal paired with the phone after one was forgotten, need app 0.9.20.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: Keeping the cameras going
sections.text:
- **The clock.** A streaming camera's clock is never changed under it, so the clock warning says how many frames it is
  out and has a **Fix** button: the director cuts to the best other camera, the stream is stopped, the clock set and the
  stream started again, and the camera goes back into the choosing once feed alignment has it in step. A phone
  restarted with nothing to tell it the time (no SIM, no internet on the camera network) comes back with its clock at
  the date its system was built, months out; from app 0.9.64 it still connects (its pairing's certificate is taken by
  its fingerprint, not its dates) and is set right automatically. Older apps turn the manager's certificate away as
  not yet valid until their clock is set by hand.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: A charger hub on a smart plug
sections.text:
The USB charger hubs for the coolers and gimbals can each sit on a smart plug, switched from the dashboard's **Power** page (Set up ›
Power; `camera_manager/plug.py`). Unlike the rest of this section, it is off until set up, and **only the buttons switch a plug**:
nothing turns one on or off around a show or on overheating.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: A charger hub on a smart plug
sections.text:
- **The plug.** A TP-Link Tapo P125M (tried here: set up, read and switched on and off from the dashboard over TPAP), or another
  plug the tapo package handles the same way. It has to have been added in the Tapo
  app once: that needs a TP-Link account. From then on the manager talks to it directly on the local network, not through
  TP-Link's cloud. Its address must be reachable from this computer, so it needs a fixed lease on the router.
- **Setting them up.** Power › *Add a plug* (administrator): its address and a name (up to 8 plugs). Power › *Tapo login*: the Tapo
  account's email and password, one for all the plugs, which they want even on the local network. The login goes in
  `secrets.json`. It is never shown again, written to the audit log or the log, or carried by a settings file, a restore point or a
  location. Saving reads the plugs at once. The plugs themselves (`plugs` in `config.json`) stay with this computer too: they are this
  network's. A manager that had the one charger plug of before keeps it as the first plug.
- **What each plug charges.** *Change this plug, or what it charges*: tick the gimbals and coolers on its charger, from those the phones
  report, and name anything else on it (spare batteries, a light). A gimbal or cooler is known by its Bluetooth address, so it stays
  on its plug when it is clamped to another phone, and it can be on one plug only: ticking it on another moves it. Each plug's card
  then says which camera each of its gimbals and coolers is on now, whether it is connected, whether that camera is armed, and a
  gimbal's battery and whether it is charging; *Not on any plug yet* lists the gimbals and coolers no plug is said to charge.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: A charger hub on a smart plug
sections.text:
- **Using them.** *Switch on* and *Switch off*, with whether each is on and whether it answers, read every 30 s: on the Power page, and
  on the Cameras page, for an administrator or an operator. Switching off asks first and lists what stops charging, and says so when
  a cooler on it is on an armed camera, whose phone will then warm up. Each switch goes in the audit log with who did it.
- **A refused login is not tried again** until it is saved again, since a Tapo plug locks itself for a while after several failed
  logins.
- **The package.** `tapo` (`requirements-plug.txt`, installed by `install-release.sh`) speaks both of Tapo's local protocols: KLAP, and
  TPAP, which recent firmware uses unless Third-Party Compatibility is on in the Tapo app. python-kasa did not speak TPAP when
  this was written. A firmware update could change the protocol again; the panel then says the plug is not answering or refused the
  login, and nothing else in the show depends on it.
- **Another make.** Everything make-specific is an entry in `plug.BRANDS` and a small device class with `on()`, `off()` and `state()`.
  Only Tapo exists today.

The demonstration manager switches two stand-in plugs, one charging Stage Left's cooler and Stage Right's gimbal and one not yet
said to charge anything (so the Drums cooler is on no plug); `tools/demo_data.py --real-plug` leaves the Power page to set up real ones.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: Keeping the computer awake through a show
sections.text:
An unattended laptop that sleeps mid-show takes the manager with it: cameras, voice calls, gimbals and the director all stop. The
Power page's **Keep this computer awake** (`camera_manager/keepawake.py`) runs macOS's own `caffeinate -i -s -w <the manager's process>`
while it is wanted: no idle sleep, and no system sleep on mains power. It is stopped when no longer wanted, and it ends by itself if
the manager quits or crashes, so the Mac is never left stuck awake. It needs no administrator password and changes no Mac setting.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: Keeping the computer awake through a show
sections.text:
- **When.** *During shows and scheduled times* (the default): while the show is live (OBS recording or streaming, or a camera
  streaming or recording) and for 15 minutes after (set from 0 to 240), so the gap between sets does not let it sleep; in each
  scheduled time; and for the next 1, 2, 4, 8 or 12 hours when asked, for setting up. *Always, while the manager runs*, or *Never*.
- **The schedule.** *Add a time*: a name, from and to (an end before the start runs past midnight), and either days of the week
  (every week) or one date. Up to 24, on this computer's own clock; the page says which comes next.
- **The screen too.** Ticked, the display stays on as well (`-d`), for a Mac whose screen is watched.
- **What no program can stop** is said on the page, read from `pmset` and `ioreg`: on battery, macOS still sleeps it when the charge
  runs low; and closing a MacBook's lid sleeps it unless it is on power with an external display. The Show page warns while the show
  is live and the Mac is not kept awake, or when one of those applies.
- Operators and administrators change it; each change goes in the audit log with who made it. Only on a Mac: elsewhere the page says
  the computer sleeps as its own settings say.

sections.doc: Keeping the cameras going: phones, coolers, plugs and the computer
sections.title: Is every camera sending every frame?
sections.text:
With the camera relay on (the default), every half minute the manager reads the last ten seconds of each streaming camera's stream
as the relay received it (without decoding it) and puts its frame rate and stalls in that camera's readiness: "Frame
rate", warning when it drops frames now and then and failing when it would stutter visibly on air.

Two causes found so far:
- **The shot chooser's stills, on the Pixel 4a and 8 (app 0.9.5 and earlier).** Each still read the whole frame back
  on the thread that feeds the encoder, about 33 MB at 4K, and cost about three frames, once every two seconds (all 93
  stalls in a recording fell within 0.3 s of a still). From app 0.9.6 the still is a small copy (about 0.4 MB) read on
  the next frame.
- **Older phones at 4K.** With six cameras at 4K the Pixel 3s ran at 25-27 fps and the Pixel 4a at about 23: too much
  for them at that size. They streamed 1440p at about 29 fps.

sections.doc: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.title: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.text: Copying the phones' own recordings is in [the offload guide](OFFLOAD.md). Back to [the manager's README](../README.md).

sections.doc: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.title: Recording each camera: on the phones, or on the PC
sections.text:
A videographer often wants every camera's own recording, to cut the show themselves, as well as the directed
programme. There are two ways to get them, and which works depends on the phones.

**On the phones (local recording while streaming).** Each phone records its own file at a higher bitrate than it
streams (20 Mb/s), and the files are copied to the PC afterwards (Recordings › Local recordings). The picture is the best there is,
but the phone encodes the picture twice and writes it to storage while it streams, and that makes a phone run hot.
On 2026-10-14 recording and streaming together ran the phones too hot to use. **It may not be possible on your
phones: test it on the intended hardware first**, recording and streaming together at the intended size for the full
length of a show plus a margin, in the place they will be mounted, and watch the Temperatures page. A phone that
reaches its heat limit (47 °C at the battery, by default) stops recording and goes on streaming.

sections.doc: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.title: Recording each camera: on the phones, or on the PC
sections.text:
**On the PC (camera files).** If the phones cannot record and stream together, the PC can keep every camera's
stream as it arrives, with no extra work for the phones and no extra encoding on the PC, while the programme is
directed, recorded and streamed as usual. Switch on "Keep each camera's own file of every programme recording" under
Recordings › PC recordings (it needs the camera relay, which is on by default): each programme recording then comes
with one file per camera and the cuts as an edit (EDL) a videographer can open and re-cut (see
[The camera relay](#the-camera-relay-the-look-ahead-and-each-cameras-own-file) below). The files have the streams'
quality (7, 12 or 25 Mb/s by stream size), which is less than the phones' own recordings; and they need disk space on
the PC: about 3, 5 or 11 GB an hour per camera at 1080p, 1440p or 4K, up to twice that while the files are made.

Either way the directed programme is saved on the PC as the show runs, and can be streamed live at the same time.

sections.doc: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.title: The camera relay: the look-ahead, and each camera's own file
sections.text:
A relay (`camera_manager/relay.py`) runs on this computer as its own service, `mcvsaid-relay`, separate from the manager so
that restarting or updating the manager never interrupts a picture. It listens on each camera's port (8999 + slot) in
OBS's place, passes every SRT message on to OBS unchanged over the PC's own loopback (UDP 9999 + slot), and writes the
same bytes to a spool in `<data>/relay/spool/<slot>/`, noting when they came. It has two jobs, switched apart:

| | Setting | Default | Costs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Holding the look-ahead** as compressed video, so OBS does not hold it as pictures | `camera_relay_enabled`, System › This computer | on | about 12 MB per camera; saves about 1.5-1.8 GB per 4K camera in OBS |
| **Camera files**: each camera's whole stream kept while the programme is recorded, for its own file and an EDL | `camera_files_enabled`, Recordings › PC recordings | off | disk: about 3/5/11 GB an hour per camera at 1080p/1440p/4K, up to twice that while the files are made |

Camera files need the relay; the look-ahead does not need camera files. Without camera files the relay keeps only
about a minute of each camera (`relay_spool_seconds`), for the pictures the director finds the performer in and the
frame-rate check, and never a recording's length; nothing is made when a recording stops.

sections.doc: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.title: The camera relay: the look-ahead, and each camera's own file
sections.text:
**Whose stream it takes.** The manager tells the relay the address each phone's control connection comes from, which
only the paired phone can make. The phone itself always gets in, as when it comes back before its old connection has
timed out. A caller from any other address is let in only while nothing is arriving from that camera (three seconds
of silence, so a phone whose address has just changed gets back in), and is replaced by the phone as soon as it
streams: nobody else on the network can put their picture in place of one that is arriving. The camera's *Stream
target* readiness warns when a stream was turned away in the last minute, or when what is arriving is not from the
phone. The relay keeps a phone's address through a restart of the manager. This is not encryption: the streams
still cross the camera network in the clear, and with the relay off OBS listens itself and takes any caller.

**Memory, measured** on the M5 Pro (48 GB), six cameras at 4K, 25 Mb/s, 5.5 s look-ahead:

| | Relay off | Relay on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OBS | 11.0 GB | 2.6 GB |
| Camera relay | | 0.13 GB |
| The whole Mac in use | 38.8 GB | 30.7 GB |

sections.doc: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.title: The camera relay: the look-ahead, and each camera's own file
sections.text:
**On by default.** A new installation has the relay on and camera files off; the manager installs and starts the relay
service itself the first time (`launchctl`/`systemctl`, as `python -m camera_manager.host service start` does). An
installation from before keeps what it had: one with the relay on keeps its camera files, as before; one with it off is
not switched on behind the operator's back. Its System › This computer page recommends the relay, with the figures above, and
switches it on in one click; the readiness check says so too when three or more cameras stream at 4K.

**Switching it off** is a troubleshooting step, under System › This computer › Advanced: troubleshooting. OBS then holds the
look-ahead in memory again, about 1.5-1.8 GB per 4K camera, and recordings get no camera files. Switching either way
points each camera's OBS source at the relay or back at the camera (only the address changes) and starts or stops the
service; a camera that is streaming drops for a few seconds. Neither switch works while the programme is recorded.

**If it cannot run here** (no libsrt, or its service will not start), the manager does not fail: every camera's OBS
source is pointed straight at its camera, as with the relay off, and the readiness check's "Camera relay" line says why
and that OBS is holding the look-ahead. Put it right (`brew install srt`, or `libsrt1.5-gnutls`), then restart the
manager.

sections.doc: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.title: The camera relay: the look-ahead, and each camera's own file
sections.text:
- **No added delay of its own.** It reads nothing in the stream, so it adds nothing measurable: against OBS listening
  directly, within a few milliseconds. (An ffmpeg relay was tried first and added about a second.)
- **It holds the look-ahead, so OBS does not.** Each camera's delay (the sync keeper's hold, about 4 s) is moved
  from OBS's delay filter into the relay while that camera is off air, leaving OBS half a second to adjust both ways.
  Switching the relay off puts it all back.
- **No extra work for the phones** and no extra encoding on this computer.
- **If the relay stops**, systemd (or launchd on a Mac) starts it again within two seconds; meanwhile those cameras' pictures stop in OBS.
  The readiness checks say so per camera. A full disk costs the spool, never the pictures.
- Needs the SRT library: `libsrt1.5-gnutls`, which comes with ffmpeg on Debian, Ubuntu and Mint; `brew install srt` on a Mac.

sections.doc: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.title: Each camera's stream is encrypted, and only its own phone can send it
trail: The camera relay: the look-ahead, and each camera's own file
sections.text:
SRT by itself neither encrypts a stream nor asks who is calling: anyone on the camera network could watch a camera, or
send a picture of their own to its port. So each camera has its own **stream passphrase**, and its stream is encrypted
with it (SRT's own encryption, AES-128). `camera_manager/streamkeys.py` has the whole of it:

sections.doc: Recordings and the camera relay
sections.title: Each camera's stream is encrypted, and only its own phone can send it
trail: The camera relay: the look-ahead, and each camera's own file
sections.text:
- **Made by the manager**, at random (43 characters), one per camera, kept in `<data>/stream-keys.json`, readable by
  its owner only. It is kept as it is, not as a hash: the relay needs the passphrase itself to decrypt the stream. No
  page or API returns it and nothing logs it; what is shown and logged is its eight-digit id.
- **Handed to the phone over the control connection only** (TLS, pinned to the manager's certificate, opened with the
  phone's own credential): in the pairing put on a phone over USB or made by the `pair` command (it leaves the pairing
