sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Performer library: privacy
sections.text:
> **Not legal advice.** This page explains how MCVSAID's performer library handles personal data and summarises
> laws that may apply. Laws change and depend on the facts. Before you use the library anywhere, and especially
> in Illinois, Texas, Washington, California or the EU/UK, get advice from a lawyer who practises there.

The performer library lets the director recognise **consenting performers** so it can give stars priority and have
chosen cameras follow chosen people. It is built so that it can't be used to identify anyone else. This page
covers what it processes, why, where the data is stored, how long it is kept and how it is deleted. It also has
consent templates and a summary of the laws. The design and measurements are in
[PEOPLE_LIBRARY.md](PEOPLE_LIBRARY.md).

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Two purposes, two consents
sections.text:
| | Purpose A: show execution | Purpose B: improving MCVSAID |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What for | Recognising a performer during a show, on the manager computer, to direct the cameras | Evaluating and tuning MCVSAID: recognition thresholds, zoom tracking accuracy, cut timing, as test fixtures and replay benchmarks |
| Needed to enrol? | **Yes**: nobody is enrolled without it | **No**: optional, asked separately, never assumed from A |
| Where the data lives | The library (`people/` in the manager's data folder) | The improvement store (`people-improvement/`), separately encrypted |
| Who it is about | That performer, under their name (seen only by the administrator) | That performer under a random pseudonym. Their name is never stored there |
| Kept for | Until the end of the show day by default. The consent may allow longer, at most 3 years | 12 months by default (configurable, at most 3 years) |
| Withdrawal | Deletes **everything** about the performer, in the library and in the improvement store | Removes them from the improvement store and lists their pseudonym as withdrawn so fixtures made from it are dropped. Their show consent stands |

The improvement purpose prefers **evaluation and threshold tuning** to training models. MCVSAID does not train any
model on performers' data. If training is ever proposed, it will be documented here first and will need its own
explicit, separately recorded consent.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: What is processed
sections.text:
| Data | Kind | Where | Who sees it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where people are in a camera's picture (boxes) | Not identifying: positions only | Memory, for one picture | The director |
| Appearance descriptors of people in a picture | Treated as biometric | Memory, for one picture. A stranger's descriptor is dropped as soon as it fails to match | Nobody |
| Face descriptors of people in a picture, where a face is clear enough | Biometric (face geometry) | Memory, for one picture, compared only with performers whose release covers their face. A stranger's is dropped as soon as it fails to match | Nobody |
| Where each person was a moment ago, per camera (to carry a performer through a look where they are turned away) | Not identifying for anyone not recognised: a box and a time, forgotten after a second | Memory | Nobody |
| Performer's name, role (performer / star), instruments | Identity | Library, encrypted | Administrator only |
| Reference thumbnails (at most 160 px, at most 8 per performer) | Identity, biometric | Library, encrypted | Administrator only |
| Reference appearance descriptors | Identity, treated as biometric | Library, encrypted | The director, under a pseudonymous id, while recognition is on |
| Reference face descriptors, only for performers whose release covers their face, and how clear the face was in each picture | Identity, biometric (face geometry) | Library, encrypted, next to the appearance descriptors; same expiry; deleted with the performer, or alone when they withdraw the face part | The director, under a pseudonymous id, while recognition is on |

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: What is processed
sections.text:
| Data | Kind | Where | Who sees it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Consent records (who gave it, who obtained it, date, scope, retention, release reference) | Identity | Library, encrypted | Administrator only |
| Improvement items: pictures with everyone else blurred, measurements | Pseudonymised | Improvement store, encrypted | Administrator. Developers only through a deliberate export |
| Operational metadata: latencies, cut timing, zoom placement error, rating scores, readiness events | Not identifying: no names, no descriptors | The usual logs and recordings | As today |

**Faces only with their own tick.** Recognition works from how a performer looks on stage: clothes, colours and
build, from a general image model (DINOv2, Apache-2.0) and a colour histogram. With Plus AI's face model in place
(docs/PEOPLE_LIBRARY.md, *Faces*), a performer's face can be used as well, where it is clear enough: only when their
release (or the production's contract) says so, recorded as its own tick beside the show consent. A release signed on
the earlier text of Consent A, which said faces are not used, does not cover it. Without that tick no face
descriptor is ever kept for them, and they are recognised by how they look only. Withdrawing it deletes their face
descriptors and keeps the rest. We treat appearance descriptors as biometric data too, even where a law might not count
them as such.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: What is processed
sections.text:
**Unknown people stay unknown.** Anyone who doesn't match an enrolled performer is "unknown". They are never
named, never given an id that lasts beyond the picture, never followed by identity from one picture to the next,
and their descriptors (appearance and face) are never stored. The matcher keeps no state between pictures. To keep a
performer recognised while they turn away for a moment, each camera remembers where each person's box was for about
a second, and, for a performer only, which performer they were named as; for anyone else, nothing but the box. Unknown people are never zoom
targets unless a camera's focus says the crowd is its subject. Even then they are framed as a crowd, not as
individuals.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Safeguards built in
sections.text:
1. **Off by default.** Recognition is turned on by the administrator for one show day (it switches off at midnight)
   or for one location. While it is on, every dashboard page shows **Performer recognition: ON**.
2. **Consent first, without paperwork in the app.** The releases themselves stay with the production (see *How consent
   is handled*). MCVSAID records only that consent was confirmed, by whom, when, and on what basis. Purpose B is a
   separate tick with its own record.
3. **Only the enrolled are identified.** Matching is limited to the library and is conservative. A match needs high
   similarity and a clear lead over every other performer, and each performer can match at most one person per
   picture. When the matcher is unsure, the answer is "unknown".
4. **Kept apart.** The library holds names. The improvement store holds pseudonyms only. The link between them is in
   the library and is deleted with it.
5. **Blurred before saving.** A picture kept for improvement is checked by the person detector at a low threshold,
   so it errs toward blurring. Everyone who isn't a performer with Purpose B consent is pixelated past recognition
   before the picture is written: strangers, crowd members, and performers who gave only Purpose A consent. If
   finding people fails, nothing is saved. *Residual risk:* someone the detector misses entirely (for example almost
   fully hidden) would not be blurred. Pictures are therefore kept only when needed, and are reviewed before any export.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Safeguards built in
sections.text:
6. **Encrypted at rest.** AES-256-GCM. The key is in the macOS Keychain or the Linux Secret Service, or failing both
   in a key file readable only by the manager's user (0600). "Delete all performer data" deletes the files and the
   key (crypto-shredding).
7. **Stays on this computer.** No cloud services. The models run locally. No names are put in prompts to the shot
   model. The library and the improvement store are left out of location and fleet exports, update bundles, logs
   and crash reports.
8. **Never published.** No names or identity data in recordings, camera files, EDLs, manifests (`.cameras.json`,
   `.cuts.json`, `.looks/`), the audit log or any export. Logs say "performer 2", never a name.
9. **Administrator only.** Only the administrator, at the manager PC, can view, enrol, export or delete. Operators
   and Stage Shots never see names or reference pictures.
10. **Readiness warnings** for: recognition on with no consent records, data past its retention, and an
    improvement export made but not confirmed as handed over.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Retention and deletion
sections.text:
- **Purpose A data** is deleted at the end of the show day by default. The administrator can choose to keep it
  for 7, 30, 90 or 365 days (for example, for a tour), and at most 3 years. Choose no longer than the releases or
  contracts allow. Once its time is up it is deleted automatically, and a
  readiness warning shows until that happens.
- **Purpose B data** is kept for 12 months by default (configurable, at most 3 years) and then deleted automatically.
- **Per performer**: the administrator can delete one performer at any time. Withdrawing Purpose A consent does
  this.
- **Everything**: "Delete all performer data" deletes the library, the improvement store and both keys.
- **Exports already handed over** can't be recalled from this computer. Each export lists the pseudonyms it holds,
  and withdrawals are recorded, so the developers can delete a withdrawn pseudonym's fixtures. The developers
  commit to doing so on their next use.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Sharing with the developers (Purpose B only)
sections.text:
Sharing is never automatic. The administrator makes an export deliberately. It contains only improvement items,
which are already pseudonymised with non-consenting people blurred. It is encrypted with a passphrase of at least
12 characters (scrypt and AES-256-GCM), and each export is recorded in the improvement store's audit trail
(pseudonyms and item counts, never names). A readiness warning stays until the administrator confirms the export
was handed over.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: How consent is handled
sections.text:
Getting consent is the production's job, done before the show the way it already handles releases: a signed
release from each performer, or a clause in their contract. MCVSAID doesn't run the paperwork. It asks for as little
as it can while still keeping a record that consent was confirmed, which BIPA and GDPR both expect you to be able to
show. On the People page, under *Consent and keeping data*, you choose one of two ways:

- **One tick per performer (the default).** Adding a performer has one checkbox: *I have this performer's signed
  release for MCVSAID to recognise them during shows*. A second, optional checkbox records Purpose B. There is no
  pop-up or form beyond these.
- **Handled by contract.** You say once that every performer you enrol has agreed in writing beforehand, by
  contract, and add an optional note (for example, "Tour agreement 2026"). Adding a performer then asks nothing
  about consent. You also say whether the contracts cover Purpose B, and the box can be unticked for anyone who
  opted out. Each performer's record says "covered by contract", with the date and your note. Switching back to
  per-performer ticks applies to new performers only.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: How consent is handled
sections.text:
Either way, Purpose B is never assumed from Purpose A. Everyone enrolled can be removed at once, and removing someone
deletes their data. **Good practice:** keep the releases or contracts where you can find them for as long as you
keep the data. Tell performers which cameras will follow them. Re-take reference pictures on the day, in what they
perform in. Delete their data when the show or tour ends. This is the default: performer data goes at the end of the
show day unless you choose to keep it longer.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Consent templates
sections.text:
Adapt these with your lawyer. Give performers the text in advance, in a language they read well, and keep the
signed copy. A signature can be electronic where the law allows. Use a parent's or guardian's consent for anyone
under 18, or the age of consent where you are.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Consent A: show execution (required to be recognised)
sections.text:
> **Performer recognition for camera direction**
>
> I, ____________________ (name), agree that **[production / band name]** may use MCVSAID, a camera direction
> system, to recognise me during **[show(s), date(s), venue(s)]** so that cameras can follow me and give me
> priority on screen.
>
> - **What is collected:** a few small reference pictures of me and descriptors of my appearance (clothes, colours,
>   build) worked out from them. This may still count as biometric information.
> - ☐ **My face too:** I also agree that a descriptor of my face (face geometry) is worked out from those pictures and
>   used, in the same way and for the same time, to recognise me when my face is clear. If I leave this unticked, my
>   face is not used.
> - **Why:** only to direct the cameras during the show(s) above. It is not used to identify me anywhere else and is
>   never published, sold or shared.
> - **Where:** encrypted on the production's computer. It is not sent to any cloud service.
> - **How long:** deleted at the end of the show day, unless I tick here ☐ to allow it to be kept until
>   ____________ (no more than 3 years), for example for a tour.
> - **Withdrawal:** I can withdraw at any time by telling ____________________. Everything held about me is then
>   deleted.
> - Saying no does not affect whether I can perform.
>
> Signed ____________________  Date __________  Obtained by ____________________  Release no. ______

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Consent B: improving MCVSAID (optional, separate)
sections.text:
> **Helping improve MCVSAID** (optional, and separate from Consent A)
>
> ☐ I agree that data about how MCVSAID recognised and followed me may be kept to test and improve MCVSAID: to check
> recognition thresholds, zoom tracking accuracy and cut timing.
>
> - **What is kept:** measurements, and pictures from the show in which **everyone else is blurred out** before
>   saving. It is stored under a random code, never my name.
> - **Not used to train** any model. Training would need a separate consent.
> - **May be shared** with MCVSAID's developers as an encrypted, coded export with no names.
> - **How long:** up to 12 months (or ____ months), then deleted.
> - **Withdrawal:** I can withdraw at any time without affecting Consent A. My data is then removed from the
>   improvement store, and the developers are told to delete what they hold under my code.
>
> Signed ____________________  Date __________  Obtained by ____________________

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Jurisdiction notes
sections.text:
This is a summary, not a complete statement of the law, and **not legal advice**. "Our approach" is how MCVSAID is
designed. Whether that is enough for your use is for your lawyer to judge.

| Where | Law | Key points | Our approach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EU / EEA (and the UK under UK GDPR) | GDPR | Biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person is special-category data (Art. 9(1)) and needs a condition such as **explicit consent** (Art. 9(2)(a)) on top of a lawful basis (Art. 6). **Purpose limitation** (Art. 5(1)(b)): a new purpose needs its own basis. Data minimisation and storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(c), (e)). Withdrawing must be as easy as consenting (Art. 7(3)). Erasure (Art. 17). Information at collection (Art. 13). Data protection by design and by default (Art. 25). A DPIA (Art. 35) is likely advisable. | Explicit written consent per purpose. Purpose B never inferred from A. Off by default. Minimal thumbnails and descriptors. Deleted at the end of the show day. One-step withdrawal and deletion. Strangers never identified or stored. Template text covers Art. 13 points. Do a DPIA before first use. |

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Jurisdiction notes
sections.text:
| Where | Law | Key points | Our approach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Illinois | Biometric Information Privacy Act (740 ILCS 14) | Covers retina or iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, and scans of hand or face geometry. Needs a **written release** after informing the person in writing of the **specific purpose and length of term** (§15(b)). Needs a public written retention schedule, with destruction when the purpose is satisfied or within 3 years of the last interaction, whichever is first (§15(a)). No selling or profiting (§15(c)). No disclosure without consent (§15(d)). Reasonable care (§15(e)). Private right of action with statutory damages. | A face is used only for performers who tick it in the written release, and BIPA is followed for everyone enrolled. The written release states the purpose and term. This page is the retention schedule. Destroyed at the end of the show day, at most 3 years. Never sold. Disclosed only as a pseudonymised Purpose B export with consent. Encrypted. |
| Texas | Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act (Bus. & Com. Code §503.001) | Covers retina or iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, and records of hand or face geometry. Requires **informing the person and getting consent before capture** for a commercial purpose. No sale or disclosure (narrow exceptions). Reasonable care. Destroy within a reasonable time, no later than the first anniversary of the purpose expiring. Enforced by the Attorney General. | Consent recorded before enrolment. No sale. Encrypted. Purpose A deleted at the end of the show day. Purpose B kept 12 months by default. |

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Jurisdiction notes
sections.text:
| Where | Law | Key points | Our approach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Washington | RCW 19.375 (biometric identifiers) and the My Health My Data Act (RCW 19.373) | RCW 19.375: notice and consent before enrolling a biometric identifier for a commercial purpose, limits on disclosure, and keeping it no longer than needed. MHMDA treats biometric data as consumer health data: **consent to collect and a separate consent to share**, a right to delete, and a private right of action. | Consent before enrolment. Sharing (Purpose B export) needs its own separate consent. Deletion on request or withdrawal. |
| California | CCPA as amended by CPRA (Civ. Code §1798.100 ff.) | Biometric information processed to identify someone is **sensitive personal information**. Notice at collection, including the retention period. Rights to know, delete and correct, and to limit the use of sensitive personal information. Applies to businesses over the thresholds. | Notice and retention in the consent text. Deletion and withdrawal at any time. Used only for the stated purposes. Not sold or shared for advertising. |
| Elsewhere in the US | e.g. Colorado Privacy Act biometric amendments, New York City's biometric signage law for commercial venues, other state privacy acts | Rules vary. Some require notices at venues that collect biometric data from customers. | Audience members are never identified, so no biometric data is collected from them. Check local law for performers. |
| Ohio | No biometric-specific statute at the time of writing | General privacy and consumer protection law still applies. | The same safeguards as everywhere else. |

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Questions people ask
sections.text:
**Can it find someone in the crowd?** No. It can only match people enrolled with consent. Everyone else is
"unknown", and nothing about them is kept.

**Can an operator see who is enrolled?** No. Operators see that recognition is on. Names, pictures and consent
records are on the administrator's dashboard only.

**What happens if a performer changes clothes?** They may not be recognised (they become "unknown") until the
administrator adds a new reference picture with the performer's knowledge. Recognition fails safe: the director
falls back to its usual framing.

sections.doc: Performer library: privacy
sections.title: Face blur
sections.text:
Face blur (an optional, separate, experimental feature, hidden unless an administrator switches it on: [FACE_BLUR.md](FACE_BLUR.md); it may miss faces) can blur everyone in the programme except the
performers this library recognises, or blur only the performers marked "Blur their face" on the People page (someone
who agrees to be recognised but not to have their face shown). It uses the library only as recognition already does: nobody else is identified,
and anyone not recognised as an enrolled, consenting performer is blurred, never shown on a guess. Face blur keeps no
face, picture or descriptor of its own: a face is a rectangle, forgotten once its moment has been shown.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Face blur (experimental)
sections.text:
**Experimental, and hidden unless an administrator switches it on.** It may miss faces, especially small, turned or
fast-moving ones (see the measurements below). Do not rely on it to hide anyone.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In short
sections.text:
**Experimental: it may miss faces, especially small, turned or fast-moving ones. Do not rely on it to hide anyone.**
Hidden, and nothing blurred, until an administrator switches it on in System › This computer › Experimental features
(`face_blur_experimental_enabled`, off by default). Then it is set on the Director page (Face blur, administrator only),
each part marked *Experimental*. Off, its settings, the People page's *Blur their face*, its part of Creator Studio and
its steps in AI assistance are all hidden, and its settings are kept for when it is next switched on. An installation
that was already blurring when the switch was added (a camera or the show set to blur, or a house of worship or Creator
Studio blurring by default) starts with it on, once, and the dashboard says so, so that an update does not silently stop
blurring live. Design, measurements and privacy: [The switch](#the-switch) and the sections after it.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In short
sections.text:
**Where the blurring happens.** For a camera whose picture must never leave it unblurred, choose **On the phone, with
this computer as a backup**: the phone finds and blurs every face itself (YuNet, the detector this computer uses, since
app 0.9.30), before its encoders, so its stream, OBS, the camera files and its own recording are all blurred for good;
and this computer keeps watching that camera ahead of OBS and covers in OBS any face the phone left showing (one
walking in before the phone's first look, one it lost for a moment), knowing which faces the phone already blurred
from the phone's own report of each frame (app 0.9.33). *Only on the phone* leaves it to the phone, and the show's
setting blurs on this computer alone, in OBS, where it can also leave consenting performers clear. The details of each
are below.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In short
sections.text:
- **What.** For the show, and camera by camera: *Off*, *Blur every face* (anonymity, a creator studio, an audience
  camera), or *Blur everyone except consenting performers* (Plus AI: only performers enrolled in the performer library
  and recognised are left clear; anyone else, and anyone not sure, is blurred), or *Blur only chosen people* (Plus AI:
  performers enrolled with their consent and marked *Blur their face* on the People page, blurred wherever they are
  recognised, from the moment they appear). Once switched on, a house of worship starts with the congregation's camera
  blurred and Creator Studio with every face.
- **Live, on time.** Each blurred camera's stream is looked at in the camera relay about 4 s before OBS shows it, ten
  times a second, and each face is covered from the looks on both sides of the moment OBS shows: placed between them,
  widened for movement, a missed look bridged, with a margin. In OBS it is built-in filters only, no plugin: pixelated
  copies of the camera (Scale/Aspect Ratio filters) cropped to each face (Crop/Pad, and an oval mask unless rectangles
  are chosen), in a layer laid over the camera in every scene
  that shows it, moving with the zoom.
- **What is covered:** the whole face and head round it; the face itself, ear to ear and forehead to chin; or only the
  eyes and nose. The smaller two hide less: people can still be recognised by hair, neck, mouth and jaw.
- **The fail-safe.** If a camera's pictures are not all looked at in time (detection stalls, falls behind the look-ahead,
  or cannot tell when OBS shows a picture), its whole picture is blurred, or it is kept off air, for exactly those
  moments, logged and shown in its readiness. It also blurs the first few seconds after starting.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In short
sections.text:
- **It can miss faces** (turned away, in profile, moving fast, partly hidden, small, dark), and a missed face is not
  blurred. Measured on the M5 Pro with faces composited into a recorded 4K street: faces down to 56 px tall in 2160
  covered in every frame live, 31 px about two-thirds of the time; 15 to 19 ms a look; six 4K cameras at ten looks a
  second took about two cores.
- **On the phone** (camera app 0.9.25 or later), camera by camera, for a picture that must never leave the phone
  unblurred: the phone finds every face itself and blurs it before its encoders, so the stream, OBS, the camera files
  and the phone's own recording are blurred for good, with no unblurred copy anywhere (the dashboard says so before
  it is switched on). Every face only: phones recognise nobody. *On the phone, with this computer as a backup* keeps
  looking at the camera here, ahead of OBS, and blurs in OBS (and in recordings afterwards) every face the phone left
  showing: one entering before the phone's first look, one it lost for a moment, one beside or partly outside its
  patch. The phone (app 0.9.33) reports where it blurred each frame, keyed by the frame's timing strip, so faces it
  blurred are told from those it missed; where it was blind, every face found is blurred here. The camera's line shows
  what the phone blurred, what was added here and how often the phone missed a face. On a synthetic clip with the
  phone simulated from its measured recall, it covered 72% of the face-frames the phone left showing (2.4% of all
  down to 0.67%), most faces entering from their first frame. *Only on the phone* leaves it to the phone. Since app 0.9.30 the phone finds faces with
  YuNet (the detector this computer uses) instead of BlazeFace: turned and small faces too, at less cost, with closer
  looks at small faces between whole looks (on test scenes 78-84% of faces found, against 31-38% before; see
  docs/FACE_BLUR.md). With no look-ahead on the phone, a face
  entering is blurred a moment late (about 4 to 7 frames); if the phone's looks stop, it blurs its whole picture. The
  show's look and fail-safe are sent with the camera's settings, and readiness shows the phone's blur and how many looks
  a second it manages.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In short
sections.text:
- **Recordings.** Camera files and the programme can be blurred afterwards, every picture looked at more closely: a
  copy beside each, or in its place. About as long as the recording per file. Exports by hand:
  `python -m camera_manager.blurfiles "<file>"`.
- **On this computer only.** YuNet (MIT, 230 KB, downloaded in AI assistance) through ONNX Runtime, or Apple's Vision on
  a Mac until it is. No face is stored: a rectangle, forgotten once its moment has been shown.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: The switch
sections.text:
`face_blur_experimental_enabled`, off by default, switched in System › This PC › Experimental features (administrator
only, `POST /api/face-blur/experimental {"enabled": true|false}`, audited as `face_blur_experimental_changed`).

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: The switch
sections.text:
- **Off:** nothing is blurred, live or in recordings, whatever the settings below say (`faceblur.enabled` gates
  `settings`, `camera_mode` and `wanted`, so the live blur, `blurfiles.Jobs`, readiness, the system check and the
  director's off-air fail-safe all see every camera as off). The dashboard shows none of it: the Director page's Face
  blur panel, the People page's *Blur their face*, Creator Studio's face blur line and face blur's steps in AI
  assistance are hidden. Changes are refused (`POST /api/face-blur` and ticking *Blur their face* answer 409); unticking
  is allowed. The settings are kept for when it is next switched on. Face blur's layers already in OBS are hidden, as
  when it is set to Off.
- **On:** everything below, as before, marked *Experimental*, with the note above where blur is turned on.
- **Installations from before the switch** (`faceblur.migrate`, once, at start-up): where face blur was in use (the show
  or a camera set to blur, or this kind of event's default: a house of worship's congregation camera, Creator Studio),
  the switch starts on, the dashboard says it was switched on by the update, and the start is audited; elsewhere it
  starts off. Either way the choice is written to `config.json`, so choosing such a kind of event later does not switch
  it on. The note goes once the administrator sets the switch themselves.
- `python -m camera_manager.blurfiles` run by hand is not affected: running it is the choice.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: The switch
sections.text:
Once switched on: optional, off by default. Faces in the programme are made unrecognisable live, placed as OBS shows each moment, and
recordings can be blurred again afterwards with every picture looked at. Code: `camera_manager/faceblur.py` (live),
`camera_manager/faces.py` (the detectors), `camera_manager/blurfiles.py` (recordings), `static/faceblur.js` (the
Director page). Tests: `tests/test_face_blur.py`.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: What can be chosen
sections.text:
For the show, and camera by camera (Director page › Face blur, administrator only):

| Choice | What is blurred |
| --- | --- |
| Off (the default) | Nothing |
| Blur every face | Every face found: anonymity (a creator studio), or a camera on an audience |
| Blur everyone except consenting performers | Every face but those of performers enrolled in the performer library (Plus AI) and recognised in that look. Everyone else is "unknown" and blurred. With no library, recognition off or not Plus, every face is blurred |
| Blur only chosen people | Only the faces of people chosen on the People page: enrolled performers (with their consent, from a camera's picture) with **Blur their face** ticked, for someone who agrees to be recognised but does not want their face shown. Recognised twice a second; once a face is recognised as theirs, it is blurred for the whole time it is in sight, from the moment it appears (the look-ahead holds what comes before the recognition), and so is any face overlapping it. With no library, recognition off or not Plus, every face is blurred, since whose is whose cannot be told |

A performer's face is left clear only when it lies in the head of exactly one person the person detector found, that
person was recognised as the same enrolled performer in every look that asked within a second either side (asked twice
a second), and no other face overlaps it. Anything less is blurred: a mistake shows a blurred performer, not an
unblurred stranger.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: What can be chosen
sections.text:
"Blur only chosen people" works the other way round, so its mistakes do too: a chosen person the camera does not
recognise (turned away for their whole time in sight, changed clothes since their reference pictures) shows unblurred.
Only people enrolled in the library can be chosen: nobody else is ever identified, so a stranger cannot be picked out
to blur; for anonymity of everyone in a picture, use *Blur every face*. In a split screen, or for the programme, a camera
blurring chosen people beside one blurring everyone but performers blurs every face.

Defaults by kind of event (`modes.py`, #108), until the administrator chooses, once the experimental switch is on (with
it off, every kind of event is off):

| Kind of event | Face blur |
| --- | --- |
| Live music, podcast, panel, theatre, cooking | Off |
| House of worship | The congregation's camera (the crowd camera) blurs every face; the others are off. Many churches do not show the congregation's faces |
| Creator Studio (`event_mode: creator`, one or a few people recording themselves) | Every face, with the fail-safe blurring the whole picture |

Also: what is covered (the whole face with a margin round it, 35% of its size by default and more above for hair; the
face itself, ear to ear and forehead to chin; or only the eyes and nose), the shape (an oval, the default, or a rectangle), the strength (at most 4, 6 or 9 blocks from
the top of a face to the bottom), the look (square blocks, or a soft blur), the fail-safe, and whether camera files and
the programme recording are blurred afterwards.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: What can be chosen
sections.text:
**The face, or only the eyes and nose.** YuNet gives each face's eyes, nose tip and mouth corners, and the patch is
placed from them in eye spacings: *the face* reaches 1.25 spacings either side of the eyes' middle (the ears' outer
edges), from a spacing above the eyes (the top of the forehead) to 0.8 below the mouth (the chin); *the eyes and nose*
half a spacing beyond each eye, from just above the eyes to a little below the nose. Both take 40% of the margin. Vision
gives no landmarks, so with Vision the places measured on frontal portraits are used (eyes 28% of the way down its box,
nose 50%, mouth 66%). Both hide less than the whole face and head: people can be recognised by their hair, neck and
outline, and with the eyes and nose only, by their mouth and jaw too. For anonymity, cover the whole face and head.

**Ovals.** Each patch shows only the oval inside its rectangle. Where more faces than patches are joined into one, that
patch stays a rectangle, so no corner of either face is left out.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Live: placed on time from the look-ahead
sections.text:
```
phone ──► relay ──(held ~4 s)──► OBS ──► programme
            │
            └─ spool ─► decoder per blurred camera (live.Follower, VideoToolbox, 1280 wide, 10 a second)
                          │  each picture with when it was taken (its timing strip)
                          ▼
                   faces found (faces.py), kept with the moment OBS shows that picture
                   (captured + that camera's own delay, as the sync keeper measures it: Director.shown_at)
                          │
                          ▼  30 times a second: what OBS shows now
                   patches from the looks on BOTH sides of the moment ─► OBS (one request batch)
```

By the time OBS shows a moment, the faces in it and in the moments either side are already known (measured: a picture
is looked at 30 to 110 ms after its bytes reach the relay; OBS shows it about 4 s later). So each patch is placed from
both sides (`faceblur.Tracker`):

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Live: placed on time from the look-ahead

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In OBS: built-in filters, no plugin
trail: Live: placed on time from the look-ahead
sections.text: For each blurred camera the manager makes, in OBS:

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In OBS: built-in filters, no plugin
trail: Live: placed on time from the look-ahead
sections.text:
- **Pixel scenes** `Face blur · <camera> · 1` … `· 4`: the camera's source stretched over the canvas, with two
  **Scale/Aspect Ratio** filters: down to a coarse grid with *area* sampling (each block the average of what it
  covers), and back up to the canvas with *point* sampling (square blocks) or bilinear (soft). Five block sizes: 6, 16,
  42, 110 and 290 rows on a 1080-row canvas. Each face uses the finest that leaves at most the strength's number of
  blocks down it (4, 6 or 9; for the soft look 2, 3 or 4, since blending between blocks let glasses and a beard show
  through at the square blocks' sizes), so a face near the camera and one at the back are both a few blocks tall.
- **Patch scenes** `Face blur · <camera> · patch 1` … `· patch 8`: each holds one item of every pixel scene (only the
  block size its face needs is shown) and two built-in filters: **Crop/Pad** cuts it to the face's rectangle on that
  block grid, and **Image Mask/Blend** (*Alpha Mask (Alpha Channel)*, stretched), switched on for an oval, keeps only the
  oval inside the rectangle: an oval picture the manager writes to `<data>/faces/oval.png`.
- **A layer** `Face blur · <camera>`: one item per patch scene, placed at its rectangle; one more, of the coarsest
  pixel scene uncropped, is the whole picture (the fail-safe). A patch moving with a face is a change of its crop and
  place, sent with the rest in one request batch.
- **The layer in every scene that shows the camera** (its full-screen scene, the split screens, the scene that keeps
  every stream open), directly above the camera's source and shaped exactly as the source is drawn there: the same crop
  (the zoom, the timing strip) in the same place (`faceblur.twin`). The director's zoom moves the layer in the same
  request batch as the camera on every step of its glide, so the patches stay on the faces as it zooms. Every few
  seconds the layers are re-placed from what OBS says, which follows anything else that moved a source.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In OBS: built-in filters, no plugin
trail: Live: placed on time from the look-ahead
sections.text:
The sync keeper does not crop the timing strip in face blur's own scenes (they must show the whole picture to line up).
"Take face blur out of OBS" (with face blur off) removes all of it.

Why not a plugin. Investigated:

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In OBS: built-in filters, no plugin
trail: Live: placed on time from the look-ahead
sections.text:
| Option | For | Against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Built-in: nested scenes + Scale/Aspect Ratio, Crop/Pad and Image Mask/Blend filters (chosen) | In every OBS on Mac and Linux, nothing to install or keep updated; pixelation by averaging is not reversible like a light blur; each face its own block size; patches are scene items, set in one request batch | A few nested scenes per camera in OBS's list; the layer has to be kept over the camera (done, including during the zoom) |
| Built-in Image Mask/Blend filter with a mask picture | One filter | OBS reloads a changed mask file at most once a second (or on a settings change, which reloads the picture): too slow and too coarse for moving faces; and it cannot pixelate on its own |
| [Composite Blur](https://github.com/FiniteSingularity/obs-composite-blur) (GPL-2.0, widely used) | Real Gaussian/pixelate on the source itself, so the zoom needs no help | One rectangle per filter instance, each blurring the whole 4K frame; a plugin to install and keep matching each OBS release on the Mac and the workstation; not installed on this Mac's OBS 32.2.2 (only OBS's bundled plugins are) |
| [obs-shaderfilter](https://github.com/exeldro/obs-shaderfilter) (GPL-2.0, widely used) with a shader of our own | One pass, any number of rectangles as uniforms, on the source itself | Same installation burden, and a custom GPU shader to maintain in the manager |
| Blurring in the relay (decode, blur, re-encode every camera) | OBS untouched | Six 4K re-encodes live: processor and latency, and the picture's quality |

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: In OBS: built-in filters, no plugin
trail: Live: placed on time from the look-ahead
sections.text:
The built-in way is clearly good enough and needs nothing installed; a shader plugin would only save the layer
keeping-up, which is done.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: The fail-safe
trail: Live: placed on time from the look-ahead
sections.text:
`face_blur_failsafe`: `blur` (the default) covers that camera's whole picture, `off_air` keeps it off air (the director
treats it as unfit, Director.fit) and covers it whole while it is on air, `off` carries on.

It is decided moment by moment from the looks themselves: a moment OBS shows is covered whole when it was not looked at
(no look within 0.4 s on both sides, `face_blur_look_gap_seconds`). That catches detection that stalls (no picture
from the relay, a decoder or detector failure), that falls behind the look-ahead (OBS about to show a moment no one
has looked at), and that loses confidence in time (a picture whose timing strip cannot be read, or a camera whose delay
is not measured, is not looked at, since when OBS shows it cannot be said). It covers exactly those moments, from the
first, and lifts only when looks have been steady for 2 s (`face_blur_recover_seconds`). Starting up, the moments
already on their way to OBS were never looked at, so the picture is blurred whole for the first 4 to 6 s. Each time it
starts and ends is logged (`face_blur_failsafe_on`, `face_blur_failsafe_off`, after a second), and the camera's
readiness says so: *warn*, whole picture blurred, and why; *fail* with no fail-safe.

`off_air` also withholds the camera as soon as its looks stop, before the uncovered moments reach OBS.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: What it cannot do
trail: Live: placed on time from the look-ahead
sections.text:
**Detection misses faces**, and a missed face is not blurred: a face turned to profile or away, moving fast, partly
hidden, small, dark or blurred by motion. The dashboard says so. On the test clip below, faces 56 px tall in a 4K
picture (2.6% of its height) were always covered live, faces 31 px tall about two-thirds of the time. Faces turned
away and occlusion were not tested (see *Not measured*). For a recording that must be anonymous, blur it again
afterwards: every picture is looked at, more closely.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Recordings: exact, afterwards
sections.text:
`blurfiles.py`, two passes of ffmpeg per file:

1. Decode at 15 pictures a second (`face_blur_file_rate`) and 1920 wide, and find the faces in the whole picture and in
   two rows of overlapping pieces (`face_blur_file_rows`): closer than live.
2. Decode again and encode: for every picture, the faces on both sides of it in time (the same `Tracker`, with the
   whole file in hand), drawn into a grey mask (one value per block size), piped to ffmpeg, which lays the matching
   pixelated copy over the picture where the mask says (`scale` area/neighbor, `alphamerge`, `overlay`). Sound copied.
   On a Mac encoded by VideoToolbox at the file's own bit rate, elsewhere x264.

`face_blur_files` (each camera file, by its camera's choice) and `face_blur_programme` (the programme recording, by the
choice of whichever camera was on air when, from the cut log; the stricter of two in a split screen; the strictest of
all before the first cut): `copy` makes `<name> (faces blurred).<ext>` beside it; `replace` puts the blurred file in its
place under its own name, so the cut log, the EDL and the camera files' manifest still name it, and no unblurred copy
is kept. Runs after the camera files are made, two files at a time; progress on the Director page.

Exports from an editor, by hand:

    python -m camera_manager.blurfiles "<export>.mp4" --model <data>/faces/face_detection_yunet_2023mar.onnx

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Face detection on this computer
sections.text:
| | On a Mac | On Linux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default | YuNet, once downloaded (AI assistance › *Face blur: download the face detector*); until then Apple's Vision | YuNet |
| YuNet | OpenCV model zoo, `face_detection_yunet_2023mar.onnx`, **MIT**, 230 KB, via ONNX Runtime (Core ML on a Mac, CUDA or CPU on Linux); checked against a pinned SHA-256 | same |
| Vision | `VNDetectFaceRectanglesRequest`, part of macOS (as `gaze.py` uses) | – |
| Both (`face_blur_detector: both`) | Vision and YuNet together, everything either finds | – |

InsightFace's detectors (SCRFD, RetinaFace weights) are not used: their published weights are for non-commercial
research only. Live, each picture is looked at whole and as two overlapping halves (`face_blur_rows` 1), which suits
YuNet's square input and doubles the size at which a 16:9 picture's faces are seen.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured on the M5 Pro (2026-10-17)
sections.text:
The recorded camera files in `~/Videos/Program/*cameras/` have no faces in them: the cameras filmed a room's ceiling,
a desk and a street with one distant walker, whose face Vision did not find in any of 132 looks (S23, 11-27-40,
225-291 s). So detection speed and the live path were measured on those files, and accuracy on a **test clip made from
one of them**: 24 s of the S23's street (11-27-40 from 232 s, 4K, its timing strip intact) with five faces from
public-domain NASA portraits composited in, moving across it at known positions: a near walker (face 267 px tall in
2160), a fast walker (133 px, 450 px/s), a far walker (56 px), a presenter close up (563 px, swaying) and a tiny one
(31 px). Truth is exact; a face hidden behind a nearer one for more than half its area is not counted. Frontal faces
only: this says nothing about profiles.

**Detection, per picture**, a 4K picture decoded 1280 wide (median):

| Detector | Whole picture | With two halves | 1920 wide, two rows of pieces (files) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vision | 5.7 ms | 13.0 ms | – |
| YuNet (Core ML) | 4.9 ms | 14.8 ms | 41 ms |
| Both | 10.4 ms | 28.5 ms | – |

**Faces found** (looks that found each face / looks it was in, 10 looks a second):

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured on the M5 Pro (2026-10-17)
sections.text:
| Face height in 2160 | 563 | 267 | 133 | 56 | 31 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vision, whole | 160/161 | 90/92 | 45/85 | 0/138 | 0/232 |
| Vision, with halves | 160/161 | 92/92 | 74/85 | 0/138 | 0/232 |
| YuNet, whole | 160/161 | 92/92 | 84/85 | 59/138 | 0/232 |
| **YuNet, with halves (live default)** | 160/161 | 92/92 | 85/85 | 133/138 | 48/232 |
| YuNet 1920, two rows, 15 a second (files default) | 241/241 | 138/138 | 128/128 | 207/207 | 240/347 |

Vision does not find a face smaller than about a twentieth of the picture's height however large the picture it is
given, hence YuNet by default.

**Live blur accuracy**: frames (30 a second) in which the whole face lay inside a patch, simulating the live path
(looks at the given rate, patches worked out for each frame OBS shows, shown with a random timing error):

| | 563 | 267 | 133 | 56 | 31 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| YuNet with halves, 10 looks/s, ±50 ms | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 67% |
| … 5 looks/s, ±50 ms | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 68% |
| Vision with halves, 10 looks/s, ±50 ms | 100% | 100% | 100% | 45%* | 37%* |
| Files (YuNet 1920, two rows, 15/s) | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 95% |

\* covered only while passing behind another face's patch. The picture was 16% blurred on average (most of it the
presenter close up, with the margin).

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured on the M5 Pro (2026-10-17)
sections.text:
**Timing.** A face is wholly covered as long as OBS's real delay is within about 0.1 s of the measured one; with the
sync keeper's reading 0.2 s out, the fast walker was wholly covered in 95% of frames (99.6% of its area); 0.3 s out,
13% (81%). Early is safer than late (0.2 s early: 100%). If a camera's delay is uncertain, raise
`face_blur_pad_seconds`. The zoom-tracking measurements (docs/PEOPLE_LIBRARY.md, the director's 5.4 s against 5.5 s)
put the director's timing within that.

**The live path with six 4K cameras**: a stand-in relay wrote six recorded 4K streams into a spool in real time (the
test clip and five 2026-10-15 camera files), decoded by `live.Followers` with VideoToolbox at 1280 wide, 10 a second,
and looked at by `FaceBlur.look` (YuNet with halves, three threads), 40 s:

| | Per camera |
| --- | --- |
| Looks a second | 8.8 to 10.1 |
| Detection | 15 to 19 ms median, 22.5 ms at most (p95) |
| Picture's age when looked at (from reaching the relay) | 27 to 86 ms median, 114 ms at most (p95) |
| Processor, all six | decoders about 1 to 1.2 cores, detection about 1 core (Both: 1.75) |

The video decoder's load (the media engine, which OBS also uses for the same six streams) was not measured: watch the
System page's *Video decoding* line when turning face blur on for many 4K cameras.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured on the M5 Pro (2026-10-17)
sections.text:
**On a busy Mac** (2026-10-17, live: load average 61 on the 18-core M5 Pro, with other work using about 12 cores), YuNet
with halves took about 45 ms a picture, every camera's looks fell 0.4 s apart and the fail-safe started every few
seconds on all four cameras. Three things made it worse, and were changed:
- The cameras were looked at in rounds, all at once, so the slowest held back the others, with three threads for four
  cameras. Now each camera is looked at again as soon as its last look is done, one look at a time, with a thread for
  every blurred camera (`face_blur_workers` at least).
- VideoToolbox, once it gave no picture for 4 s, was given up for good: all four decoders were left on the processor at
  about 40% of a core each. Now it is tried again after a minute, then after longer each time (up to 10 minutes), and
  on a new connection once a minute has passed.
- Neither was shown. Each camera's line now says how long finding the faces takes (median and most) and what decodes
  its pictures, as does the fail-safe's reason ("looks were 0.6 s apart (finding the faces took 45 ms a picture, at
  most 80 ms; decoded on the processor)").

**Recordings**: a 60 s 4K camera file took 63 s (about 2.8 cores); two at once, 90 s for both. A two-hour show with six
camera files and the programme is an overnight job; blur only the cameras that need it.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Not measured
sections.text:
- **OBS itself.** The live OBS on this Mac was not touched (a show could be running). The OBS side was tested against a
  model of OBS's compositor (`tests/test_face_blur.py`: crop, bounds, nested scenes, Scale/Aspect Ratio with area and
  point sampling), which checks that the patches land on the face through the zoom, in the split screens and the scene
  that keeps streams open, and nowhere else. To check in OBS, off air: turn face blur on for one camera, look at its
  scene in the preview, and watch OBS's render time (Stats) with several faces.
- Faces turned away, in profile, occluded, at night or blurred by motion; real audiences.
- Recognition of performers for "everyone except performers": that needs a consenting rehearsal (as the performer
  library itself does).
- The Linux workstation: YuNet's speed there (CUDA or CPU).

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Blurring on the phones
sections.text:
For a camera whose picture must never leave the phone unblurred (strict anonymity, an untrusted network): Director ›
Face blur › camera by camera › *On the phone*. The camera app (0.9.25 or later) then finds the faces itself and blurs
every one before its encoders, so the stream, the relay's spool and camera files, OBS, and the phone's own recording are
all blurred. **For good: no unblurred copy exists anywhere**, and the dashboard says so before it is switched on.

- **Every face only.** The phone does not recognise anyone, and must not: *everyone except consenting performers* and
  *only chosen people* stay with the manager. The show's look (margin, strength, style, what is covered, shape) and its
  fail-safe apply on the phone too.
- ***On the phone, with this computer as a backup*** keeps looking at that camera here too, and blurs in OBS every
  face the phone left showing (*The backup*, below); ***Only on the phone*** leaves it to the phone, and nothing more is
  done for that camera here, live or afterwards.
- **Sent with the camera's settings.** The manager compares the phone's own account (telemetry `face_blur.chosen`) with
  what it should be and sends `faceblur.settings` when they differ, again every 15 s while they still do. It takes
  effect at once, streaming or not (switching it on or off redraws the picture's filters: a moment's pause). An app
  too old to blur is shown as *fail* in the camera's readiness, never taken to be blurring.
- **Readiness** has a line for it: looks a second, how long each takes, faces now; or the fail-safe, and why.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: How it works on the phone
sections.text:
`FaceBlurFilter` in the app is drawn after the timing strip (`TimecodeFilter`), whose rows it never blurs. Up to 8 times
a second (`face_blur_phone_rate`) the frame as it comes in is drawn 640 pixels wide a row of `face_blur_phone_rows`
(1280 at the default 2) into a small buffer and read back on the next frame (`SmallPicture`, the same way the shot
chooser's pictures are made, so the encoder never waits), and handed to `FaceFinder` on a thread of its own. Since app
0.9.30 that runs OpenCV's **YuNet** (2023mar, MIT; the detector this computer uses, converted for LiteRT with its input
fixed, 230 KB) through **LiteRT** (formerly TensorFlow Lite, Apache-2.0) on the processor, over the picture in 640 × 384
pieces at its own size: one at rows 1 (640 wide), four at 2, nine at 3 (1920). After each whole look, while small faces
are being followed (under 12% of the picture's height), they are **looked at closer** once before the next:
squares of the full frame four times their size (at least a tenth of its height), drawn 320 pixels and looked at with
YuNet's 320 × 320 input, at most four a look; a distant face is then several times larger to the model. A closer look
moves the faces' tracks on, but says nothing of the rest of the picture, so it never counts as a look for the
fail-safe. 0.9.25 to 0.9.29 used MediaPipe's BlazeFace full-range in 192-pixel squares (*Which detector*, below). The
faces go to `FaceTracker`, which for each frame says where to blur. A shader pixelates (or softens: since 0.9.31 it blends the averages of the
nearest blocks, half as many down a face) up to 8 rectangles or ovals given as uniforms; more faces are joined
into fewer rectangles, never left out. The manager's small pictures from a blurring phone are taken after the blur.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: How it works on the phone
sections.text:
- **No look-ahead**, so each face is followed from look to look: covered where it was last seen and where its measured
  speed has taken it since, widened by what a misjudged speed could do; a face seen only once is given room for a brisk
  walk; a face lost (a missed look, turned away) is held 0.6 s, spreading. A face **entering** is covered from the first
  look that finds it: late by half a look's interval on average, plus the look's time and a frame.
- **The fail-safe.** When no picture taken in the last 0.7 s has been looked at (detection stopped, fell behind, or the
  model failed), the whole picture is blurred (in 110-row blocks, the strip left clear) until looks have been steady for
  1.5 s, and the phone reports it (`face_blur.state` `failsafe`, with why and for how long). It is blind from the start
  too, so the first second and a half after arming is blurred whole. With the show's fail-safe *off* it is reported
  but not blurred; with *off air*, the director also keeps the camera off air while its phone is blind.
- **A graphics chip that refuses the shader** never lets faces through: the filter falls back to blurring the whole
  picture, then to black, and readiness says so. That happened on every phone with 0.9.25: the shader named a variable
  `half`, a word GLSL ES keeps for itself, so face blur blurred the whole picture (and found no faces) until 0.9.26.
  The app's checks now look for such words (`tools/tests/ShaderWordsTest.java`), and the shaders were compiled on an
  S23+'s Adreno 740 before 0.9.26 was released.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: How it works on the phone
sections.text:
- **Holding the encoder back** a few frames, so that a face entering could be covered from both sides as the manager
  does, was weighed and not built: it would need about 5 frames held (the look interval and its time), that is 165 ms
  more delay, sound and picture 5 frames apart, and 5 copies of the frame on the graphics chip (about 165 MB at 4K),
  which the Pixel 3 and 4a do not have to spare. *On the phone, with this computer as a backup* gives that layer instead (*The backup*, below).

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured
sections.text:
**Which detector, since 0.9.30** (on the Mac, the app's own looks; 57 public-domain NASA photographs of audiences,
classrooms, stages, crowds and races, framed 1920 × 1080, each also shrunk to a half and to 0.3 into an empty room
recorded by the cameras, 171 pictures, 2,410 faces). The reference is Apple's Vision run on the full picture and on
enlarged overlapping pieces of it, with what YuNet and BlazeFace each found there surely (0.8) added, checked by eye
on samples: it misses some faces in crowds, so the share found is a share of the faces the reference knows. Vision
also says how far each face is turned (*frontal* under 20°, *turned* 20–50°, *profile* beyond); 1,267 faces were
found only by the others, mostly small ones. A face is found when a box overlaps it by a quarter or the two hold each
other's middles. Faces under 16 pixels tall in 1080 are under 6 pixels in the 640-wide picture, and none is found
there.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured
sections.text:
- **YuNet finds about two and a half times as many faces as BlazeFace at the same setting**, turned and in profile as
  well as frontal (a profile is found as often as a frontal face: the misses are small faces and faces seen from above
  or behind), and the whole picture at 640 wide finds more than BlazeFace's 28 squares. Its *unmatched* finds were
  looked at one by one (rows 2): nearly all were real heads the reference had missed, many from behind, in profile or
  looking down; a few were hands or bright shapes. For blurring those are on the safe side.
- **Closer looks** add most where faces are small: at rows 1 they find a fifth more of the frontal faces, at rows 2 the
  smallest faces (16–24 px) go from 70% to 78%. Here they were aimed at the faces the whole look had just found in the
  same picture; in the app they are aimed at the faces being followed, in newer frames, so they also move those faces
  on between whole looks (more looks a second for the faces that matter).
- **People, for following** (EfficientDet-Lite0 at 0.4, 640-wide picture, the 462 people Vision found in the same
  pictures): following steers by a face or, when none is found in the top of a person's box, by the person. The share
  of people it has something to steer by:

| People | BlazeFace face (0.9.27–0.9.29) | YuNet face | **YuNet face or the person (0.9.30)** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| full size (154) | 38% | 67% | 92% |
| half size (154) | 18% | 50% | 69% |
| 0.3 size (154) | 9% | 23% | 43% |
| all (462) | 22% | 47% | 68% |

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured
sections.text:
Of the 246 people whose face YuNet did not find, 98 (40%) were found as people. EfficientDet-Lite2 (448 pixels,
  7.6 MB) found 87% of the people against Lite0's 76% at 0.3 (62% at 0.4), but with more false finds and at more than
  twice the time; Lite0 at 0.4 was kept. A head is estimated from a person's box as measured on these pictures (a
  face's height is about 0.3 of the box's width, half of them 0.24 to 0.35; its middle about its own height below the
  top).

**Which model, and how the picture is cut, 0.9.25 to 0.9.29** (on the Mac, the same decoding as the app; 192 camera frames from the
2026-10-16 recordings, 1920×1080, with three heads from public-domain NASA portraits put into each at random places,
24 frames a face size; the picture scaled to 640 wide as the phone does; recall: faces found with their box overlapping
the true one by a quarter or more; no false finds in the 12 empty frames except where said):

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured
sections.text:
| Model, squares | ms a picture on the M5 Pro | 24 px | 32 | 44 | 60 | 80 | 120 | 200 | 360 (of 1080) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| short-range, whole picture | 4.4 | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 92% | 100% |
| short-range, rows 1–2 (3 false finds) | 12.0 | 0% | 0% | 11% | 91% | 96% | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| full-range, whole picture | 5.5 | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 1% | 54% | 100% | 100% |
| full-range, row 1 | 9.2 | 0% | 0% | 0% | 30% | 70% | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| **full-range, rows 1–2 (10 squares, the default)** | 20.1 | 11% | 39% | 89% | 97% | 99% | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| full-range, rows 1–3 (28 squares; 1 false find) | 46.8 | 49% | 86% | 99% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% |

The short-range model (224 KB) is made for faces near a phone held at arm's length and finds nothing a stage camera
would show at a distance; the full-range model needs the picture cut into squares too. A 960-wide picture added
nothing over 640 with rows 1–2 (with rows 1–3 it found more of the smallest faces: 62% at 24 px, against 49%).

**How late a face entering is covered** (`FaceTracker` itself, in a simulation of 400 faces each, entering at a random
moment, a frame every 33 ms; a look's time varied ±20%):

sections.title: Measured
sections.text:
| Looks | Each takes | Late by (frames, median / 90% / worst) | Uncovered after that |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| every 125 ms (8 a second) | 40 ms | 4 / 6 / 6 | none |
| every 125 ms | 80 ms | 5 / 7 / 7 | none |
| every 125 ms | 150 ms | 7 / 10 / 12 | none |
| every 200 ms | 80 ms | 6 / 9 / 10 | none |
| every 250 ms | 150 ms | 9 / 12 / 14 | none |
| every 500 ms | 300 ms | 18 / 24 / 27 | 9.5% of frames for a face walking half the width a second |

Once found, a face walking up to half the picture's width a second was covered in every frame; one running across the
whole width in a second can be uncovered for 2 frames before its speed is known (`tools/tests/FaceTrackerTest.java`).

**The detectors on a phone, since 0.9.30** (2026-10-22, from the shell, the app's own YuNet, People and Faces classes and LiteRT
1.4.2 on 2 threads, on a 1920 × 1080 test scene with 30 faces, drawn as the app draws it; 15 looks each, the camera app
not armed):

| Look | Galaxy S23+ (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2), median (slowest) | Pixel 8 (Tensor G3) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| YuNet rows 1: 640 wide, 1 piece | 10 ms (19) | 11 ms (24) |
| **YuNet rows 2: 1280 wide, 4 pieces (the default)** | 39 ms (41) | 44 ms (47) |
| YuNet rows 3: 1920 wide, 9 pieces | 85 ms (89) | 97 ms (101) |
| A closer look: 4 crops of 320 | 15 ms (18) | 17 ms (20) |
| People (EfficientDet-Lite0), while following | 20 ms (30) | 24 ms (35) |
| BlazeFace, 2 squares (following, 0.9.27–0.9.29), for comparison | 10 ms (17) | 12 ms (32) |
| BlazeFace, 10 squares (blur, 0.9.25–0.9.29), for comparison | 49 ms (58) | 55 ms (73) |

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured
sections.text:
- The **graphics chip** (LiteRT's GPU delegate 1.4.2) was slower for every one of these small models, on both phones:
  YuNet rows 2 took 58 ms on the S23+'s Adreno 740 (130 on the Pixel 8), a closer look 33 (52) and the people model
  46 (124), against 39, 15 and 20 on the processor, besides more than half a second to load. **4 threads** were no faster than 2. The app runs them on the processor, 2
  threads.
- Following alone (blur off) is a YuNet look at rows 1 and the people model: about 35 ms a look on the Pixel 8, 8 a
  second, against 10–12 ms for BlazeFace's 2 squares before, for three times as many people to steer by. Blur at the
  default costs a little less than before (39 ms against 49 on the S23+) and finds two and a half times as many faces.

**In the app, since 0.9.30** (signed test builds of 0.9.30 on a Galaxy S23+, live manager, 2026-10-22; 4K at 25 Mb/s,
*Only on the phone*, the show's look; stream only; read from the phone's telemetry every 10 s). The camera saw a desk
with one person at it, about a quarter of the picture tall, turning now and then; with following on, the gimbal was
not connected, so the phone looked for people too but turned nothing:

| Looks | Looks a second | A look, median (range) | Frames | Phone |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Blur, rows 2 | 6.0–6.4 | 67–94 ms (as it warmed) | 30 fps, none dropped | 31–39 °C |
| Blur and following (people too) | 5.0 (4.6 lowest) | 115 ms (104–120) | 30 fps, none dropped | 34–38 °C |
| Blur alone, the same minutes | 6.0 | 77 ms (69–80) | 30 fps, none dropped | 34 °C |

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured
sections.text:
- **The person was blurred** throughout, turned away included (checked on frames from the relay), and the fail-safe
  never covered the whole picture. The S23+ looked about as fast as with BlazeFace in 0.9.26 (94 ms a look at 4K),
  while finding far more faces (above). A look slows by about a third as the phone warms from 31 to 39 °C.
- **Following costs about 38 ms a look** on top of blur at 1280 wide. The first build took 85 ms more: it averaged
  every pixel of the picture for the people model, nearly a million reads a look; four spread over each of its pixels
  are enough. Alone (blur off) following looks at 640 wide, where the people model's picture is a quarter of that.
- **Closer looks** did not run: the only face was too large to need one (a quarter of the picture's height; only faces
  under 12% get them), as intended. They were first written to fit between whole looks, and at 4K on an S23+ none
  ever fitted (a whole look took 70 ms of the 125 between them); now one follows each whole look while small faces are
  followed. Their drawing and decoding were checked from the shell (above) and by tools/tests, not yet in the app on a
  small face.
- **Not measured:** steering the gimbal by a person's body (no gimbal was connected), recording on the phone at the
  same time, the Pixel 3, 4a and the S20 FE.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured
sections.text:
**The detector on a phone, 0.9.25 to 0.9.29** (Galaxy S23, Snapdragon 8 Gen 2, 2026-10-22). The app's own look (BlazeFace.java, the
same sampling and LiteRT 1.4.2 with XNNPACK) was run from the shell on a 640×360 picture with faces 200, 90 and 50 px
tall in 1080, 20 looks each, with the camera app not armed:

| Squares | A look, median (most) | The model's share | Found |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| rows 1 (2 squares) | 15 ms (16) | 12 ms | 200 and 90 px |
| **rows 1–2 (10 squares, the default)** | 71 ms (74) | 60 ms | all three |
| rows 1–3 (28 squares) | 196 ms (203) | 169 ms | all three, the 50 px face surer (0.96 against 0.84) |

About 6 ms a square, against 2 on the M5 Pro; 2 or 4 threads were no faster than 1 from the shell. At 8 looks a second
the default keeps one core about 57% busy. The older phones are expected to be 2 to 4 times slower: still inside the
fail-safe's 0.7 s at rows 1–2, with faces entering blurred later (the simulation above gives 7 to 12 frames at 150 ms
a look).

**In the app, on the phones, 0.9.26** (camera app 0.9.26, live manager, 2026-10-22, no show on). Two phones streamed to the
relay and OBS, stream only, with *Only on the phone* and the show's look (strong, soft, the face itself, oval, margin
0.2), 20 minutes each at 1080p (7 Mb/s) and 4K (25 Mb/s), then about 5 minutes with face blur off for comparison. Read
from their telemetry every 10 s. The cameras saw a room, and a person now and then (1 or 2 faces at most):

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Measured
sections.text:
- **No frames were lost to face blur.** Both phones held 30 frames a second throughout, the same as with it off; the
  few frames dropped in sending (1 and 10) are the network's, as often with it off.
- **Detection time** stayed inside the fail-safe's 0.7 s everywhere: the whole picture was never blurred for want of a
  look. The S23+ took about 93 ms a look at either size; the Pixel 8 about 125 ms cool, slowing to 250 ms as it warmed
  to 41 °C (Android's thermal status "moderate") in its 1080p run, and back to 127 ms once cooler at 4K. Both slower
  than the S23+ benchmark from the shell (71 ms), since the camera, encoder and network share the processor.
- **Battery:** face blur adds roughly 5 to 20 percentage points an hour (the comparison runs were only 5 minutes, so
  this is coarse). Battery temperature followed the room and the phones' coolers more than face blur: no rise was
  seen that face blur alone explains, except perhaps the Pixel 8's 41 °C at 1080p.
- **A face entering**, from the simulation above at the measured rates: about 5 frames late (median) on the S23+
  (7 looks a second, about 95 ms each), and 6 to 10 on the Pixel 8 (4 to 6 looks a second, 125–190 ms). Not measured
  with people walking in on cue.
- **Not measured:** the Pixel 3, 4a and the other Pixel 8, the S20 FE and the S23 were not connected; one S23+ ran
  another session's test build and was left out. Recording on the phone at the same time (a second encoder) was not
  tried. The older phones are expected to look 2 to 4 times slower: if one cannot keep its looks within 0.7 s (its whole
  picture then stays blurred), set `face_blur_phone_rows` to 1 (since 0.9.30 the picture 640 wide: faces from about 30 px; before, 2 squares, from about 120 px) or lower
  `face_blur_phone_rate`.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: The backup: this computer catching what the phone missed
sections.text:
*On the phone, with this computer as a backup* (`face_blur_phones` `both`) has the phone blur every face, as above, and
this computer keep looking at the camera's relay stream ahead of OBS as it does for any blurred camera, covering in
OBS every face it finds that the phone left showing. The phone has no look-ahead; this computer has four seconds of it,
so it can cover a face entering from before the phone's first look, one the phone lost for a moment, and one beside or
partly outside the phone's patch, from both sides of the moment.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: The backup: this computer catching what the phone missed
sections.text:
- **The phone says where it blurred** (app 0.9.33): each frame's patches, as fractions of the picture as it goes out
  (turned for a phone set to 180°), keyed by the time in that frame's timing strip, and whether the frame was blind or
  blurred whole (`CoverLog` in the app; message `face_blur_cover`, twice a second: a few numbers a frame). It is sent only to a
  manager that asked since it connected (`cover` in `faceblur.settings`, sent only to an app whose capabilities say
  `face_blur_cover`), since an older manager closes the connection on a message it does not know.
- **Each look here is judged against that very frame** (the strip's time read from the picture is the phone's own):
  a face whose covered part (the show's area) lies inside the phone's patches, all but 15% of it, or in a frame blurred
  whole, is the phone's (*covered*); one with a patch on part of it is *partly* missed; one with none, or in a blind
  frame, *missed*. Only those go to the tracker and are blurred here, placed from both sides as usual. A look waits up
  to `face_blur_phone_wait_seconds` (1.5 s) for its frame's report, well inside the look-ahead; a frame not reported by
  then (*unreported*), or from a phone that cannot report, has every face found blurred here.
- **The fail-safe.** A moment this computer did not look at is blurred whole by its own fail-safe, unless the phone
  reported blurring that frame (its faces, or the whole picture): then the phone stands, as *Only on the phone* would,
  and with *off air* the camera is not kept off air for it. Where neither looked, the whole picture is blurred.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: The backup: this computer catching what the phone missed
sections.text:
- **The picture itself is not used as a cue.** A blurred patch looks flat (block averages), so it was tried as a cue
  for when a report is late: on the measurement below, faces the manager found inside the phone's patches had a median
  flatness (the share of a face's box with next to no fine detail) of 0.44 and 0.79 on the two runs, and faces left
  showing 0.36 and 0.39, with a tenth of them above 0.89: compressed, a smooth face looks as flat as the phone's blocks,
  and YuNet still finds small pixelated faces whose blocks are not flat. A cue that wrong would leave misses unblurred,
  so a late report means every face found is blurred here.
- **What it shows.** The camera's line on the Director page and its readiness: what the phone blurred in the frames
  looked at here, how many faces it left showing that were blurred here (and how many partly outside its blur), as a
  share of the faces seen, over the last minute and since the manager started; whether the phone is reporting; and when
  the phone is blind. Each face caught is logged (`face_blur_backup_caught`). The share over-counts with the soft blur:
  YuNet finds about half the faces the phone softened, and their boxes reach past its oval (blurred again here, which
  does no harm).
- **Recordings.** A backed-up camera counts as *every face* for the recordings' pass (*Recordings*, above): its camera
  file, and the programme while it is on air, are looked at again afterwards and every face found is blurred; in a file
  the phone already blurred those are the faces it left showing (and now and then a small face found through its
  blocks). *Only on the phone* gets no pass here.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: The backup: this computer catching what the phone missed
sections.text:
- **Patches before and after a face is seen** now reach along its movement (*Live*, above), for every camera.

**Measured** (`tools/blur_backup_bench.py`, 2026-10-23, on the M5 Pro). A synthetic clip, 30 frames a second, twice
120 s (two random seeds): 12 people in each, cut from 14 public-domain NASA portraits and put into recorded camera
pictures, standing, appearing, walking in from either side or hurrying across, 40 to 220 px tall in 1080; now and then
a face is hard to find for 0.4–1.6 s (drawn blurred and darker: turned, in shadow, moving). The phone is simulated as
`FaceTracker` works (ported), looking 8 times a second, each look ready 40–80 ms later, finding each face with the
chance measured for YuNet at rows 2 with closer looks for its size (a hard face a quarter as often), and its blur drawn
into the picture (medium, oval, margin 0.35), compressed (JPEG 80). The manager is the real `FaceBlur` with YuNet,
looking ten times a second at 1280 wide, with the phone's reports 0.5 s after each frame. A face is *showing* in a frame
when over a quarter of its box is outside the phone's blur; *caught* when under a tenth of it is outside both.

sections.title: The backup: this computer catching what the phone missed
sections.text:
| | Seed 3 | Seed 11 | Both |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Face-frames | 5,173 | 4,805 | 9,978 |
| Left showing by the phone | 100 (1.9%) | 139 (2.9%) | 239 (2.4%) |
| … covered by the manager | 52 (52%) | 120 (86%) | 172 (72%) |
| Left showing by both | 48 (0.93%) | 19 (0.40%) | 67 (0.67%) |
