sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: The backup: this computer catching what the phone missed
sections.text:
- **A face entering** (23 episodes, 89 frames): 78% of its frames caught, 11 of the 23 from their first frame; the
  look-ahead is what the phone lacks. Missed: a face only partly in the picture at the edge, which YuNet does not find either.
- **A face hard to find** (15 episodes, 144 frames): 72% caught, but unevenly (30% on seed 3, 98% on seed 11): this
  computer uses the same detector as the phone, so a face the phone cannot find is often hard here too; its gain is
  more looks and both sides of each moment, not a better detector.
- **Lost a moment** (4 episodes, 1–3 frames each): none caught; all were slivers of a face leaving at the edge.
- **The reports save doubled-up patches**: faces the phone had blurred were covered here too in 388 and 306 face-frames
  with reports, against 2,112 and 1,815 without (a late report, or an older app), where every face found is blurred
  here; patches on no face at all, 163–176 patch-frames against 244–293. What reaches OBS is no less safe without them.
- **Patches reaching along a face's movement** before and after it is seen made little difference here (86.3% against
  84.2% on seed 11, the same on seed 3).
- **Not measured:** real phone-blurred footage with people walking in (the cameras were not used for this); real
  faces turned away rather than drawn blurred; the phone's real misses, which this simulates from its measured recall.
  The dashboard's own count of the phone's misses (above) is the measurement to watch in a show.

sections.doc: Face blur (experimental)
sections.title: Privacy
sections.text:
- Nothing leaves this computer: pictures are decoded and looked at in memory, and the detectors run here.
- Blurring on the phones: each phone looks at its own pictures, in memory, overwritten by the next. It tells the
  manager how many faces it is blurring, how fast it looks, and whether its fail-safe is on; and, only for a manager
  backing it up that asked, the rectangles it blurred in each frame, over the camera network to this computer, kept
  here 30 s. Never a picture of a face, or anything else about one.
- A face is a rectangle and a confidence, kept only until its moment has been shown (20 s live), or until the file is
  made. No face pictures, descriptors or identities are stored. Logs say which camera's fail-safe started and why,
  never anything about a face.
- "Everyone except consenting performers" uses the performer library under its own rules
  ([PRIVACY_PERFORMER_LIBRARY.md](PRIVACY_PERFORMER_LIBRARY.md)): only enrolled, consenting performers are ever
  recognised; nobody else is identified, and anyone not recognised is blurred.
- Blurring is not a guarantee of anonymity: detection misses faces, and people can be recognised by their voice,
  clothes, build, tattoos or where they are. For strict anonymity keep the fail-safe on, blur recordings afterwards
  with `replace`, and check the result before publishing.

sections.doc: Locations, and moving a set-up to another PC
sections.title: Locations, and moving a set-up to another PC
sections.text: Back to [the manager's README](../README.md).

sections.doc: Locations, and moving a set-up to another PC
sections.title: Locations
sections.text:
A location is a set of cameras with its own way of running a show: the fleet (which cameras the manager answers for,
the name it goes by there, the certificates they expect) and the settings (what each camera shows, the stage picture,
how shots are chosen, the look-ahead). One PC keeps several and has one in use at a time. System › Locations &
backups, for the administrator, does all of this:

- **Switch** puts the location in use away exactly as it stands and brings another out. The manager restarts, and
  then lets in that location's cameras only. It is refused while cameras are connected.
- **New location** starts with no cameras, to pair some into: a set can be made ready here for a PC somewhere else.
- **Export** seals a location, cameras and settings together, with a passphrase; **Add a location from a file**
  adds one to the list without touching the one in use.
- **Restore points** keep the state of the location in use. One is made before a switch, an import or a restore,
  and whenever asked for; restoring brings back the settings, or the settings and the cameras. Forty are kept for
  each location, the ones made by hand outlasting the automatic ones.

sections.doc: Locations, and moving a set-up to another PC
sections.title: Cameras a location does not use, and removing a camera
sections.text:
A location can have a camera paired that it does not always use: a spare, or one kept for another kind of show.
**Set aside** (on the camera's card under *Maintenance*, or System › Cameras › Paired cameras; the
administrator) sets it aside at the location in use. It stays paired, with its settings, and is left out of the
show: the director never chooses it or puts it in a split, “Start All” leaves it out, *Refresh OBS scenes* makes
nothing for it, and it is not checked for readiness, so it never makes the set-up “Not ready”. It is folded into a
short *Not in use here* list on the Cameras page, with **Use here** to bring it back. If it connects anyway it is
let in and shown there as connected, and nothing more. What is set aside (`cameras_set_aside`) is a setting of the
location: each location keeps its own, and switching brings back that location's.

sections.doc: Locations, and moving a set-up to another PC
sections.title: Cameras a location does not use, and removing a camera
sections.text:
**Rename…** (beside it, on the camera's card and in the paired cameras) changes the name a camera is shown by, at
any time, streaming or not: 1 to 80 characters, no two cameras alike whatever their case. Everything else stays: its
slot, its settings (kept by camera, not by name), its pairing, and its place in OBS, which is found by its port. When
OBS is running its source takes the new name, and so do its scenes: `Cam <name>`, the split screens `Split <name> +
<other>` and face blur's own. Only names change: each scene keeps its contents, the programme stays on air (the
director knows a rename from a cut), and a default shot naming one of those scenes, in the settings and in this
location's band profiles, is given the new name. A new name something else in OBS already has is left alone, and
said why. Recordings already on this computer stay in the folder of its old name; new ones go in a folder with the
new name. The audit log has `camera_renamed`, with both names, and `obs_names_refreshed`, with what OBS was given.

sections.doc: Locations, and moving a set-up to another PC
sections.title: Cameras a location does not use, and removing a camera
sections.text:
**Remove camera…** unpairs a camera for good, after a confirmation. The hash its credential is checked against
goes, so the phone can no longer connect with it (one connected is disconnected); its slot is free for another;
its pairing files are deleted; and everything set for it is cleared: what it shows, its solo zoom, its place on the
stage picture, its microphone, telephoto, decoding and colour calibration, the crowd camera when it was that, and
the performers it followed. Its recordings and temperature history stay. It is refused while the camera streams,
records or is on air. A restore point is made first, and the audit log has `camera_removed`. To use the phone
again, pair it again (Add a phone). Only the location in use is changed: another location with the same camera
keeps it.

Locations are kept under `data/locations/`, private like the rest of the data folder. What belongs to the PC rather
than the place never moves with a location: addresses, folders, passwords, what is offered to the network.

sections.doc: Locations, and moving a set-up to another PC
sections.title: Moving a set-up to another PC
sections.text:
Two exports, on System › Locations & backups under "Move or copy this set-up" and as commands
(`export-settings`, `import-settings`, `export-fleet`, `import-fleet`):

- **Settings**: how shots are chosen, what each camera shows, the stage picture, the look-ahead. A plain file with
  nothing secret in it. Addresses, folders, what is offered to the network and every secret stay with the PC.
- **The fleet**: the cameras, the name the manager goes by, and the certificates the cameras expect, with their
  private keys. Always encrypted with a passphrase of twelve characters or more (scrypt, AES-256-GCM); without it
  the file is noise. A PC that brings a fleet in is, to those cameras, the same manager, and they connect to it
  with nothing done to them.

To replace a PC: run `bootstrap.sh` on the new one, bring the fleet in, load the settings, then switch the old
manager off or give it another name. Two managers answering to one name fight over the cameras. A fleet is only
brought to a PC with no cameras of its own and none connected. Passwords, recordings, history and OBS (which
exports its own Scene Collection and Profile) are not carried.

sections.doc: Backing up the manager's data
sections.title: Backing up the manager's data
sections.text:
`scripts/backup-data.sh` makes a dated archive of everything that is the installation's own, and
`scripts/restore-data.sh` puts one back. Neither needs the manager stopped to make a backup; a restore does.

sections.doc: Backing up the manager's data
sections.title: What is saved
sections.text:
One file, `mcvsaid-data-YYYY-MM-DD-HHMMSS.tar.gz`, in `~/.local/share/mcvsaid/backups` (`MCVSAID_BACKUPS` names another
folder), readable by its owner alone. Inside:

- `data/`: the database (`registry.sqlite3`: cameras, pairings, shows, users' activity), the certificate and key, the
  pairing files, the people library with its face data, calibrations, set pictures, locations, names and the small JSON
  files. The database is copied with SQLite's online backup, so the copy is consistent while the manager is running, and
  is checked (`PRAGMA integrity_check`) before it is archived.
- `config/`: `config.json` and `secrets.json` from `~/.config/mcvsaid` (`MCVSAID_CONFIG`).
- `MANIFEST.txt`: when it was made, and what is and is not in it.

**Archives hold password hashes, the model server's key, the certificate's private key and face data.** Keep them as private
as the installation itself.

sections.doc: Backing up the manager's data
sections.title: What is left out
sections.text:
Recordings and other media (`*.mov`, `*.mp4`, `*.mkv`, `*.m4a`, `*.wav`), the camera relay's spool, the downloaded models
(`speech/`, `spotter/`, `*.onnx`, `*.tflite`), the camera app's APK, colour `captures/` pictures, the database's `-wal` and
`-shm` side files (their content is in the copy), and the `*.before-*` and `*.new` files the manager keeps while changing
something. Models and the APK come back by themselves (or from the dashboard) when needed; recordings are copied off by
the offload, not here. Bundled tools (`~/.local/share/mcvsaid/tools`), installed releases and the update source are not
data and are not saved.

sections.doc: Backing up the manager's data
sections.title: How often, and how many
sections.text:
The newest 14 are kept (`--keep N`; `--keep 0` keeps all). Only `mcvsaid-data-*.tar.gz` files made by the script are ever
deleted; `before-restore-*` and `before-move-*` archives and anything else in the folder are left alone.

Nightly at 02:30 (a computer that was off or asleep runs it when it is next on). One command sets that up:

```bash
scripts/backup-data.sh --install-schedule
```

On Linux it installs the systemd user timer `mcvsaid-backup.timer` (and `mcvsaid-backup.service`) and enables it; on a Mac,
the launchd agent `com.mcvsaid.backup`, whose log is `~/Library/Logs/mcvsaid/mcvsaid-backup.log`. The installers do not
do this by themselves: a backup schedule is chosen. Run it from the installed copy
(`~/.local/share/mcvsaid/current/scripts/backup-data.sh`), which is where the schedule points. To stop it:
`systemctl --user disable --now mcvsaid-backup.timer`, or on a Mac
`launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.mcvsaid.backup`.

sections.doc: Backing up the manager's data
sections.title: Restoring
sections.text:
1. Stop the manager: `systemctl --user stop mcvsaid-manager` (Mac: `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.mcvsaid.manager`).
2. `scripts/restore-data.sh ~/.local/share/mcvsaid/backups/mcvsaid-data-2026-11-16-023000.tar.gz`
3. Start it again (`systemctl --user start mcvsaid-manager`; Mac: `launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.mcvsaid.manager.plist`).

The script refuses while the manager is running or any program has the database open; checks that the archive is one of
its own and its database is sound; first saves the current data and settings to
`backups/before-restore-<date>.tar.gz` (restore that one to undo); then replaces the database and the files in the
archive and prints what it did. Files in the data folder that are not in the archive are left as they are.

sections.doc: Backing up the manager's data
sections.title: Copying archives off the machine
sections.text:
A backup on the same disk does not survive the disk. Copy the folder somewhere else, for example:

```bash
rsync -a --chmod=F600,D700 ~/.local/share/mcvsaid/backups/ user@other-machine:mcvsaid-backups/
```

or to an external drive with `cp -p`. Use a destination only you can read, or encrypt first
(`gpg -c <archive>`), because of what the archives hold.

sections.doc: Backing up the manager's data
sections.title: Not covered by tests
sections.text:
The tests run the scripts against temporary folders with a real SQLite file, and check the schedule's files are
installed (with stand-ins for `systemctl` and `launchctl`). The timers themselves, firing at 02:30 and catching up after
sleep, have not been seen running; nor has the Linux `tar` (the tests ran with macOS's).

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Security model
sections.text:
The camera initiates WSS; there is no new camera LAN listener. Android's existing
ADB loopback API remains loopback-only and requires its separate token.

Every camera has a random 256-bit provisioning credential. Linux stores its
SHA-256 digest. The device stores its own credential in private preferences;
Android backup is disabled. The APK contains no production credentials.
Provisioning JSON files contain secrets: transfer privately, never commit them,
and keep their permissions at 0600. Linux's generated data directory uses 0700.
The initial setup command must run as the regular user, not root.

The manager generates an ECDSA TLS certificate with an explicit IP/DNS SAN.
Android verifies the leaf certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint and validity dates,
and retains OkHttp's standard hostname/SAN verification. A mismatched, expired,
or wrong-host certificate must not connect. Compare the pairing fingerprint
through a trusted channel when importing. Pinning allows a locally issued
certificate without installing a system CA. It does not disable hostname checks.
Certificates expire after two years; renew and provision new pins before expiry.
Clock skew can reject commands and certificates. Set devices' clocks correctly;
this check is not a claim that media clocks are synchronized.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Security model
sections.text:
The dashboard defaults to HTTP loopback only, with a random private password,
scrypt password hashing, HttpOnly/SameSite=Strict session cookies, eight-hour
session expiry, mutation CSRF tokens and exact configured origins. Remote
binding is refused without explicitly enabling dashboard TLS. HTTPS needs a
certificate with the matching dashboard hostname/IP and a trusted browser
certificate. Do not expose either listener to the internet. OBS WebSocket remains
loopback and authenticated; this milestone does not change its configuration.

Dashboard requests and agent messages are bounded to 16 KiB; commands have
bounded parameters and deadlines. Login attempts and command submissions are
rate-limited. Camera output telemetry has a bounded WebSocket queue and reconnect
backoff. Audit records contain command names, IDs, outcomes and connection state,
not passwords, provisioning bundles or setting values. No secrets are printed
by initialization or pairing commands. Do not add access-header logging.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Security model
sections.text:
To rotate a camera credential: stop the manager, rerun `pair` for the same slot,
import the new bundle on the disarmed phone, then restart the manager. The stable
camera ID remains unchanged, and the old token no longer authenticates. Avoid
pairing while the manager is running: existing authenticated connections need to
be closed and durable pending requests need reconciliation. Certificate rotation
requires re-pairing every device. To revoke a camera for good (a lost or retired
phone), the administrator uses **Remove camera…** on its card: the stored digest is
deleted, so its credential no longer authenticates, a connected phone is closed
with 1008, and its pairing files are deleted (`camera_removed` in the audit log).
A restore point taken just before keeps the digest, so restoring "settings and
cameras" from it lets that phone in again. To disconnect an agent, use the phone's visible
Disconnect Manager button; media capture continues independently.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Security model
sections.text:
Physical Arm is required after process restart/disarm unless the app has been
made device owner on that phone; then an authenticated `camera.arm` command starts
the capture service idle (no stream, no recording) and `system.reboot` restarts
the phone. Device owner is set once over USB by the operator and can be released
from the phone's screen. The agent never bypasses camera/microphone permissions
and never re-arms by itself on reconnect or after a restart. From 0.7.0 the agent
starts after a phone restart or app update without being opened, and its settings
(pairing credential included) are kept in device-protected storage so this works
before the screen lock is first entered; that storage is encrypted with a key tied
to the phone, not to the screen-lock PIN. Commands from a 0.7.0 manager carry a
relative time-to-live, so the two-minute wall-clock check applies only to older
managers; the certificate validity check still depends on the phone's clock. Physical
Stop is authoritative. An UNKNOWN command outcome means its execution is
uncertain, and requires a status check before retrying with a new request ID.
Completed duplicate IDs replay their saved outcome rather than execute again.
The Android ledger retains approximately 900–1024 recent requests; deduplication
is bounded, not indefinite. Linux keeps command history until manually archived.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Security model
sections.text:
This is a commissioning preview. No independent penetration test has run.
Production hardening still requires long-run testing, log/DB retention,
provisioning UX review, device power-management verification and reconnect tests
on every supported Android release. Rooted devices weaken Android credential
isolation; do not share root access or the provisioning files.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Who can log in
sections.text:
Everyone logs in by name, with their own password, to an account with one role (`camera_manager/users.py`): for
example Avery as an administrator, Eric as an operator, Sam as a setup tech, Cody for Stage Shots.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Who can log in
sections.text:
| Login | Where | Can |
|---|---|---|
| Administrator account | At the manager PC; from the camera network too once allowed, with an authenticator code (see Administering from the camera network) | Everything, including the Users page; on the network, all but what is kept to the PC |
| Operator account | At the PC, or from the camera network when the dashboard is offered there | Run a show: cameras, streams, recording, shots, the charger plugs' switches, the director, sync, temperatures, offload of recordings |
| Setup tech account | At the PC, or a phone at `https://calibrate.mcvsaid.local` (or `https://operate.mcvsaid.local`) on the camera network | Calibrate (Set up › Calibrate): measure lip sync and fit each camera's colour from a phone held up on stage. And the Operate page for setting gimbal positions before the show: aiming, zoom, Stop gimbal, Set home and the Positions (save, update, rename, try, delete), with nothing that puts a camera on air, arms, streams, records or changes the director. Every other page sends them to Calibrate, and every other request is refused (`authorize(..., tech=True)` marks the few that are theirs) |
| Stage Shots account, or the Stage Shots passcode | A phone on the camera network | Choose the shot, switch automatic choosing on or off (the layout is set up at the dashboard, on Stage layout) |
| Teleprompter PIN | A tablet on the camera network | Move the teleprompter's script: section, line, play, speed, follow; at karaoke night, the singer's screen and Next singer (see [Teleprompter and karaoke](TELEPROMPTER_AND_KARAOKE.md)) |

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Who can log in
sections.text:
| Login | Where | Can |
|---|---|---|
| No login: the night's code | A guest's phone on the camera network, at karaoke night | Sign up to sing (a first name and a song from the list) and see their place in the line; nothing else (see [Karaoke night](TELEPROMPTER_AND_KARAOKE.md#karaoke-night-a-line-of-singers-the-words-lit-as-they-are-sung)) |

An operator cannot delete recordings from the phones, update, restart, pair, rename, remove or set aside cameras, send a camera's
stream anywhere but to this manager, change how they find the
manager, change the model server, or change any password, passcode or account. Unless administering from the camera
network is switched on, an administrator's password is refused from there even when it is right (an administrator's
open login on a tablet, from before they were made one, keeps an operator's rights there). An operator account also opens the phone Stage Shots page; a Stage
Shots account opens nothing else.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Who can log in
sections.text:
- **Users** (administrators, `/users`): add someone (name, role, and a password typed or made here and shown once),
  rename them, give them a new password, another role, or remove them. Only each password's hash is kept, with the
  accounts in `secrets.json`. What an account may do is looked up at every request, so a change holds at once for
  whoever is logged in to it: an upgrade opens what the new role opens; a downgrade logs them down, or out where the
  new role does not open that page (an operator made Stage Shots is logged out of the dashboard; their phone page
  goes on); a new password or removal logs the account out everywhere, live pictures included. The last
  administrator cannot be removed or given another role.
- **From before accounts**: an installation that had an administrator password and an operator password keeps both
  working. Each becomes an account with no name yet, opened by its password with the name left empty, as before. The
  administrator is asked for a name at their next login; the operators' shared account is named, or replaced by one
  account per operator, on the Users page. The old `password_hash` and `operator_password_hash` settings are gone
  from the files once that is done (`accounts_made_from_role_passwords` in the audit log).
- System › Logins ("Who else can log in") offers the dashboard to the camera network (`dashboard_remote_enabled`,
  port 8444, after a restart), lists who is logged in, by name, and logs any of them out; the accounts themselves are
  on the Users page.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Who can log in
sections.text:
- **Administering from the camera network** (`camera_manager/twofactor.py`), for a PC that is out of reach once it is
  installed. An administrator logs in on the network dashboard (port 8444, `https://operate.mcvsaid.local` or any
  page of it) with their password and a six-digit code from an authenticator app (the standard time-based codes:
  Google or Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password, Authy and the like). Ticking **Trust this device for 30 days** when
  giving the code means that browser is asked only for the password until then; the trust is a random token in a
  cookie (only its hash is kept), shared by the easy addresses as the login is (see Easy addresses), so a device
  trusted at `operate.mcvsaid.local` is trusted at `remote.` and `calibrate.` too, while the address with its port
  is trusted separately. How it is set up and held:
  - Each administrator sets up a code on the Users page (**Set up a code…**: scan the QR code, made on the manager,
    or type the key, then type the first code). Ten backup codes are shown once, for a lost phone; each opens one
    login. The Users page also makes new backup codes, sets up a new code, removes it, and lists and forgets
    trusted devices. A new password forgets every trusted device of that account. A used code is not taken again.
  - System › Logins › **Let administrators work from the camera network** (`dashboard_remote_admin`) is switched on
    only at the PC, and only once an administrator has a code; it can be switched off from anywhere, which makes
    every administrator on the network an operator at once. An administrator without a code is an operator there,
    and is told to set one up at the PC.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Who can log in
sections.text:
- Administrator rights on the network rest after 30 minutes without an administrator change: the next
    administrator request asks for the password again, in a dialog, and is then sent (`/api/login/confirm`). Running
    the show goes on meanwhile. Changing accounts, the network settings or the fleet asks for the password within
    the last 5 minutes. Wrong codes and passwords count as wrong guesses, slowed as below.
  - **Kept to the PC** (`remote_admin_at_pc_only`, chosen only at the PC): any of users and passwords, the camera
    network settings, updates and AI keys, setting up phones on their cable, and settings and fleet files. Only the
    fleet files are kept there to begin with, as they let another PC stand in for this one. Switching the
    administrator's dashboard off on the network, from the network, is refused: it would shut the page being used.
  - Logins, codes given, trusted devices, backup codes used and every change are in the audit log
    (`administrator_second_step`, `device_trusted`, `authenticator_code_set`, `remote_admin_changed`, ...).
  - Other things on the PC (OBS's own window, the operating system, its updates) are reached with the operating
    system's own remote access, such as macOS Screen Sharing; switching that on is a setting of the PC, not of the
    manager.
- **Easy addresses** (`camera_manager/webnames.py`, `web_names`, on by default): with the dashboard offered on the
  camera network, `https://operate.mcvsaid.local` opens it at the Operate page (operator login) and
  `https://remote.mcvsaid.local` at the Remote page's keys (the same login); there `/` is that page, so the Show page
  is at `/show` (the side bar's Show and the logo go there, and a reload stays on it). With Stage Shots
  offered, `https://stageshots.mcvsaid.local` opens that, and with the teleprompter offered,
  `https://teleprompter.mcvsaid.local` and `https://karaoke.mcvsaid.local` open it (its PIN; the guests' sign-up
  at `/join`), with no port to type. Alongside any of them, `https://calibrate.mcvsaid.local` opens the **calibration
  pages** for a phone or tablet held in front of the cameras, with no login: **Sync flash** (`/sync-flash`, for
  Calibrate sync) and the **Colour card** (`/colour-card`): a 24-patch chart laid out and coloured as the
  ColorChecker the Colour page fits to (`colour.CHART`, from `/colour-chart.json`), an 18% grey and a white for a
  white balance lock, a grey scale in even L* steps for exposure, 75% and 100% colour bars, and black, with the
  patches' names on or off, full screen and the screen kept awake. Logged in there as a setup tech or an operator
  (or an administrator with their authenticator code, once administering from the network is on), the same page drives Calibrate (see [Calibrate from the stage](COLOUR_AND_CALIBRATION.md#calibrate-from-the-stage));
  nothing else of the dashboard opens under that name: the login, the session and `/api/calibrate` only. `calibrate_page: false` leaves it out; `calibrate_page: true` offers it on its own, with
  nothing else offered (which starts the listener on 443 and 80). Alongside them too, `https://recipe.mcvsaid.local`
  opens **the host's recipe page** (see [Cooking](RECIPE_AND_KITCHEN.md#the-hosts-own-recipe-page)), with no login; `recipe_page` false or true as for `calibrate_page`. The same pages are at `/calibrate` on the dashboard,
  and the Sound page's Calibrate sync links to the easy address once it is up. The names go under the manager's own
  name when it has one (`operate.kitchen.local`), are announced beside it, and are in the web certificate. A name
  leads only to an address, so the manager also listens on 443 and passes each request on by the name asked for,
  exactly as if it had come in on 8444, 8443 or 8445 (an operator, or an administrator with their code, or the PIN, as there).
  **One login serves the dashboard's easy addresses**: logged in at `operate.mcvsaid.local` is logged in at
  `remote.` and `calibrate.` (and logged out at all of them by Log out at any). The login is kept in a cookie of its
  own (`cc_names_session`, and `cc_names_trusted` for a trusted device) set for the manager's name and every name
  under it (`Domain=mcvsaid.local`, or the manager's own name), only for a request that came in by one of those names,
  Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Strict. What that changes: the browser also sends it to `stageshots.`,
  `teleprompter.` and `karaoke.` (the same manager, where it opens nothing: they keep their own logins), and to any
  other name under `mcvsaid.local`, so a device on the camera network that announced such a name and was opened in a
  browser that accepted its certificate (clicking through the warning) would be sent it; a host-only cookie is exposed
  to the same device announcing `operate.mcvsaid.local` itself, so it is little more. A tablet that trusts only the
  installation's authority sends it nowhere else. Acting still wants the page's CSRF token and an easy address's own
  Origin (never Stage Shots' or the teleprompter's). The address with its port, and the PC, keep their own login
  (`cc_session`) and take nothing from the shared one; port 80 sends plain `http://` for the
  same names on to `https://`. macOS allows 443 and 80 without the administrator only on every address, so both refuse
  anything not from the camera network and any other name. The addresses with their ports always work too; on Linux,
  where 443 needs the administrator, set `web_names_https_port` (and `web_names_http_port`) to free ports, and the
  names carry that port. iPhones, iPads and Macs find `.local` names; Windows 10 and 11 usually do; Android 12 and
  later should.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Who can log in
sections.text:
- Pages opened in a browser from the network are served with a certificate signed by the installation's own
  authority (`data/web/`). A tablet that installs `https://<manager>:8444/authority.crt` and trusts it stops
  warning, for the dashboard and for Stage Shots, and stays trusting when the certificate is renewed.
- Wrong passwords, passcodes and PINs from the network slow the device that sent them and no other: five are let by,
  then it waits 30 seconds, a minute, two, up to fifteen minutes after each further one, until a right one or an hour
  without any. They are counted together as well, against a short code tried from many addresses in turn: sixty in ten
  minutes, and devices that have not logged in within the last twelve hours wait out the ten minutes; one device
  cannot bring that about, and those already in use are not held up. The PC itself is never made to wait this way.
  A Stage Shots passcode you choose is 6 to 64 characters and a teleprompter PIN 6 to 8 digits; shorter ones set
  before 2026-11 keep working until changed.
- The dashboard's command route sends a camera only what the pages send, by role; the settings the manager sends by
  itself (camera Wi-Fi, battery protection, silence, face blur, voice) are not sent for anyone from a browser.
- Every listener caps a request's body as it arrives, sends `Content-Security-Policy` (with `base-uri 'none'`,
  `form-action 'self'`, `object-src 'none'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and
  `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, and `Cache-Control: no-store` on everything but scripts and stylesheets, which the
  browser keeps and asks about each time (`no-cache`, answered 304 when unchanged) and which are gzipped. A client's
  address is the one that connected: `X-Forwarded-For` is not believed.

sections.doc: Security model
sections.title: Who can log in
sections.text:
- Everything logged at a person's request says who asked, by name: `"who": "Eric (operator) at 10.20.30.44"`;
  logins, refused logins and account changes name the account (`"user": "Eric"`).

sections.doc: The computer: decoding and what was measured
sections.title: The computer: decoding and what was measured
sections.text: Where OBS decodes each camera, and the figures measured on the manager's computers. The short version is in [What the PC needs](../README.md#what-the-pc-needs).

sections.doc: The computer: decoding and what was measured
sections.title: Decoding on the graphics card or the processor
sections.text:
OBS decodes every camera, by default on the graphics card's video decoder, and that is the first limit a set-up meets.
Each camera's OBS source can decode on the processor instead. On System › This computer, **Decoding** sets this per camera,
shows how busy the decoder and the processor are, and has **Measure this computer**: about two minutes of decoding the real
phone footage captured for the tests (`capture-footage`), on each, adding streams until they fall behind. It then
suggests where each camera should go: all start on the processor, and the largest move to the graphics card one at a
time only while the processor would be over half busy (and the decoder stays under 80%). "Use the suggestion"
applies it. Costs are what OBS was seen to use, learned as cameras stream (OBS costs about twice what ffmpeg alone
measures on the processor, and more on the graphics card too); with nothing known about the processor, every camera
stays on the graphics card. A camera streaming on air is changed once it is off air, since a change restarts its OBS source. Nothing is
measured while a camera streams or the programme is recorded.

Measured on the workstation (2026-10-15):

| | 4K camera | 1440p camera | Most at real time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Graphics card (RTX 4090 Laptop), ffmpeg | 12% of its decoder | 7% | 6 at 4K; 8 fell behind |
| Graphics card, as OBS uses it (seen live) | about 20% | about 9% | |
| Processor (i9-14900HX, 32 threads), ffmpeg | 1.3% of the processor | 0.5% | 8 at 4K, at 12% (the most tried) |

sections.doc: The computer: decoding and what was measured
sections.title: Decoding on the graphics card or the processor
sections.text:
Live, in OBS (2026-10-15): **six 4K cameras all decoded on the processor took about 16% of it**, every picture showing
and no frame skipped, recording included. On the graphics card, which the shot-choosing model also keeps busy, three
4K and three 1440p cameras had filled the decoder (85-100%) and pictures went missing. So the processor comes first
here. On a PC with a weaker processor the same rule sends the largest cameras to the graphics card. A processor
working hard runs warmer, which on a laptop over a long show is worth watching on the Processor readiness line.

sections.doc: The computer: decoding and what was measured
sections.title: Measured on the Mac
trail: Decoding on the graphics card or the processor
sections.text:
Six cameras at 4K (25 Mb/s each), a 1080p programme and a 5.5 s look-ahead, on 2026-10-15 and 16:

| | Camera relay off (OBS holds the look-ahead as pictures) | Camera relay on (the relay holds it compressed) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OBS | 11.0 GB (about 1.8 GB per 4K camera) | 2.6 GB |
| Camera relay | | 0.13 GB |
| Shot-choosing model | about 2.4 GB of its own, plus 5.7 GB of weights held by the graphics | the same |
| Manager | 0.08 GB | 0.08 GB |
| **The whole Mac in use**, other apps included | **38.8 GB**, memory pressure normal | **30.7 GB** |

- Processor 42% busy, graphics 65%. Decoding six 4K streams in hardware cost OBS 27% of one core.
- The model answered in about 0.56 s idle, and took about 2.2 s to rate six cameras during the show (about 1 s on the
  Linux workstation's RTX 4090).
- Observed in use, not measured as above: with **five cameras at 4K, the Mac's memory in use approaches 40 GB**, read for
  the whole Mac (a 4K OBS canvas or recording and other open apps likely count towards it).

So: **48 GB for five or six 4K cameras with the model**, with the camera relay on (the default), which saved about
1.4 GB per 4K camera here. 32 GB is enough only for fewer or smaller cameras. On a laptop, run it on power and watch the Processor line
in readiness over a long show.

words.brief: Stay on the busy station; the host when they talk to camera.
words.listen: Listen to the kitchen: chopping, frying, the blender and the host’s voice favour their cameras
words.named: A station you named is looked for in the picture, but cannot be listened for.
words.give: Give it a station so the model knows what it shows.

places.cook_host: At eye height across the counter from the host, a little to one side, so they can look into it.
places.board: Overhead, looking straight down at the board: on a boom arm or a shelf above. The zoom keeps to the hands and the knife.
places.mixer: Above and to one side of the bowl, close enough to see into it, out of the way of splashes.
places.counter: Overhead or at a steep angle over the counter where the food is prepared and the plates are put together.
places.stovetop: Above and in front of the hob at about 45 degrees, to see into the pans; well clear of the heat and the steam.
places.oven: Low, facing the oven door from a little to one side, so the shelf shows when the door is open.
places.grill: Beside the grill, upwind of the smoke, looking down across the grate.
places.kitchen_wide: In a corner, high, with the host and every station in frame.

modes.about: Cameras show singers and instruments; solos are heard and favoured; the crowd camera is shown when the crowd is lively.

modes.name: House of worship
modes.about: Pastor, worship leader and band, choir, readers and the congregation. Music is followed as at a concert; while someone speaks, their camera is favoured.

modes.name: Podcast / talk show
modes.about: Two to six people at microphones, a camera on each and a wide shot. The camera of whoever is talking is favoured, from their own microphone when a mixer gives one; the wide shot when several talk or nobody does.

modes.name: Panel / conference / meetup
modes.about: Moderator, panelists, a speaker at the lectern and questions from the audience, each with a microphone. Whoever is speaking is favoured.

modes.name: Theatre / comedy / open mic
modes.about: Performers on stage, the whole stage and the audience. The audience is shown more often, when it laughs or applauds.

modes.name: Cooking / recipe
modes.about: A recipe from several angles: the host, the cutting board from above, the mixer, the counter, the stovetop, the oven and the grill. The busy station is favoured, also by its sound (chopping, frying, the blender); shots are calmer, and each step of the recipe can be marked for the edit.

modes.name: Creator Studio
modes.about: Build your own: define the framings each camera follows, how close it shoots, and when it cuts.

modes.name: Karaoke night
modes.about: Guests sing one after another: the singer, a duet partner, the host, the stage and the crowd. Guests sign up from their phones; the words are on a screen facing the singer, lit as they are sung (the Karaoke page).
